Overall Phase Separation Overview: FUS (P35637) undergoes self-driven phase separation (class_: PS-self) forming liquid droplets in vitro and in vivo within the nucleus and cytoplasm (PubMed:38971830, 39473462, 39535884, 35787038, 35767424, 37204199, 37782826). It associates with stress granules (colocalizing with G3BP1), nucleoli, paraspeckles, and DNA damage foci (PubMed:38971830, 35662392, 37204199, 38070499, 39168125, 29677514). The condensates typically exhibit liquid-like properties (spherical droplets, fusion, rapid FRAP recovery) but undergo pathological liquid-to-solid transitions to fibrillar or hydrogel states upon aging, stress, or disease mutations (PubMed:38971830, 39473462, 37204199, 35620440, 37782826).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, FUS phase separation regulates mRNA triage in stress granules during cellular stress, facilitates DNA repair via PARP1-mediated compartmentalization at damage sites, and activates transcription by forming nuclear condensates with lncRNAs (e.g., TMPO-AS1) or transcriptional machinery (PubMed:38971830, 37804508). Pathologically, dysregulated liquid-to-solid transitions driven by mutations (P525L, R522G, G156E), aging, or loss of chaperoning cause cytoplasmic amyloid aggregation linked to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTLD) (PubMed:38971830, 39473462, 37204199, 35620440, 37782826). These irreversible aggregates disrupt nucleocytoplasmic transport, impair RNA processing, and induce cytotoxicity (PubMed:36690069, 38070499, 37204199).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal Low-Complexity Domain (LCD/PLD) enabling π-π interactions via tyrosine residues and C-terminal RGG domains facilitating cation-π interactions via arginine residues (PubMed:38971830, 37204199, 35787038, 36758221, 38070499, 38056002, 37179431, 24268778, 29677515). ALS-associated mutations (R522G, P525L, G156E, R244C) disrupt nuclear localization, enhance cytoplasmic condensation, and accelerate liquid-to-solid transitions (PubMed:38971830, 39473462, 37204199, 35620440, 38070499, 37179431, 39920231). Post-translational modifications regulate phase separation: phosphorylation (e.g., at S42/S54/S61) inhibits LLPS by introducing electrostatic repulsion, while arginine methylation (e.g., R234/R242/R244 by PRMT1) reduces phase separation propensity (PubMed:36256816, 36361989, 38056002, 37179431, 39455581).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Extrinsic regulators include: (1) RNA, which nucleates phase separation at low stoichiometries but dissolves condensates at high concentrations (PubMed:38070499, 34357401, 35531473, 29677515); (2) Protein partners like G3BP1 (stress granule recruitment), PARP1 (enriched partitioning via PARylation), and chaperones (Hsp70/Hsp27 inhibit pathological transitions) (PubMed:38971830, 39496836, 35620440, 37204199); (3) Ions, where intermediate salt concentrations (~0.3M) promote LLPS following the Hofmeister series, while CsCl induces irreversible solidification (PubMed:39473462, 39535884, 33597515); (4) Chemicals including JSF1 (enhances LLPS in dark, triggers light-induced fibrillation) and graphene quantum dots (inhibit/reverse phase separation) (PubMed:38971830, 37204199); and (5) Stress conditions (oxidative, osmotic) that trigger condensate formation (PubMed:37204199, 37853127).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TDP-43 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro and in vivo, forming dynamic liquid-like condensates primarily in the nucleus and cytoplasm (PubMed:39817908, 36227471, 36075972, 37431963). It associates with Stress Granules under cellular stress, Cajal bodies, paraspeckles, neuronal RNP transport granules, and anisosomes (PubMed:39817908, 37431963, 35646935, 36930291, 37937963). These condensates typically exhibit liquid properties (spherical droplets, fusion capability, rapid FRAP recovery) but undergo pathological transitions to gel-like or solid states, including amyloid fibrils, under conditions such as prolonged stress, mutations, high protein concentration, or aging (PubMed:36075972, 36227471, 37434215, 30814253).
Functional Summary: Physiological phase separation enables RNA processing (splicing, stability, transport), nuclear body assembly, and stress granule-mediated mRNA sequestration during cellular stress (PubMed:37431963, 35646935, 39817908). Dysregulation due to mutations, PTMs, or prolonged stress drives aberrant liquid-to-solid transitions, forming pathological inclusions in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) (PubMed:36075972, 37434215). These aggregates cause nuclear depletion, loss of RNA processing functions (e.g., STMN2/UNC13A cryptic exon inclusion), disrupted nucleocytoplasmic transport, and cytotoxicity (PubMed:38079474, 37431963, 30853299, 35495061). Co-aggregation with α-synuclein or RNA-binding proteins exacerbates neurodegeneration, while therapeutic strategies targeting phase separation (e.g., monoclonal antibodies, oligonucleotides) mitigate toxicity (PubMed:38052886, 37662377, 37434215, 30826182).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the C-terminal low-complexity domain (LCD; residues 263-414), particularly its conserved helical region (residues 320-343) and hydrophobic residues like W334, which mediate self-assembly via helix-helix interactions and transient hydrophobic contacts (PubMed:37579155). N-terminal domain (NTD)-mediated oligomerization is essential for physiological LLPS (PubMed:37431963, 29438978). Disease-associated mutations (e.g., M337V, Q331K, A315T, G294A, G376V) enhance cytoplasmic phase separation, promote aggregation, and accelerate liquid-to-solid transitions (PubMed:38079474, 37431963, 35646935). Post-translational modifications critically regulate behavior: phosphorylation at S409/S410 promotes pathological aggregation (PubMed:37434215, 30853299); arginine methylation at R293 permits physiological LLPS while reducing aggregation (PubMed:39817908); acetylation at K145/K192 reduces RNA binding and enhances aberrant phase separation (PubMed:36930291, 25556531); and methionine oxidation disrupts LLPS by inducing conformational changes (PubMed:37782781).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TDP-43 co-phase separates with RNA, which promotes physiological LLPS but inhibits it at high concentrations (PubMed:38052886, 29650702, 34380047). Key protein partners include hnRNP A1 (enhanced by PAR polymers), α-synuclein (promoting liquid-to-solid transitions), SARS-CoV-2 N protein, MATR3, FUS, and granulins (GRNs), with redox state modulating GRN interactions (PubMed:30728452, 38052886, 39201466, 31019288, 35490297). Ions and chemicals regulate phase behavior: intermediate salt concentrations promote LLPS following reentrant phase transitions; TMAO enhances LLPS while suppressing aggregation; and PARylation levels modulate stress granule dynamics (PubMed:33597515, 36227471, 30728452). Small molecules like compound A2 suppress phase separation, while JSF1 and graphene quantum dots inhibit pathological transitions (PubMed:37937963, 39901566).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: G3BP1 undergoes RNA-dependent liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) to form stress granules (SGs) in the cytoplasm, with additional localization to the nucleus under energy stress conditions (PubMed:36151083, 40145738). As a core scaffold protein, it primarily self-assembles (PS-self) via its multivalent domains but requires RNA and partner proteins for physiological SG nucleation (PubMed:32302571, 36692217, 36256816). SGs exhibit liquid-like material states with fusion dynamics and rapid component exchange, though aging, disease mutations, or specific stressors can induce pathological liquid-to-solid transitions (PubMed:32302572, 30893049, 36151083). G3BP1 also associates with DMLC granules, neuronal granules, and P-bodies (PubMed:37437058, 37401177, 32302570).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, G3BP1 condensates regulate mRNA storage during stress, coordinate antiviral responses via RIG-I/cGAS activation, and stabilize damaged endolysosomes for repair (PubMed:36151083, 34779554, 37968398). Pathologically, chronic SG persistence or liquid-to-solid transitions drive neurodegeneration (ALS/FTD, Parkinson's) through TDP-43/hnRNP sequestration and α-synuclein aggregation (PubMed:30893049, 39951026, 39621905). In cancer, SGs promote malignancy in Cr(VI)-transformed cells but suppress tumors by sequestering oncogenic mRNAs (e.g., c-Myc) (PubMed:39306064, 35072355). Viral pathogens (e.g., SARS-CoV-2) co-opt or disrupt condensates to evade immune responses, highlighting G3BP1 as a therapeutic target (PubMed:35652658, 34400613).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is driven by three key domains: the N-terminal NTF2-like (NTF2L) dimerization domain essential for oligomerization, the RNA-binding domain (RRM), and arginine-glycine-glycine (RGG) motifs that confer RNA-binding multivalency (PubMed:32302571, 36256816, 39079611). Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) regulate assembly: IDR1 (acidic) suppresses LLPS, while IDR3 (basic) facilitates RNA interactions; their interplay fine-tunes condensation thresholds (PubMed:32302571, 36806943). Post-translational modifications critically modulate behavior—arginine methylation (R447) inhibits LLPS, S149/S232 phosphorylation relieves autoinhibition, and K63-linked ubiquitination disrupts condensation (PubMed:36256816, 32302572, 36692217). Disease mutations (e.g., S38F) impair dimerization or RNA binding, promoting aberrant solidification (PubMed:32302570, 36806943).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RNA binding is essential, with G-quadruplex structures, dsRNA, and polyA sequences acting as primary cofactors (PubMed:36350614, 36150385, 29262335). Protein partners include Caprin-1 (CTD enhances LLPS; GIM suppresses it), TDRD3 (restores methylation-inhibited phase separation), and UBAP2L (co-nucleates SGs) (PubMed:36279435, 39097054, 32302570). Negative regulators include SARS-CoV-2 N protein (blocks NTF2L domain), FLNA (sequesters G3BP1), and 14-3-3γ (disrupts condensates) (PubMed:34400613, 36806943, 36931259). Small molecules modulate behavior: perillaldehyde (PAE) promotes protective SG assembly, proline suppresses condensation via repulsive interactions, and arginine-rich dipeptides (R-DPRs) drive pathological transitions (PubMed:39951026, 39642205, 39621905). Ions and nucleic acid nanostructures further tune material properties (PubMed:39704478).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Tau (MAPT) undergoes both self-driven and partner-induced liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), classified as PS-self or PS-other depending on context (PubMed:36894559, 37673952, 31971365, 31481790, 28819146). It forms condensates primarily in the cytoplasm and nucleus (PubMed:35298090, 35405154, 31481790, 39558004), associating with stress granules, nuclear speckles, and the nuclear pore complex (PubMed:35298090, 36373666, 35405154, 33848474). Initial condensates exhibit liquid-like properties but undergo frequent liquid-to-solid/gel transitions, particularly when aged or under pathological conditions (PubMed:35298090, 37673952, 36373666, 38545836, 39510192).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, Tau LLPS enables microtubule nucleation, mRNA regulation in stress granules, and chromatin organization (PubMed:31481790, 28877466, 38429335, 33017094). Pathologically, condensates serve as nucleation sites for amyloid fibrils, with liquid-to-solid transitions generating seeding-competent species that propagate neurofibrillary tangles in Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia (PubMed:35298090, 39510192, 32499559). These transitions disrupt nucleocytoplasmic transport, induce synaptic loss, and cause mitochondrial dysfunction (PubMed:35298090, 39558004, 32087196). Mutations (e.g., P301L) and PTMs (e.g., hyperphosphorylation) exacerbate toxicity by enhancing condensate stability and aggregation propensity (PubMed:35405154, 32499559).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is driven by Tau's microtubule-binding domain (MTBR; residues 244-441) and proline-rich region (PRD; residues 151-244), which facilitate electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions (PubMed:35298090, 36258016, 36373666, 32997736). Disease mutations like P301L, P301S, ΔK280, and K274Q enhance LLPS propensity and accelerate pathological transitions (PubMed:36258016, 31971365, 35405154, 32499559, 39421885). Phosphorylation exerts bidirectional regulation: sites like S262/S356/S324 promote LLPS, while hyperphosphorylation or AT8 epitope formation disrupts it (PubMed:35298090, 28819146, 40074668). Acetylation at K274 enhances phase separation, whereas N-terminal acetylation inhibits it (PubMed:29734651, 31036717).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Tau co-phase separates with RNA, heparin, and polyanions via complex coacervation (PubMed:35298090, 39510192, 37293933, 31971365, 28683104). Molecular crowders (PEG/dextran) induce LLPS, while ions modulate behavior: Zn²⁺/Al³⁺ promote condensation, whereas Ca²⁺ collaborates with RNA G-quadruplexes to trigger rapid liquid-to-solid transitions (PubMed:35405154, 32229582). Proteins including TRIAD3A, EB1, G3BP1, and HP1α recruit Tau into condensates, with EB1 delaying pathological transitions (PubMed:39009640, 38445984, 38429335). Small molecules exhibit concentration-dependent effects: suramin forms benign droplets, methylene blue/gallic acid induce gelation, and shikonin inhibits LLPS (PubMed:36894559, 37673952, 38545836, 35120943).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: hnRNPA1 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) mediated by its low-complexity domain (LCD), forming dynamic condensates primarily in the nucleus and cytoplasm (PubMed:39535884, 36256816, 37130439). It associates with stress granules under cellular stress and nuclear speckles during RNA processing, exhibiting liquid-like material states that can pathologically transition to hydrogel or solid fibrillar aggregates (PubMed:26412307, 31043593). These transitions are concentration-dependent and influenced by environmental factors (PubMed:38999934, 33577679).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, hnRNPA1 phase separation organizes RNA processing at nuclear speckles, maintains telomere integrity via TERRA sequestration, and enables stress granule assembly for mRNA sequestration during cellular stress (PubMed:39313323, 37130439). Pathologically, dysregulated liquid-to-solid transitions form cytotoxic amyloid aggregates linked to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), inclusion body myopathy, and multisystem proteinopathy, driven by mutations (e.g., D262V, P288A) or prolonged stress (PubMed:23455423, 31043593, 34291734). These transitions are exacerbated by viral proteins (e.g., SARS-CoV-2 N) and dipeptide repeats (GR/PR), potentiating neurodegeneration (PubMed:35384603, 27768896).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by aromatic residue patterning (e.g., Tyr, Phe, Trp) within the LCD (residues 186-320) and RGG-rich domain, where tyrosine spacing balances LLPS promotion against aggregation (PubMed:32029630, 39535884, 31043593). Key regulators include: 1) Post-translational modifications—phosphorylation at C-terminal serines (S361-S368) reduces condensation propensity, while arginine methylation (R196/R206/R218) suppresses LLPS (PubMed:35864335, 36256816); 2) Disease mutations (e.g., D262V, P288A) enhance phase separation and accelerate pathological liquid-to-solid transitions (PubMed:37130439, 34291734); 3) Engineered mutations altering net charge or aromatic content directly modify saturation concentrations and condensate material properties (PubMed:39356108, 32029630).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Extrinsic regulators include: 1) Binding partners—RNA promotes LLPS but suppresses it at high ratios, FUS engages in heterotypic co-phase separation via electrostatic interactions, TDP-43 co-condenses in a PAR-dependent manner, and SARS-CoV-2 N protein accelerates pathological solidification (PubMed:29650702, 37684240, 30728452, 35384603); 2) Ions/Chemicals—phase separation follows the Hofmeister series, strengthened at intermediate NaCl concentrations but inhibited at >200 mM, while crowding agents (PEG) and reduced pH enhance condensation (PubMed:33577679, 38999934); 3) PAR polymers dramatically enhance LLPS and enable co-condensation with TDP-43 via the PAR-binding motif (PBM) (PubMed:30728452).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NPM1 undergoes both self-driven (PS-self) and partner-dependent (PS-other) phase separation, primarily localizing to the nucleolar granular component (PubMed:38987300, 35325178, 37705750, 37683610). It forms dynamic liquid-like condensates in physiological conditions (PubMed:35325178, 36543022, 37683610) but exhibits material state plasticity, transitioning toward gel/solid states under crowding (PubMed:36463407) or with specific partners (PubMed:39528457). These condensates display rapid fusion and FRAP recovery in their liquid state but develop viscoelastic properties when complexed with rRNA or client proteins (PubMed:37683610, 37705750).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, NPM1 phase separation scaffolds the nucleolar granular component, enabling ribosomal subunit assembly via rRNA processing factor concentration and vectorial particle maturation (PubMed:38987300, 37683610, 37705750). It maintains nucleolar integrity by buffering concentration noise and restricting heterochromatin invasion (PubMed:31974256, 39738032). Pathologically, dysregulation causes: 1) Ribosomopathies when liquidity is impaired by mutations (DDX24E271K) or methylation defects (PubMed:37705750, 39169036); 2) Neurodegeneration via poly(PR)-induced condensate dissolution and rRNA sequestration in ALS/FTD (PubMed:30981631); 3) Cancer through AML mutations disrupting nucleolar localization and stress response pathways like p53/ARF regulation (PubMed:36743470, 36220893); 4) Viral exploitation where adenovirus hijacks LLPS for core assembly (PubMed:39162498).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically governed by: 1) N-terminal oligomerization domain enabling pentamer assembly, providing multivalency (PubMed:36743470); 2) Central intrinsically disordered region (IDR) featuring acidic tracts (A1/A2/A3) for heterotypic interactions and basic tracts (B1/B2) for RNA binding (PubMed:37540843, 30498217); 3) Phosphorylation at S125 (IDR) reducing oligomer stability to increase droplet fluidity, while mitotic hyperphosphorylation (T199/T219/T234/T237) inhibits RNA binding and suppresses LLPS (PubMed:37540843, 35513709, 35864335); 4) Mutations like AML-associated C-terminal truncations disrupting nucleolar partitioning, and A-tract mutations impairing partner recruitment (PubMed:36743470, 30981631).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Key extrinsic modulators include: 1) Protein partners: Ribosomal proteins (RPL5, RPL7/uL30) and R-motif carriers (SURF6, GNL2) drive heterotypic LLPS via electrostatic complementarity (PubMed:36543022, 30981631, 29483575); DDX24 stabilizes liquid state, while its E271K mutant reduces partitioning (PubMed:37705750); p14ARF induces gel-like transitions via hydrophobic crosslinking (PubMed:39528457); Viral protein VII triggers condensate assembly in adenovirus infection (PubMed:39162498). 2) RNA: rRNA scaffolds condensates and modulates material properties through entanglement (PubMed:37683610, 36463407). 3) Chemical regulators: PEG crowding agents promote homotypic LLPS and liquid-to-gel transitions (PubMed:36463407); Poly(PR) dipeptides dissolve native condensates at high concentrations (PubMed:30981631). 4) Ions: Physiological salt concentrations maintain extended conformations favoring heterotypic LLPS (PubMed:29483575).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SQSTM1 undergoes phase separation requiring binding partners such as ubiquitin chains to form liquid-like condensates (PubMed:29507397, 31857589, 33473217). It localizes primarily to the cytoplasm and nucleus (PubMed:34385323, 39418304, 37802024), associating with membrane-less organelles including p62 bodies, stress granules, damaged lysosomes, mitochondrial clusters, and nuclear condensates (PubMed:37194327, 37802024, 37683611, 34385323). These condensates typically exhibit liquid properties but undergo pathological transitions to gel-like or solid states under conditions like KEAP1 retention, HSP27 depletion, or prolonged stress (PubMed:37306101, 36701233, 37837191).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, phase separation enables selective autophagy by sequestering ubiquitinated cargo (damaged lysosomes, mitochondria) for degradation and facilitates stress granule clearance (PubMed:37194327, 33473217, 29457785). Nuclear condensates serve as proteolytic hubs, stabilizing PML bodies by degrading RNF4 (PubMed:34385323, 39418304). Pathologically, dysregulation contributes to neurodegeneration: ALS/FTD mutations impair lysophagy condensates; Alzheimer's involves autophagy-disrupting accumulations; Huntington's features accelerated PolyQ aggregate coarsening (PubMed:36701233, 37774095, 37837191). In cancer, persistent condensates drive hepatocellular carcinoma via Mallory-Denk bodies and confer chemoresistance through NRF2 hyperactivation (PubMed:37192622, 38994016). Myotoxicity arises from synergistic defects with TIA1 mutations in stress granule clearance (PubMed:29457785).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the PB1 domain (mediating oligomerization) and UBA domain (binding ubiquitin chains), with deletions (ΔPB1/ΔUBA) abolishing condensation (PubMed:37194327, 37847732, 37837191). Key regulatory post-translational modifications include: phosphorylation at Ser403/Ser407 enhancing ubiquitin binding and phase separation (PubMed:37306101, 29343546); acetylation at Lys420/Lys435 disrupting UBA dimerization to promote condensation (PubMed:31857589); asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA) at Arg183/Arg217 by PRMT6 boosting oligomerization (PubMed:38994016); and cysteine oxidation under mitochondrial stress (PubMed:33822768). Disease-associated mutations (e.g., ALS-associated point mutations (unspecified)) impair phase separation (PubMed:37194327, 29343546).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Essential co-scaffolds include polyubiquitin chains (PubMed:29507397, 37113335) and partner proteins like NBR1 (modulating liquidity), KEAP1 (altering material states), and HSP27 (maintaining condensate fluidity) (PubMed:37847732, 37306101, 37194327). Recruitment of LC3B via LIR domains enables autophagosome engagement (PubMed:37802024), while MOAP-1 disassembles condensates by disrupting oligomerization (PubMed:33393215). Phase separation is induced by lysosomotropic agents (chloroquine), tyrosine kinase inhibitors (gefitinib), and ferroptosis inducers (RSL3) (PubMed:37847732, 38994016). Cellular stressors (nutrient deprivation, oxidative/proteotoxic stress) also promote condensation (PubMed:31857589, 34385323).

MLO Types: Inclusion body; P-body; Postsynaptic density; Stress granule; Synapsin condensate; α-synuclein condensates
Overall Phase Separation Overview: Alpha-synuclein (αS) undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) forming liquid-like condensates in the cytoplasm and nucleus that transition to solid amyloid aggregates over time (PubMed:39384788, 35276458, 37238596, 33386842). It associates with multiple membrane-less organelles including stress granules, P-bodies, Lewy body-like inclusions, and synapsin condensates (PubMed:35688132, 38052886, 39384788, 33774037). Initial liquid droplets exhibit fusion and rapid FRAP recovery but undergo pathological liquid-to-solid transitions facilitated by aging, concentration, or mutations, forming hydrogels or fibrillar states (PubMed:35276458, 37238596, 37585526, 36802433).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, αS condensates regulate synaptic vesicle clustering and mRNA metabolism via P-bodies, linking membrane trafficking to RNA turnover (PubMed:33386842, 35688132). Pathologically, liquid-to-solid transitions drive Lewy body formation in Parkinson's disease, with mutations (A30P/E46K/A53T) and ionic dysregulation (Ca²⁺/Mn²⁺) accelerating amyloid aggregation and neurodegeneration (PubMed:39384788, 35276458, 34871547). Co-aggregation with TDP-43 in stress granules underlies comorbidities in FTLD and MSA, while disrupted P-body function stabilizes disease-relevant mRNAs (PubMed:38052886, 35688132). Pharmacological stabilization of liquid droplets (e.g., by claramine or β-synuclein) reduces toxicity, highlighting therapeutic strategies targeting phase transitions (PubMed:38714700, 39384788).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by αS's domain architecture: the N-terminal domain (residues 1-60) mediates electrostatic interactions and membrane binding, the hydrophobic NAC domain (61-95) enables aggregation, and the acidic C-terminus (96-140) facilitates client-scaffold binding (PubMed:35688132, 36459561, 38951707). Mutations profoundly alter behavior—E46K promotes condensation; A30P reduces droplet formation; A53T decreases fluidity and accelerates aggregation; H50Q enhances aggregation; while A53E inhibits solidification (PubMed:39384788, 37238596). Phosphorylation at S129 marks pathological aggregates but doesn't drive transitions (PubMed:37585526, 34165838).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Ions and lipids critically modulate phase separation: Ca²⁺ promotes droplet formation and accelerates aggregation; Mn²⁺ induces direct solid condensates; RNA G-quadruplexes scaffold aggregation-prone complexes (PubMed:35276458, 34871547, 39426376). Protein partners include β-synuclein (enhances liquidity and delays solidification), TDP-43 (enables αS partitioning as a Pickering agent that nucleates heterotypic amyloids), synapsin 1 (recruits αS into synaptic vesicle clusters), VAMP2 (orchestrates LLPS via electrostatic interactions), and SERF (promotes co-phase separation and fibrillation) (PubMed:39384788, 38052886, 33774037, 38951707, 38272228). Chemicals like claramine stabilize liquid states, while LL-III inhibits fibril maturation (PubMed:38714700, 34165838).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: BRD4 undergoes phase separation primarily through co-condensation with partners (class: PS-other) but exhibits self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) in specific contexts (PubMed:37924814, 37156794). It localizes to the nucleus and associates with membrane-less organelles including transcriptional condensates, super-enhancers, and PML/RARα microspeckles (PubMed:39136995, 35646539, 37924814). BRD4 condensates typically exhibit liquid-like properties (PubMed:39136995, 35646539, 37924814).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, BRD4 condensates organize transcriptional machinery at super-enhancers, enabling DNA damage protection, mRNA export, and chromatin looping (PubMed:38874522, 37924814, 39136995). Pathologically, dysregulated phase separation drives: leukemia via PML/RARα-BRD4 condensates activating oncogenes (MYC, BCL2) (PubMed:39136995); atherosclerosis through ox-LDL-induced BRD4-MED1 condensates promoting inflammatory genes (IL-1β, IL-8) (PubMed:35646539); impaired DNA repair via gel-like BRD4-KU80 condensates blocking NHEJ in MiDAC deficiency (PubMed:38423014); and cancer progression through aberrant condensates in NUT carcinoma, myxoid liposarcoma, and squamous cell carcinoma (PubMed:37488172, 34357401, 37924814). Condensate disruption (e.g., by JQ1 or IDR deletion) suppresses oncogenesis and inflammation (PubMed:39136995, 35646539).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by BRD4's intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), particularly the C-terminal IDR (residues 674-1351) and N-terminal low-complexity domain (LCD) of the long isoform (PubMed:37924814, 38874522, 31065677). Bromodomains (BD1/BD2) enable multivalent acetyl-lysine interactions essential for condensation (PubMed:38423014, 31543265). Key regulatory features include: splicing-dependent mechanisms where the short isoform (BRD4S) drives condensation via its BID domain (PubMed:32203489); phosphorylation that diminishes phase separation (PubMed:32203489); and reentrant phase behavior at extreme salt concentrations mediated by electrostatic forces (PubMed:33597515). Disease-associated mutations (e.g., N140A/BD1, N433A/BD2) disrupt phase separation (PubMed:38423014).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: BRD4 co-phase separates with multiple partners including PML/RARα, MED1, KU80, NUP153, YTHDC1, and FUS-CHOP (PubMed:39136995, 35646539, 38423014, 37924814, 34375583, 34357401). External modulators include: ox-LDL and crowding agents (PEG) that enhance condensation (PubMed:35646539); curcumin and bromodomain inhibitors (JQ1) that dissolve condensates (PubMed:35646539, 39136995); RNA which exhibits concentration-dependent modulation (low concentrations promote, high concentrations dissolve) (PubMed:33333019); and light-activatable systems (e.g., dCas9-CRY2Clust) enabling synthetic condensate formation (PubMed:37000871). Ions regulate phase separation through electrostatic interactions, showing reentrant behavior at low/high salt concentrations (PubMed:33597515).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: HP1α undergoes self-driven phase separation (PS-self), forming liquid-like condensates primarily in the nucleus, with frequent localization to heterochromatin and stress granules under oxidative stress (PubMed:35447032, PubMed:37398008, PubMed:36943889). Autonomous phase separation occurs when phosphorylated, but DNA or RNA scaffolds are often required (PubMed:35725842, PubMed:38048471, PubMed:33514913). Typical material states are liquid, but pathological liquid-to-solid transitions occur with prolonged incubation or disease-associated mutations (PubMed:37398008, PubMed:38664966).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, HP1α LLPS enables heterochromatin compaction, gene silencing, and stress granule assembly during oxidative stress (PubMed:35447032, PubMed:37398008, PubMed:31543422). Pathologically, liquid-to-solid transitions driven by mutations (e.g., ALS-linked variants) or RNA dysregulation contribute to neurodegenerative diseases and genomic instability (PubMed:37398008). Disrupted phase separation impairs chromatin organization, linking to diseases like Alzheimer's (PubMed:38429335).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the disordered N-terminal extension (NTE) and hinge region (HR), where phosphorylation of NTE serines (S11-S14) by CK2 enhances LLPS propensity (PubMed:35447032, PubMed:37398008, PubMed:40138713). The chromoshadow domain (CSD) enable H3K9me3 binding and dimerization, while the C-terminal extension (CTE) inhibits LLPS via auto-inhibition (PubMed:33661100, PubMed:28636604). Mutations in key regions (e.g., K91Q in HR, K42Q in CD) disrupt phase separation(PubMed:38048471, PubMed:40138713).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: DNA and RNA (e.g., L1 RNA, MSR RNA) are essential scaffolds that lower the critical concentration for LLPS, with longer DNA increasing condensate viscosity (PubMed:33514913, PubMed:38048471, PubMed:33661100). Protein partners include 53BP1 (mutual co-phase separation at heterochromatin), Tau (co-condensation under low salt), and IRTKS (SUMOylation-enhanced LLPS) (PubMed:35042897, PubMed:38429335, PubMed:39192031). Ions modulate LLPS following the Hofmeister series, with intermediate salt concentrations promoting droplet formation (PubMed:37398008, PubMed:36537242). Chemicals like 1,6-hexanediol dissolve condensates, while ligands (e.g., Sgo1 peptide) enhance phase separation (PubMed:36537242).

Protein Name: Cytotoxic granule associated RNA binding protein TIA1
Overall Phase Separation Overview: TIA1 undergoes self-driven phase separation primarily in the cytoplasm, though nuclear localization is also observed, and is a core structural component of stress granules across diverse cellular stressors including osmotic stress, ER stress, heat shock, and oxidative stress (PubMed:38668381, 37437058, 35902691, 37853127, 37401177, 11121440, 38714852). Its condensates typically exhibit liquid-like properties with dynamic exchange, but undergo pathological liquid-to-solid transitions to fibrillar states accelerated by ALS-associated mutations (e.g., P362L, A381T) (PubMed:34310938, 28817800, 37401177). TIA1 also associates with specialized condensates like DMLC granules during LINE-1 RNA processing (PubMed:37437058).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, TIA1 condensates mediate mRNA triage during stress, enabling translational regulation, LINE-1 RNA processing in DMLC granules, and IRE1α-XBP1 pathway enhancement via stress granule coalescence (PubMed:11121440, 37437058, 38714852). Pathologically, mutation-induced persistent stress granules accumulate ubiquitinated proteins, misfolded aggregates (e.g., TDP-43), and undergo irreversible liquid-to-solid transitions, driving cytotoxicity in ALS, FTD, and inclusion body myopathy (PubMed:28817800, 34310938, 29457785). These aberrant phase transitions disrupt proteostasis and nucleocytoplasmic shuttling, directly linking TIA1 dysregulation to neurodegenerative disease progression (PubMed:36373666, 34310938).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by TIA1's prion-like domain (PrLD) and RNA recognition motifs (RRMs), with RRM2 histidines (H94/H96) enabling Zn²⁺-mediated multimerization that maintains dynamic liquid states while suppressing fibrillization (PubMed:35911965, 38193795). The low-complexity domain (LCD) facilitates concentration-dependent assembly, while disease mutations (P362L, A381T, E384K, N357S) enhance phase separation propensity and accelerate liquid-to-solid transitions by strengthening intermolecular interactions (PubMed:28817800, 34310938, 29457785). Arginine methylation by PRMT1 reduces phase separation capacity, whereas tandem nucleic acid binding sites (≥2 UC/TC motifs) sequence-specifically trigger condensation and amyloid formation (PubMed:37401177, 33621982).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RNA serves as an essential scaffold, with poly(A)⁺ mRNA and specific sequences (e.g., p53 3' UTR) driving phase separation (PubMed:11121440, 33621982). Zn²⁺ enhances liquid droplet formation and inhibits pathological aggregation, while FUS RGG domains cooperatively promote nucleic acid-induced LLPS (PubMed:35911965). Protein partners include G3BP1, which lowers saturation concentrations cooperatively; TDP-43, which co-aggregates in condensates; and SQSTM1/p62, which associates with persistent granules (PubMed:32302571, 28817800, 29457785). Osmotic strength bidirectionally regulates condensation (hyperosmotic promotion, hypoosmotic inhibition), and chemicals like GR/PR dipeptides or G4-ligands (pyridostatin/RHPS4) induce stress granule assembly (PubMed:37853127, 27768896, 35902691).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: YAP undergoes both self-driven and partner-dependent phase separation (PubMed:36989141, 31792379, 33606996). It forms liquid-like condensates primarily in the nucleus and cytoplasm (PubMed:36989141, 36908026, 31792379, 37494632), associating with transcriptional condensates, stress-induced biomolecular condensates, and nuclear puncta (PubMed:36908026, 36732631, 38784009, 39865973). These condensates exhibit rapid dynamics with fusion and FRAP recovery but can transition to less dynamic/viscous states upon TEAD binding (PubMed:36908026).
Functional Summary: Phase separation of YAP into nuclear condensates is essential for efficient somatic cell reprogramming within dynamically responsive hydrogels(PubMed:36989141), while YAP also drives oncogenesis in hepatoblastoma and ependymoma (PubMed:36908026, 36732631) and contributes to anti-PD-1 therapy resistance via CD155 expression(PubMed:33606996). Pathologically, irreversible transitions promote cytotoxicity in endothelial cells during HLA-II antibody response (PubMed:39865973) and tumor progression via aberrant transcriptional activation (PubMed:33850322, 38784009). In development, condensates determine stem cell lineage specification by facilitating YAP phosphorylation (PubMed:36640330) and modulate osteogenesis in hydrogel microenvironments (PubMed:37494632).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by YAP's coiled-coil domain and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), particularly the C-terminal IDR (PubMed:33606996, 36989141, 36908026). The coiled-coil domain enables oligomerization essential for condensation (PubMed:36732631), while phosphorylation at Ser127 inhibits phase separation (PubMed:36908026). Disease-associated mutations enhance condensation: YAP5SA (dephosphorylation mimic) promotes nuclear foci formation (PubMed:36908026), and hydrophobic residue mutations (e.g., L308E/L311E/L318E/L325E) in the coiled-coil domain disrupt phase separation (PubMed:33606996). Motifs in fusion partners (e.g., MAMLD1) also drive phase separation via oligomerization (PubMed:36732631).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: YAP co-phase separates with TEAD transcription factors (TEAD1/TEAD3/TEAD4), which stabilize condensates and alter material properties to a viscous state (PubMed:36908026, 31792379, 38784009). Key partners include TAZ (PubMed:31792379, 37494632), BRD4, MED1, and EP300 in transcriptional hubs (PubMed:36732631, 33606996), and SRC-1 in oncogenic condensates (PubMed:33850322). Phase separation is induced by hyperosmotic stress (PubMed:31792379), low elastic modulus hydrogels (PubMed:37494632), and HLA-II antibody ligation (PubMed:39865973). Inhibitors include FUS (PubMed:38172614), verteporfin (disrupts YAP-TEAD) (PubMed:36989141, 38784009), and 1,6-hexanediol (dissolves liquid condensates) (PubMed:36989141, 36732631, 39865973).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: EWSR1 undergoes both self-driven and partner-dependent phase separation (PubMed:35787038, 34304571, 26286827, 29650702; PubMed:35033560, 36444977, 37243594, 39112465). It localizes to the nucleus and cytoplasm, associating with membrane-less organelles including engineered synthetic organelles on microtubules, DNA damage foci, and centromeres (PubMed:35033560, 26286827, 37243594). EWSR1 forms dynamic liquid-like condensates that can transition to solid or hydrogel states, particularly under prolonged incubation or reduced O-GlcNAcylation (PubMed:36444977, 34304571, 24267890, 29930090).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, EWSR1 phase separation maintains centromeric chromatin integrity via RNA-mediated CENP-A retention, ensuring chromosome stability (PubMed:37243594), organizes PAR-dependent DNA repair compartments (PubMed:26286827), and forms transcriptional hubs that activate gene expression (PubMed:29930090). Pathologically, the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion drives Ewing sarcoma oncogenesis through aberrant transcriptional condensates (PubMed:29930090, 24267890). Reduced O-GlcNAcylation promotes toxic liquid-to-solid transitions linked to aggregation (PubMed:34304571), while disrupted RNA buffering or partner interactions (e.g., with FUS) exacerbates amyotrophic lateral sclerosis pathology (PubMed:30937520).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is driven by intrinsically disordered regions, including the N-terminal low-complexity domain (LCD; residues 47-266) and prion-like domain (PLD) (PubMed:36444977, 26286827, 29650702). The SYGQ2 motif within the PLD and RNA-recognition motif (RRM) are essential for condensate formation and function, with deletions (ΔCABD/ΔRRM) abolishing phase separation (PubMed:37243594). O-GlcNAcylation of the LCD reduces phase separation propensity and maintains fluidity, preventing pathological liquid-to-solid transitions (PubMed:34304571). The EWSR1-FLI1 fusion oncoprotein leverages the PLD for aberrant transcriptional hub formation (PubMed:31171724, 29930090).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: EWSR1 co-phase separates with partners including FUS in synthetic organelles and DNA damage foci, TAF15 in heterotypic condensates, and CENP-A at centromeres (PubMed:35033560, 26286827, 37243594). RNA critically modulates behavior: centromeric RNA stabilizes condensates, while high total RNA concentrations suppress phase separation (PubMed:37243594, 29650702). Poly(ADP-ribose) (PAR) nucleates DNA damage-induced condensates (PubMed:26286827), and maltose-binding protein (MBP) dissolves nuclear condensates upon recruitment (PubMed:39112465). RNA Polymerase II C-terminal domain partitions into condensates under ATP depletion (PubMed:32929202).

Protein Name: Mediator of RNA polymerase II transcription subunit 1
Gene Names: MED1 ARC205 CRSP1 CRSP200 DRIP205 DRIP230 PBP PPARBP PPARGBP RB18A
MLO Types: Mediator condensate; Nuclear speckle; Transcriptional condensate
Overall Phase Separation Overview: MED1 undergoes partner-driven phase separation, primarily forming transcriptional condensates in the nucleus (PubMed:35646539, 36603581, 37973889). It associates with membrane-less organelles including super-enhancer condensates, Nuclear speckle, Mediator condensates, and stress granules (PubMed:29930091, 31563432, 33606996). MED1 typically forms liquid-like droplets with rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), exhibiting spherical morphology and fusion capabilities (PubMed:31391587, 36603581, 37973889). While pathological state transitions are not commonly observed for MED1 alone, its condensates can undergo material property changes when complexed with partners like polyQ-expanded transcription factors (PubMed:32386547).
Functional Summary: MED1 condensates serve as organizational hubs for transcription by selectively partitioning positive regulators (RNA Pol II, CTR9, SPT6) while excluding repressors like NELF, thereby enhancing transcriptional efficiency of super-enhancer-driven genes(PubMed:36603581, 39300145). They facilitate chromatin looping, RNA polymerase II elongation, and hormone-responsive gene activation (e.g., AR-targeted KLK2/KLK3) (PubMed:36229685, 36755093). Pathologically, disrupted MED1 condensation contributes to atherogenesis (via ox-LDL), cancer (via aberrant MYC activation), and developmental disorders like synpolydactyly (via TF unblending) (PubMed:35646539, 32386547). Inhibition of MED1 phase separation reduces inflammatory gene expression and tumor growth (PubMed:35646539).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: MED1 phase separation is intrinsically regulated by its large intrinsically disordered region (IDR, residues 948-1574), particularly through alternating blocks of charged residues (|NCPR| ≥ 0.5) and serine/lysine-rich low-complexity domains (PubMed:36603581, 37973889). The IDR's electrostatic properties drive multivalent interactions, with charge-pattern mutations (e.g., EDtoA, RHKtoA) abolishing phase separation (PubMed:36603581). Methylation at Cys83 within the ZnF1 domain disrupts phase separation by inhibiting ubiquitin binding (PubMed:37379216). Alanine repeat expansions in partner proteins cause unblending from MED1 condensates (PubMed:32386547).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: MED1 co-phase separates with diverse partners including BRD4, RNA Pol II, β-catenin, TAZ, TEAD4, and nuclear receptors (AR, ER, GR) to form transcriptional hubs (PubMed:30449618, 31563432, 33606996, 36229685). Nucleic acids exhibit concentration-dependent modulation: low RNA/DNA concentrations promote MED1 condensation via electrostatic interactions, while high concentrations dissolve condensates (PubMed:33333019). Chemical modulators include curcumin (inhibitor via P300 suppression), SIRT1 agonists (enhancers), and phospholipids like PIP₂ (induces irregular morphology via Mg²⁺-bridging) (PubMed:35646539, 35879450, 37973889). Post-translational modifications in partners regulate incorporation; for example, phosphorylated p53 incorporates more efficiently into MED1 droplets (PubMed:36634798).

MLO Types: DNA damage foci; Nucleolus; Transcriptional condensate
Overall Phase Separation Overview: TAF15 undergoes self-driven phase separation (class_ 'PS-self'), forming liquid-like condensates primarily in the nucleus (PubMed:35662392, 26286827, 29930090, 37131610) and cytoplasm (PubMed:29650702, 30937520). It associates with membrane-less organelles including nucleolar CITIs, DNA damage foci, stress granules, and transcriptional hubs (PubMed:35662392, 26286827, 29930090). Material states are typically liquid (PubMed:35662392, 36444977, 37094074), though hydrogel formation occurs in vitro via prion-like domain polymerization (PubMed:24267890).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, TAF15 condensates facilitate DNA repair at damage foci, mediate chromatin tethering to nucleoli, and activate transcription via RNA Pol II recruitment (PubMed:26286827, 35662392, 29930090). Pathologically, dysregulated phase separation drives oncogenesis in fusion proteins (e.g., EWS::FLI1), increasing gene fusion frequency and aberrant transcription in leukemia (PubMed:29930090, 35662392, 24267890). TAF15 also acts as a chaperone, inhibiting FUS liquid-to-solid transitions and mitigating aggregation in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (PubMed:30937520).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the prion-like domain (aa 1-216) and N-terminal IDR (aa 2-205), with tyrosine-arginine motifs in the RNA-binding domain enabling low saturation concentrations (PubMed:26286827, 36444977, 29961577). The low-complexity domain (LCD) mediates multivalent interactions essential for transcriptional hubs (PubMed:29930090). Hypomethylation – induced by AdOx – promotes nucleolar puncta formation, suggesting arginine methylation regulates phase behavior (PubMed:37131610). Tyrosine residues are critical for droplet integrity; mutations reduce phase separation propensity (PubMed:24267890).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RNA suppresses phase separation at high concentrations but depletion induces condensate formation (PubMed:29650702). TAF15 is recruited to SFPQ/NONO scaffolds in nucleolar CITIs and co-assembles with FUS/EWSR1 in heterotypic condensates at DNA damage sites and stress granules (PubMed:35662392, 26286827, 30937520). PARP1 recruits TAF15 to DNA repair condensates via PAR-dependent mechanisms (PubMed:38320550, 26286827). Chemical modulators include AdOx (induces nucleolar puncta) and glycine (alters fixation artifacts) (PubMed:37131610, 36444977). In transcriptional hubs, TAF15 recruits RNA Polymerase II, with LCD interactions stabilizing DNA binding (PubMed:29930090, 24267890).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: DDX4 undergoes self-driven phase separation (PubMed:35975930, 25747659, 28894006, 39505696) forming reversible liquid-like condensates primarily in the cytoplasm and nucleus (PubMed:38721279, 37973889, 25747659, 31974256). It associates constitutively with nuage (germ granules) (PubMed:37973889, 25747659, 28894006, 39505696) and exhibits high environmental sensitivity, dissolving upon increased ionic strength, temperature shifts, or arginine methylation (PubMed:25747659, 28894006, 37980572). Condensates maintain liquid properties including fusion competence and rapid FRAP recovery, with no observed irreversible transitions to solid states (PubMed:25747659, 28894006, 39505696, 31974256).
Functional Summary: DDX4 phase separation forms nuage condensates essential for germ cell biology, regulating mRNA processing and RNA stability during spermatogenesis (PubMed:25747659, 28894006, 37980572, 39505696). Ca²⁺ signaling modulates condensate morphology and function in this context (PubMed:37980572). The dense phase provides a selective solvent environment that concentrates single-stranded nucleic acids while excluding double-stranded DNA (PubMed:25747659) and enables G-quadruplex unfolding (PubMed:39505696). In somatic cells, it reduces stochastic protein concentration noise in the nucleoplasm during interphase, with dissolution during mitosis eliminating this buffering capacity (PubMed:31974256). When fused to editors like V1, the IDR enhances RNA editing efficiency but shows dose-dependent suppression of gene activation in synthetic transcriptional systems due to inadequate co-regulator recruitment (PubMed:38721279, 37094074).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR; residues 1-236) featuring clustered FG/RG motifs and charge patterning that enable multivalent cation-π/electrostatic interactions (PubMed:25747659, 28894006, 39505696). Phenylalanine residues are essential, as Phe→Ala mutations (e.g., 9FtoA, 14FtoA) abolish phase separation (PubMed:35975930, 25747659, 28894006, 39505696). Charge-altering mutations in the acidic cluster (Ddx4N0-N4 series) modulate ion sensitivity (PubMed:37980572), while arginine methylation destabilizes condensates by reducing transition temperatures (PubMed:25747659). Alternative splicing (e.g., Ddx4N2 variant) also regulates phase separation capacity (PubMed:25747659).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is extrinsically regulated by ions and biomolecular partners. Multivalent cations (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Y³⁺) stabilize condensates via charge inversion of acidic residues, with maximal stability at net charge +13 (pH 4.5) (PubMed:37980572). Salt concentration critically modulates behavior, as high NaCl abolishes phase separation while intermediate concentrations promote it (PubMed:25747659, 28894006, 35975930). DDX4 recruits nucleic acids including ssDNA and ssRNA (24-mer) into condensates, with Ca²⁺ enhancing RNA partitioning (PubMed:25747659, 37980572). It unfolds G-quadruplex DNA (MHT24) within droplets (PubMed:39505696) but is inhibited by the SH3 protein through weak interactions that raise phase separation thresholds (PubMed:35975930). In synthetic systems, phase separation requires Ferritin Core binding (PubMed:30500534).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: hnRNPA2 (P22626) undergoes self-driven phase separation, forming dynamic liquid-like condensates in vitro and in cells within both the cytoplasm and nucleus (PubMed:38072051, 39349455, 26544936). It associates with stress granules and transport granules, where it regulates RNA metabolism (PubMed:38072051, 30397184, 33349959). While initial condensates exhibit liquid properties (spherical morphology, fusion/fission, and rapid FRAP recovery), they progressively mature toward hydrogel-like states or irreversible solid aggregates over time—a transition dramatically accelerated by disease-associated mutations like D290V and P298L (PubMed:38072051, 26544936, 32870271).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, hnRNPA2 phase separation enables mRNA regulation—facilitating localized translation in transport granules, stress granule assembly during cellular stress, and alternative splicing in 40S hnRNP particles (PubMed:39349455, 35687109, 33349959). Pathologically, mutations like D290V/P298L drive irreversible liquid-to-solid transitions, forming cytotoxic fibrillar aggregates that disrupt RNA metabolism, cause cytoplasmic mislocalization, and contribute to multisystem proteinopathy, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and inclusion body myopathy (PubMed:38072051, 23455423, 32870271). These transitions are exacerbated by RNA dysregulation or chemical triggers, linking phase separation dyshomeostasis to neurodegeneration (PubMed:33349959, 23455423).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by hnRNPA2's low-complexity domain (LCD; residues ~190-341), which forms labile cross-β polymers through tyrosine/phenylalanine-rich motifs (e.g., Y278, Y283, F291, F309) and RGG repeats (PubMed:26544936, 33349959, 29358076). Critical residues include Y236/Y240/Y243, where tyrosine-to-serine mutations impair phase separation (PubMed:33349959). Disease mutations D290V and P298L within the LCD enhance phase separation propensity, promote cytoplasmic aggregation, and stabilize fibrils (PubMed:38072051, 23455423). Arginine methylation (R191/R201/R216/R254) reduces phase separation, while the conserved region (CR) helix integrity modulates material state transitions (PubMed:29358076, 34380047).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is modulated by RNA and protein partners: A2RE RNA inhibits hnRNPA2 phase separation by competing with LCD-RGG interactions (PubMed:32870271), while poly(A) RNA and specific mRNAs (e.g., Fsip2) lower saturation concentration and enhance droplet formation (PubMed:39349455). Proteins like Fyn-SH3 induce co-phase separation, with Fyn incorporating into hnRNPA2 droplets (PubMed:30397184), while hnRNPF, ch-TOG, and TDP-43 partition into hnRNPA2 condensates via heterotypic interactions (PubMed:33349959, 29358076). Salt concentration follows the Hofmeister series, with intermediate levels promoting phase separation, whereas high salt or low pH suppresses it (PubMed:33469149, 38072051). Tyrosine phosphorylation reduces phase separation and prevents partner recruitment (PubMed:33349959).

Protein Name: DNA-directed RNA polymerase II subunit RPB1
Overall Phase Separation Overview: RNA polymerase II subunit RPB1 (POLR2A) undergoes phase separation primarily through partner-driven mechanisms (class: PS-other) but exhibits self-driven capacity via its C-terminal domain (CTD) under specific conditions (PubMed:39266551, 34667177, 30127355, 29849146). It localizes to the nucleus and associates with transcriptional condensates, nuclear speckles, and spliceosomes (PubMed:36979361, 39266551, 34667177, 26455390). The protein typically forms liquid-like condensates (PubMed:37851801, 36979361, 39266551), with phosphorylation-dependent material state transitions: unphosphorylated CTD forms initiation condensates, while phosphorylation dissolves these and enables transitions to elongation/splicing condensates (PubMed:39266551, 31391587).
Functional Summary: Phase separation enables transcription initiation by concentrating machinery at promoters/super-enhancers, with ANLN-enhanced condensates regulating oncogenic pathways (e.g., Wnt signaling) in cancer (PubMed:39894879, 36979361). Phosphorylation-driven transitions to elongation/splicing condensates facilitate RNA processing, while nuclear hubs serve as reservoirs for rapid gene activation (PubMed:31391587, 30127355). Dysregulation—via CTD truncation, phosphomimetic mutations, or impaired transitions—causes aberrant splicing, transcriptional defects, and pathological accumulation in initiation condensates (PubMed:39266551, 36979361). Compartmentalization with PHF3 links transcription to mRNA decay, and recruitment into viral condensates (e.g., HSV-1 ICP22) enables viral replication (PubMed:34667177, 39383039).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by the C-terminal domain (CTD), where heptad repeat length (52 repeats in humans) determines stability—longer repeats enhance condensation while truncation impairs it (PubMed:39266551, 30127355). Key post-translational modifications include: Ser5 phosphorylation promotes initiation condensate formation; hyperphosphorylation dissolves condensates but enables splicing factor partitioning; and O-GlcNAcylation by OGT is essential for biomolecular condensate assembly (PubMed:36979361, 39266551, 37851801). Phosphomimetic mutations (e.g., T4E/S7E) abolish condensation, while tyrosine phosphorylation (Tyr1) regulates pause-release transitions (PubMed:39266551, 36979361).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is extrinsically modulated by partner-driven co-condensation: hypophosphorylated CTD partitions into mediator complexes (e.g., MED1), while hyperphosphorylated CTD incorporates into splicing factor condensates (e.g., SRSF2) (PubMed:31391587). Recruitment occurs in PHF3 condensates (Ser2-phosphorylated CTD), FUS LC droplets, PSPC1 transcription hubs, and mSWI/SNF PLD condensates (PubMed:34667177, 26455390, 34916619, 38326345). Regulatory proteins like ANLN enhance CTD phase separation and clustering; MPRIP mediates PIP2-associated transitions; and PIN1/SCAF6/SRSF2 induce phospho-CTD condensation (PubMed:39894879, 36979361, 39266551). Kinases (CDK7, CDK9) and pre-phosphorylation by CAK critically regulate partitioning (PubMed:31391587, 29849146).

MLO Types: Cytoplasmic Nucleoporin Granule; Nuclear body; Nuclear pore complex; Transcriptional condensate
Overall Phase Separation Overview: NUP98 undergoes self-driven phase separation via its FG-repeat domain, forming liquid-like condensates both in vitro and in vivo (PubMed:37100914, 25562883, 34163069, 39648588). It primarily localizes to the nucleus and cytoplasm, associating with nuclear pore complexes (PubMed:37100914, 32706158) and transcriptional condensates in fusion proteins like NUP98-HOXA9 (PubMed:36304323). The material state is typically liquid but undergoes concentration- and pH-dependent transitions to solid (amyloid) or gel states (PubMed:36138110, 39648588, 34903620). DNA binding competes with homotypic FG interactions, altering condensate morphology and dynamics (PubMed:36304323, 34903620).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, NUP98 phase separation forms the nuclear pore permeability barrier, enabling selective nucleocytoplasmic transport and mRNA export (PubMed:37100914, 25562883). Pathologically, fusion proteins (NUP98-HOXA9/NSD1/PHF23) drive leukemogenesis via aberrant transcriptional condensates that concentrate coactivators, establish super-enhancer chromatin looping, and activate oncogenes (HOXA, MEIS1) (PubMed:36304323, 35073946, 34163069, 39922194). Liquid-to-solid transitions form cytotoxic amyloids (PubMed:36138110, 39648588), while FG-repeat mutations abolish transformation capacity (PubMed:34903620, 39922194). Under FXR deficiency, aberrant cytoplasmic granules impair nuclear envelope assembly, linking to fragile X syndrome (PubMed:32706158).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by FG-repeat motifs (GLFG, FSFG, TFG) within the N-terminal intrinsically disordered region, with valency (repeat number/spacing) critically regulating condensation propensity (PubMed:37100914, 34163069, 34903620, 39648588). Key residues Phe92, Phe96, Phe102, Phe117, Phe120, Gln105, and Gln111 in the aggregation-prone segment (residues 85-124) mediate amyloid formation (PubMed:36138110). Phosphorylation inhibits phase separation (PubMed:37100914), while arginine methylation reduces propensity (PubMed:39648588). Disease-associated mutations (e.g., FG→AA substitutions) impair condensation efficiency, and DNA-binding domain mutations (e.g., ΔDNA) cause aberrant condensate morphology (PubMed:36304323, 34903620, 39922194).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: DNA acts as a scaffold for condensate formation, with chromosomal DNA essential for normal organization in transcriptional condensates (PubMed:36304323, 34903620). NUP98 co-phase separates with nuclear transport receptor NXF1 and mRNA, the latter exhibiting concentration-dependent biphasic regulation (PubMed:37100914). In leukemogenic fusions, it recruits transcriptional coactivators (KMT2A/B, BRD4, EP300, SMARCA5, BPTF) via FG-repeat-dependent partitioning (PubMed:39922194). Phase separation is modulated by ions (salt sensitivity following Hofmeister series), PEG (accelerating liquid-to-gel transitions), and pH (reversible aggregation at pH 7) (PubMed:37100914, 39648588, 36138110, 33469149). Importin β binds FG motifs without suppressing condensation (PubMed:25562883).

MLO Types: DNA damage foci; Nucleolus; Stress granule; Transcriptional condensate
Overall Phase Separation Overview: p53 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) forming dynamic condensates primarily in the nucleus and cytoplasm (PubMed:35618207, 36108750, 36350030, 38435052, 39661689). It associates with transcriptional condensates, stress granules under oxidative stress, DNA damage foci (as a client in 53BP1 condensates), and nucleolar compartments where mutant p53 accumulates (PubMed:36350030, 31267591, 36634798). Condensates typically exhibit liquid-like properties initially but undergo pathological transitions to gel-like or solid states due to aging, mutations, or environmental stressors; wild-type p53 shows reversible liquid behavior while cancer mutants (e.g., R273C, R175H) form irreversible solids (PubMed:35618207, 36350030, 36634798, 38435052, 39661689).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, LLPS enables p53 to form transcriptional hubs activating target genes (e.g., p21) for cell-cycle arrest and DNA repair, with recruitment into 53BP1/TIP60 condensates facilitating damage response (PubMed:35618207, 36108750, 31267591, 39965267). Pathologically, cancer mutations (R248Q, R175H, R273C/L) drive irreversible liquid-to-solid transitions, causing loss of tumor-suppressor function via sequestration, gain-of-function oncogenesis, and chemoresistance through drug entrapment in aggregates (PubMed:36350030, 38435052, 39661689). Lactylation impairs tumor-suppressive LLPS, while aberrant phase separation with poly-PR/GR may contribute to neurodegeneration in ALS/FTD (PubMed:38653238, 34768862).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by multivalent interactions involving the N-terminal transactivation domain (TAD), DNA-binding domain (DBD), tetramerization domain (TET), and disordered C-terminal domain (CTD) (PubMed:35618207, 36108750, 36350030). Tetramerization via TET is essential for multivalency, with oligomerization-disrupting mutations (e.g., R337C, L344P) impairing LLPS (PubMed:36108750, 34588591). Phosphorylation at Ser392 enhances fluidity and stabilizes transcriptional condensates, while Ser46/Ser15 phosphorylation promotes recruitment into functional droplets (PubMed:35618207, 36634798). Cancer-associated DBD mutations (R248Q, R273H, M237I) and tetramerization defects accelerate liquid-to-solid transitions, and lactylation at K120/K139 inhibits LLPS by impairing DNA binding (PubMed:36350030, 38653238, 38435052).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: p53 co-phase separates with transcriptional scaffolds MED1 and RNA polymerase II, with specific DNA (e.g., p21/p53AIP1) essential for incorporation into condensates (PubMed:35618207, 36634798). It partitions into 53BP1 DNA repair foci and TIP60 nuclear puncta for damage response (PubMed:31267591, 39965267). Nucleic acids critically modulate behavior: non-specific DNA/RNA promote LLPS and maintain liquid states, while target DNA dissolves condensates; poly-PR/GR peptides induce LLPS via TAD2 interactions but accelerate solidification at high concentrations (PubMed:36350030, 39661689, 34768862). Small molecules exert context-dependent effects—doxorubicin induces LLPS in wild-type p53 and partitions into mutant condensates to drive chemoresistance, while high salt concentrations dissolve droplets (PubMed:38435052, 39541973). Lactylation by AARS1 inhibits phase separation (PubMed:38653238).

MLO Types: P-body; RNP transport granule; Stress granule
Overall Phase Separation Overview: Caprin1 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) via its C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR), forming dynamic liquid droplets primarily in the cytoplasm (PubMed:40028898, 39172789, 34074792, 35072355). It localizes to stress granules as a core scaffold component and associates with P-bodies and mRNA transport granules (PubMed:36279435, 34074792, 35072355). The condensates exhibit reentrant behavior, dissolving at low/high NaCl or ATP-Mg concentrations but forming stable droplets at intermediate levels (PubMed:40028898, 34074792). Pathological liquid-to-solid transitions occur when client proteins like SOD1 aggregate within condensates (PubMed:39172789).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, Caprin1 LLPS nucleates stress granules to protect mRNA during cellular stress and regulates mRNA metabolism by accelerating CNOT7-mediated deadenylation while inhibiting translation (PubMed:36279435, 31439799, 39079611). Pathologically, it contributes to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) by promoting SOD1 unfolding/aggregation in condensates (PubMed:39172789) and influences cancer progression via circVAMP3-driven sequestration of oncogenic mRNAs (e.g., c-Myc) in hepatocellular carcinoma (PubMed:35072355). Dysregulation through RGG mutations or aberrant PTMs impairs stress response and correlates with neurodegeneration and tumorigenesis (PubMed:39079611, 35072355).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by Caprin1's C-terminal IDR (residues 607-709), featuring arginine-rich regions and RGG motifs that mediate multivalent interactions (PubMed:36279435, 34074792, 39079611). Critical mutations include RGG→AGG substitutions that impair stress granule formation and RNA binding (PubMed:36279435, 39079611). Post-translational modifications regulate LLPS: tyrosine phosphorylation reduces net charge and eliminates reentrant behavior (PubMed:40028898), O-GlcNAcylation at S644/S649 disrupts key interaction hotspots (PubMed:34074792), and specific phospho-tyrosine patterns (e.g., pY625/pY636) control co-phase separation selectivity with partners like FMRP (PubMed:31439799).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Ions modulate LLPS: Na⁺/Cl⁻ enable reentrant phase behavior through electrostatic effects, while ATP-Mg enhances condensation at intermediate concentrations but dissolves droplets above 20 mM (PubMed:40028898, 34074792). RNA scaffolds—including circVAMP3, polyA RNA, and cellular mRNAs—promote phase separation and induce subcompartmentalization (PubMed:35072355, 31439799). Key protein partners include G3BP1, with which Caprin1 reciprocally enhances condensation via RNA-mediated co-assembly (PubMed:36279435, 35072355); PRMT1, recruited via Caprin1's C-terminal domain for stress granule maturation (PubMed:39079611); phosphorylated FMRP, forming translation-repressive condensates (PubMed:31439799); and SOD1, which undergoes concentration-dependent unfolding within Caprin1 droplets (PubMed:39172789).

MLO Types: Centrosome; Destruction complex condensate; Wnt signalodroplet
Overall Phase Separation Overview: Axin1 (O15169) undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) to form dynamic, liquid-like biomolecular condensates primarily in the cytoplasm, with additional localization to the nucleus during specific cellular responses (PubMed:36037369, 39384753, 38279052). It associates with multiple membrane-less organelles including β-catenin destruction complex condensates, Wnt signalodroplets at the plasma membrane, centrosomal structures, and antiviral condensates (PubMed:36266931, 37611590, 36037369, 39384753, 38279052). These condensates exhibit liquid properties—demonstrating fusion, fission, and rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP)—and serve as scaffolds for macromolecular complex assembly (PubMed:37611590, 36037369, 38279052).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, Axin1 condensates: (1) Scaffold the β-catenin destruction complex, concentrating kinases (GSK3β/CK1α) to degrade β-catenin and suppress Wnt signaling, maintaining intestinal homeostasis (PubMed:37611590, 36037369, 38279052); (2) Assemble Wnt signalosomes with Dvl2/Lrp6 to activate β-catenin signaling (PubMed:36266931, 36342472); (3) Facilitate antiviral defense by recruiting TBK1/IRF3 to enhance interferon production (PubMed:39384753); (4) Enable β-catenin nuclear translocation and incorporation into transcriptional condensates for Wnt target gene activation (PubMed:38279052). Pathologically, disrupted condensation—via mutations (e.g., DIX domain), APC truncations, or USP10 dysregulation—abrogates β-catenin degradation, driving Wnt hyperactivation and colorectal cancer progression (PubMed:36037369, 38279052, 37873736).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by Axin1's DIX domain, which enables polymerization via electrostatic interactions, and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs; notably aa209-679), which provide multivalency for condensation (PubMed:37611590, 37721093, 38279052, 33060621). Key regulatory features include: (1) Phosphorylation by TBK1 at serine/threonine residues promotes phase separation during antiviral responses (PubMed:39384753); (2) Charge-neutralizing mutations in the DIX domain (e.g., Axin1-DA) or IDR deletions (e.g., Δ209-464, Δ497-679) disrupt condensation (PubMed:37611590, 38279052); (3) Cancer-associated truncations impair kinase recruitment without abolishing phase separation (PubMed:38279052). The RGS domain facilitates subcellular localization but does not directly drive phase separation (PubMed:37721093).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is modulated by extrinsic partners and conditions: (1) Dvl2 co-condenses with Axin1, attenuating destruction complex stability while recruiting it to dynamic Wnt signalosomes and introducing PP1 for Axin1 dephosphorylation (PubMed:36342472, 37721093, 36266931); (2) APC stabilizes condensates via multivalent IDR interactions, though truncated mutants (e.g., R1450*) fail to recruit kinases GSK3β/CK1α (PubMed:38279052, 33060621); (3) USP10 enhances condensate size/stability through scaffolding via its polybasic region, independent of deubiquitinase activity (PubMed:37611590); (4) Lrp6 recruits Axin1 to membrane-proximal signalodroplets in a density-dependent manner (PubMed:36266931); (5) Viral nucleic acids (e.g., poly(I:C)) or TBK1 activation trigger antiviral condensate formation (PubMed:39384753); (6) Wnt pathway activation dissolves centrosomal condensates to enable β-catenin stabilization (PubMed:36037369).

MLO Types: Nuclear body; PML nuclear body; PML/RARα microspeckle
Overall Phase Separation Overview: PML (P29590) undergoes self-driven phase separation to form nuclear biomolecular condensates, primarily localized in the nucleus (PubMed:39136995, 35194189, 37655965, 35163537, 34072343). It scaffolds PML nuclear bodies (NBs) with liquid-like properties including fusion, spherical morphology, and fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) (PubMed:35194189, 37655965, 35163537). These condensates associate with membrane-less organelles including canonical PML NBs, PML/RARα-assembled microspeckles in APL, and ALT-associated PML bodies (PubMed:39136995, 37655965, 34072343). Material state transitions occur under stress: arsenic trioxide (ATO) induces liquid-to-gel transitions (PubMed:37655965), while oxidative stress triggers liquid-to-solid transitions in isoforms like PML-I and PML-II (PubMed:34072343).
Functional Summary: PML phase separation is functionally critical for tumor suppression via genome stability maintenance, DNA repair, apoptosis regulation, and antiviral defense (PubMed:35194189, 39418304, 27374333). In acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), PML-RARA microspeckles recruit BRD4 to activate leukemogenic genes (e.g., MYC, BCL2), driving cell proliferation (PubMed:39136995). ATO therapy cures APL by inducing PML-RARA gel transitions that enable SUMO-triggered ubiquitination and degradation (PubMed:37655965). PML NBs act as oxidative stress sensors: C213 oxidation regulates dynamics and UBC9/KAP1 sumoylation (PubMed:37655965). SQSTM1 condensates protect PML from degradation by sequestering RNF4 (PubMed:39418304). Isoform-specific roles include PML-I in DNA damage repair, PML-II in nuclear lipid droplet regulation, and PML-V in telomere lengthening in ALT cancer cells (PubMed:34072343). Disrupted phase separation (e.g., by SAMHD1 deficiency or PML-RARA expression) impairs NB functions and promotes disease (PubMed:36150385, 35194189).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by the B-box 2 (B2) α1-helix (residues C213-L218), which drives trimerization via hydrophobic interactions and acts as an oxidation-sensitive rheostat (PubMed:37655965). The intrinsically disordered region (IDR; aa 205-589) enables multivalent interactions (PubMed:39136995). Sumoylation at K490 modulates dynamics by creating immobile fractions within condensates, while K490R mutation disrupts this and enhances liquidity (PubMed:35163537). Isoform-specific features govern behavior: PML-II's C-terminal domain enables charge-driven phase separation, PML-V's α-helical motif promotes hyperstable oligomerization, and PML-I's SIM motif facilitates SUMO-dependent scaffolding (PubMed:34072343). Disease mutations like C213S disrupt NB assembly, L218G impairs trimerization, and A216V causes clinical ATO resistance (PubMed:37655965, 34072343).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Extrinsic regulators include partner proteins and small molecules. SQSTM1 (p62) stabilizes PML NBs by sequestering RNF4 via PB1-PR domain interactions, preventing PML ubiquitination and degradation (PubMed:39418304). BRD4 co-scaffolds transcriptional hubs with PML-RARA in microspeckles (PubMed:39136995). SUMO2 localizes to PML bodies in a conjugation-dependent manner, enhancing phase separation through SUMO-SIM interactions (PubMed:35235714, 27374333). DAXX recruitment occurs via SUMO-SIM binding (PubMed:35194189). Small molecules modulate material states: arsenic trioxide (ATO) binds C213, inducing liquid-to-gel transitions and hyper-sumoylation (PubMed:37655965), while antimony trioxide exhibits similar effects (PubMed:37655965). MALL requires PML for nuclear condensate localization and stabilizes NB integrity (PubMed:35399121).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: UBQLN2 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro and forms biomolecular condensates primarily in the cytoplasm, with some nuclear localization observed under stress conditions (PubMed:29526694, PubMed:34129687, PubMed:33431932). It associates with stress granules under diverse proteotoxic stressors and forms distinct UBQLN2 bodies (PubMed:29526694, PubMed:30442662, PubMed:34129687). The condensates are typically liquid-like with dynamic properties but undergo pathological liquid-to-solid transitions to amyloid-like states with ALS-linked mutations or prolonged incubation (PubMed:30925840, PubMed:30982635, PubMed:30333186). Ubiquitin binding reverses LLPS through UBA domain interactions, causing liquid-to-disperse phase transitions (PubMed:29526694).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, UBQLN2 condensates function in protein quality control by concentrating ubiquitinated substrates and proteasomal components, protecting K63-linked substrates from degradation while enabling linkage-specific interpretation of the ubiquitin code (PubMed:39121161, PubMed:34029402). They regulate stress granule dynamics by suppressing FUS phase separation and maintaining RNP fluidity (PubMed:30442662). Pathologically, ALS-linked mutations impair condensate assembly, reduce liquidity, and promote irreversible liquid-to-solid transitions that form cytotoxic amyloid aggregates. These sequester proteasome subunits and TDP-43, disrupting proteostasis and contributing to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia pathogenesis (PubMed:30333186, PubMed:30982635, PubMed:34129687).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by multivalent interactions involving the STI1-II domain (residues 379-486), essential for oligomerization; the UBA domain (promotive); the UBL domain (inhibitory); and the Pxx region that acts as a molecular 'sticker' (PubMed:29526694, PubMed:34029402, PubMed:30982635). ALS-linked mutations (P497H, P497S, P497L, P506T) reduce saturation concentrations, enhance oligomerization, and promote liquid-to-solid transitions (PubMed:30982635, PubMed:34129687). Hydrophobic/aromatic substitutions in sticker positions (e.g., P506W) decrease saturation concentrations and increase viscoelasticity, while acidic substitutions disrupt phase separation (PubMed:30925840). The ubiquitin-binding-deficient L619A mutation increases puncta formation and aggregation propensity (PubMed:30333186).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Extrinsic regulation is dominated by ubiquitin chains: K63-linked chains strongly promote phase separation, while K48-linked chains exhibit biphasic/re-entrant behavior; free ubiquitin dissolves condensates via UBA domain binding (PubMed:39121161, PubMed:29526694, PubMed:30982635). UBQLN2 recruits E6AP AZUL to condensates through UBA interactions (PubMed:36827983) and incorporates proteasomes and deubiquitinases, inhibiting their enzymatic activity within condensates (PubMed:39121161). It co-localizes with FUS in stress granules, increasing FUS-RNA complex dynamics to suppress aberrant phase separation (PubMed:30442662). Under pathological conditions, it induces HDAC6-dependent aggresome formation with microtubule-related proteins (PubMed:33097688).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: G3BP2 undergoes phase separation to form liquid-like condensates primarily in the cytoplasm, where it serves as a core scaffold protein for stress granules (PubMed:35652658, 37398029, 34400613, 39951026). Its phase separation efficiency exceeds that of G3BP1 due to higher arginine content in its RG-rich region and is RNA-dependent, requiring RNA for condensation under low crowding conditions (PubMed:32302572). G3BP2 associates predominantly with stress granules across multiple biological contexts, with liquid-like material properties confirmed by rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) (PubMed:39951026). No material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: G3BP2-mediated phase separation organizes stress granules that fluidize the cytoplasm, enabling mRNA storage and cellular adaptation during stress (PubMed:37398029). This process is linked to cancer cell fitness and neurodegeneration (PubMed:37398029). Viral subversion occurs when SARS-CoV-2 N protein disrupts G3BP2 condensates to suppress antiviral responses and promote replication (PubMed:34400613, 33495715). In Parkinson's disease models, stress granule induction via PAE preserves dopaminergic neurons, reduces α-synuclein aggregation, and ameliorates motor deficits, highlighting neuroprotective roles (PubMed:39951026).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of G3BP2 is intrinsically driven by its RG-rich region, which provides enhanced multivalency through increased arginine residues compared to G3BP1, boosting phase separation efficiency (PubMed:32302572). The NTF2 domain mediates critical protein interactions, including binding with viral partners (PubMed:34400613). Oligomerization occurs at neutral pH, though RNA remains essential for phase separation under physiological conditions (PubMed:32302572). RNA-binding domains and protein interaction motifs collectively support its scaffolding function in condensate assembly (PubMed:37398029).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: G3BP2 phase separation is extrinsically regulated by RNA and viral proteins. Cellular mRNAs, particularly poly-adenylated RNAs, are essential for stress granule nucleation and lower the saturation concentration for condensation (PubMed:37398029, 32302572). The SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid (N) protein binds G3BP2 via the NTF2 domain, inhibiting phase separation and disrupting stress granule assembly as a viral immune evasion strategy (PubMed:34400613, 33495715). Perillaldehyde (PAE) chemically induces G3BP2-RNA condensate formation, enhancing stress resilience (PubMed:39951026).

MLO Types: DNA damage foci; Nucleolus; ViPR body
Overall Phase Separation Overview: Fibrillarin (FBL) undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) primarily within the nucleus, specifically localizing to the dense fibrillar component (DFC) of the nucleolus (PubMed:27212236, 31540874, 34326237, 38745030, 39579766). It also associates with DNA damage foci during double-strand break repair (PubMed:37582658).
