HSPB1 maintains liquid-like properties of these condensates (PubMed:36075972, 32231288, 36701233) and prevents pathological liquid-to-solid transitions (PubMed:36075972, 32231288).
Functional Summary: HSPB1 maintains proteostasis by preventing pathological condensate transitions: it preserves TDP-43 liquidity to enable stress recovery and prevent ALS-associated aggregation (PubMed:36075972); sustains SQSTM1/p62 condensate dynamics for autophagosome biogenesis during lysophagy, with defects linked to neurodegeneration (PubMed:37194327, 36701233); and inhibits FUS amyloid formation, protecting against ALS (PubMed:32231288). Dysregulation of HSPB1-mediated control correlates with irreversible liquid-to-solid transitions in TDP-43/FUS condensates, driving cytotoxicity in ALS and FTD (PubMed:36075972, 32231288).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: HSPB1's regulatory function is governed by its N-terminal domain (NTD) and oligomerization state (PubMed:32231288). Phosphorylation at S15/S78/S82 disrupts multimerization, switching its activity: under basal conditions, multimeric HSPB1 inhibits client phase separation; under stress, phosphorylated HSPB1 partitions into condensates to preserve liquidity (PubMed:32231288). Phosphorylation is essential for recruitment to SQSTM1/p62 condensates (PubMed:36701233). The alpha-crystallin domain (ACD) directly binds client proteins like FUS to inhibit amyloid formation when exposed by demultimerization (PubMed:32231288).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: HSPB1 partitions into TDP-43 condensates, delaying liquid-to-gel transitions and inhibiting fibrillization (PubMed:36075972). It co-localizes with SQSTM1/p62 on damaged lysosomes, maintaining condensate liquidity for lysophagy (PubMed:37194327, 36701233). For FUS, HSPB1 inhibits phase separation under non-stress conditions but co-phase separates upon phosphorylation to prevent amyloid transitions (PubMed:32231288). HSPB1 is recruited to SOD1-positive stress granules during proteotoxic stress (PubMed:28377462) and requires partner proteins (TDP-43, SQSTM1, FUS) for condensate incorporation (PubMed:36075972, 36701233, 32231288).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: U1-70K (SNRNP70) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in the nucleus, forming dynamic liquid-like condensates that can transition to solid aggregates (PubMed:36073763, 31723601). It associates with nuclear condensates, nuclear bodies, and nuclear speckles, where it co-localizes with CPSF6, PABPN1, and U2 snRNA (PubMed:36073763, 31723601, 38381607). The protein also co-phase separates with partners like SRSF1 in vitro (PubMed:39023093). Liquid-to-solid transitions occur in cellular environments and are modulated by concentration, time, and environmental factors (PubMed:31723601, 36073763).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, U1-70K LLPS regulates RNA processing by recruiting CPSF6 to alternative polyadenylation sites and modulating PABPN1-mediated repression, while co-phase separation with SRSF1 ensures spliceosome assembly fidelity (PubMed:36073763, 39023093). Pathologically, liquid-to-solid transitions—accelerated by prolonged expression or environmental stressors—promote cytotoxic aggregate formation linked to Alzheimer’s disease, where U1-70K co-aggregates with tau (PubMed:31723601, 36073763). These transitions are driven by LC domain motifs and represent a key mechanism in neurodegeneration (PubMed:31723601).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by low-complexity domains LC1 (residues 231-306, also termed BAD1) and LC2 (residues 317-407), which contain repetitive basic-acidic motifs enabling multivalent electrostatic interactions (PubMed:36073763, 31723601, 39023093). The LC1 domain undergoes a conformational switch from α-helix to β-strand/random coil upon partner binding (PubMed:39023093). Arginine-to-alanine mutations in LC1 disrupt phase separation and partner interactions (PubMed:36073763). Basic residues are essential for droplet formation, while acidic residues stabilize morphology (PubMed:31723601).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: U1-70K co-phase separates with protein partners including PABPN1 (driving its liquid-to-aggregate transition), CPSF6 (recruited to nuclear condensates), and SRSF1 (via BAD1-phosphorylated RS domain interactions) (PubMed:36073763, 39023093). This co-assembly is regulated by phosphorylation of both U1-70K BAD1 and SRSF1 (PubMed:39023093). Small molecules modulate material states: aspartic acid induces solid aggregates, while arginine maintains liquid states but disrupts droplet morphology (PubMed:31723601). Phase separation is sensitive to pH and salt concentrations, with larger droplets forming at acidic pH (PubMed:31723601).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: HSP70 (P0DMV8) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but is recruited into various membraneless organelles through heterotypic interactions (PubMed:33335017, 39804774). It localizes to both nucleus and cytoplasm, associating with stress-induced condensates including BAG2 degradation condensates (80.7% colocalization), TDP-43 anisosomes (6-16× enrichment in liquid cores), p62 nuclear condensates, TDP-43 nuclear condensates (NCs), and Negri bodies (PubMed:35654899, 33335017, 34385323, 28680096, 39804774). Within these compartments, HSP70 maintains liquid-like states with rapid fluorescence recovery (t½=3s in anisosome cores), but its delocalization can trigger liquid-to-gel transitions in client condensates (PubMed:33335017, 39804774).
Functional Summary: HSP70 serves as a chaperone guardian in biomolecular condensates, preventing pathological transitions: in BAG2 condensates, it enables ubiquitin-independent proteasomal degradation of clients like Tau (PubMed:35654899); in TDP-43 assemblies, it sustains liquidity to avert neurotoxic aggregation linked to ALS/FTD (PubMed:33335017, 36930291); in p62 hubs, it facilitates stress-responsive protein quality control (PubMed:34385323); and in Negri bodies, it supports viral replication machinery concentration (PubMed:28680096). Dysregulation—through delocalization (e.g., during prolonged poly-PR stress), ATP depletion, or inhibition—triggers gelation of TDP-43 condensates, causing phospho-TDP-43 oligomerization, cytotoxicity (7.7% LDH increase), and TDP-43 proteinopathy (PubMed:39804774, 33335017).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains or features driving autonomous HSP70 phase separation are identified, as it lacks self-assembly capability (PubMed:33335017, 39804774). Its regulatory function in condensates is mediated by ATP-dependent chaperone activity, where ATP hydrolysis maintains liquidity of host condensates like TDP-43 anisosomes and nuclear condensates (PubMed:33335017, 39804774). Inhibition of HSP70 ATPase activity reduces fluidity and promotes pathological transitions in client condensates (PubMed:33335017, 39804774).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: HSP70 recruitment requires partner-driven condensation: it co-phase separates with BAG2 in degradation condensates during hyperosmotic/proteasome stress (PubMed:35654899), enriches in TDP-43 anisosomes dependent on RNA-binding deficient TDP-43 variants (PubMed:33335017), partitions into p62 nuclear condensates under heat/oxidative stress (PubMed:34385323), incorporates into Negri bodies via viral P protein interactions (PubMed:28680096), and maintains TDP-43 NC fluidity through NEAT1 RNA scaffolding (PubMed:39804774). Key modulators include ATP levels (depletion causes irreversible liquid-to-solid transitions), proteasome inhibition (enhances TDP-43 demixing), and poly-PR dipeptide (induces NC maturation) (PubMed:33335017, 39804774).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Histone H1.4 (P10412) undergoes phase separation exclusively through partner-dependent mechanisms (class: PS-other) primarily in the nucleus (PubMed:32111972). It forms liquid-like condensates with short dsDNA (300-bp) in vitro (PubMed:37432033) and associates with heterochromatin (chromocenters) and nucleoli (PubMed:32111972). With chromatin scaffolds, its C-terminal domain promotes a transition toward solid-like material states characterized by increased density and reduced dynamics (PubMed:31543265). No material state transitions were explicitly reported across studies.
Functional Summary: H1.4 phase separation regulates chromatin architecture by promoting longer nucleosome linkers in higher eukaryotes (PubMed:31543265) and organizing heterochromatin domains (PubMed:32111972). Pathologically, its failure to be displaced by MeCP2 in Rett syndrome results in aberrant H1.4-dominated chromatin architecture, contributing to neurodevelopmental defects (PubMed:32111972). The evolutionary conservation of H1 expression correlates with its role in tuning chromatin phase separation properties (PubMed:31543265).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the disordered C-terminal domain (CTD), which is necessary and sufficient for altering chromatin condensate density and dynamics (PubMed:31543265). Post-translational modifications, particularly acetylation of histone tails, modulate the material properties of chromatin droplets (PubMed:31543265). While the lysine-rich CTD is implicated in DNA-driven phase separation, this remains inferred rather than experimentally validated (PubMed:37432033).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: H1.4 requires nucleic acid scaffolds: short dsDNA (300-bp) is essential for droplet formation but inhibited by longer DNA (PubMed:37432033), while nucleosomal arrays/chromatin enhance phase separation (PubMed:31543265, 32111972). It competes with MeCP2 for chromatin binding, forming mutually exclusive condensates where functional MeCP2 displaces H1.4 from heterochromatin to nucleoli. Rett syndrome mutations in MeCP2 abolish this competition, trapping H1.4 in heterochromatin (PubMed:32111972).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SON forms immiscible, viscoelastic condensates within nuclear speckles in the nucleus, exhibiting minimal molecular dynamics (PubMed:38381607). Its material properties are regulated by phosphorylation: dephosphorylation increases cohesion (rendering it more viscoelastic), while phosphorylation decreases cohesion (making it more liquid-like) (PubMed:39755675). As a core scaffold, SON maintains nuclear speckle integrity, with depletion disrupting speckle organization (PubMed:39798570).
Functional Summary: SON phase separation regulates alternative splicing of chromatin-related mRNAs and organizes nuclear speckle subcompartments that selectively enrich clients like SRSF1 and U2 snRNA (PubMed:38381607). Phosphorylation-dependent cohesion dynamics directly control mRNA retention within speckles, with dephosphorylation increasing nuclear mRNA retention (PubMed:39755675). SON depletion disrupts pre-mRNA 3' end processing genome-wide and enlarges RBBP6 foci, confirming its essential role in maintaining nuclear speckle structure for efficient gene expression (PubMed:39798570).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of SON is intrinsically regulated by phosphorylation states. Dephosphorylation enhances condensate cohesion and viscoelasticity, whereas phosphorylation reduces cohesion, promoting liquid-like dynamics (PubMed:39755675).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SON's phase separation is extrinsically modulated by phosphatase PP1 (complexed with NIPP1), which dephosphorylates SON to increase cohesion and mRNA retention in nuclear speckles (PubMed:39755675). Conversely, the kinase DYRK3 phosphorylates SON, reducing cohesion and promoting mRNA release (PubMed:39755675). SON also functionally interacts with SRRM2 as a co-scaffold; their co-depletion disrupts nuclear speckle integrity (PubMed:39798570).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TFEB undergoes self-driven phase separation (PubMed:35293953, 33290690, 33290695), forming liquid-like condensates primarily in the nucleus, where it associates with transcriptional condensates (PubMed:33290690, 33290695). Under specific conditions (e.g., high salt), it also forms cytoplasmic condensates (PubMed:35293953). These condensates exhibit liquid properties including rapid fluorescence recovery and spherical morphology, but demonstrate rigid interfacial boundaries and low fusion propensity (PubMed:35293953). Material state transitions occur from liquid to solid-like states in aged droplets, accelerated by small molecules or in disease models (PubMed:35293953).
Functional Summary: TFEB phase separation facilitates the assembly of dynamic transcriptional condensates that activate autophagy and lysosomal gene expression (PubMed:33290690, 33290695). Modulation of condensate material properties by Ro-3306 or vanillic acid enhances TFEB transcriptional activity, increasing lysosomal biogenesis and clearance of toxic aggregates (e.g., mutant huntingtin) independently of nuclear translocation (PubMed:35293953). Inhibition of phase separation by IPMK suppresses this transcriptional program and lysosomal function (PubMed:33290690, 33290695). Pathological liquid-to-solid transitions, accelerated by small molecules or disease conditions, impair condensate dynamics and may contribute to cytotoxicity (PubMed:35293953).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of TFEB is intrinsically driven by its basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) domain (PubMed:35293953, 33290690, 33290695). Charged residues (arginine/lysine) within this domain regulate fusion propensity, interfacial tension, and viscosity (PubMed:35293953). Mutation of eight basic residues to alanine (bHLH-B8A) reduces the LLPS concentration threshold, increases fusion frequency, and decreases surface rigidity (PubMed:35293953). Deletion of the bHLH domain abolishes phase separation capacity (PubMed:33290690, 33290695).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TFEB phase separation is modulated by several extrinsic regulators. The protein IPMK binds directly to TFEB's bHLH domain, inhibiting phase separation and dissolving preformed condensates (PubMed:33290690, 33290695). Within nuclear condensates, TFEB co-localizes with the transcriptional co-activator MED1 and associates with target mRNAs like LAMP1 (PubMed:33290690, 33290695). Sodium ions (Na⁺) are essential for condensation, with droplet formation showing salt-concentration dependence and high salt inducing cytoplasmic puncta (PubMed:35293953). Small molecules Ro-3306 and vanillic acid initially increase droplet size and fusion but promote pathological liquid-to-solid transitions over time (PubMed:35293953).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: APC undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) to form biomolecular condensates (PubMed:37047451, 38279052, 33060621). It primarily localizes to the cytoplasm and nucleus, associating with destruction complex condensates and centrosome-associated structures (PubMed:35867833, 36037369, 38279052). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties, evidenced by droplet fusion and rapid FRAP recovery, but undergo pathological liquid-to-solid transitions when aged or under specific conditions (PubMed:33060621, 38279052).
Functional Summary: APC phase separation organizes the β-catenin destruction complex, concentrating kinases (GSK3β/CK1α) to enable efficient β-catenin phosphorylation and degradation, thereby suppressing Wnt signaling (PubMed:36037369, 38279052, 33060621). In colorectal cancer, truncating mutations (e.g., R1450*/R876*) maintain condensate formation but disrupt kinase recruitment, leading to β-catenin accumulation, nuclear translocation, and Wnt-driven tumorigenesis (PubMed:38279052, 33060621). Centrosomal association with Dvl2 condensates fine-tunes Wnt signal transduction during cell cycle progression, dissolving during mitosis while remaining dispensable for pathway activation (PubMed:35867833). Pathological liquid-to-solid transitions generate cytotoxic aggregates linked to disease progression (PubMed:33060621).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by multiple disordered regions: the ASAD domain (residues 396-426) utilizes hydrophobic patches (Leu3/Ile7/Tyr10/Trp17) and charged residues (PubMed:37047451), while 20R repeats (e.g., 20R3 SLSAL motif, 20R5 SLSSL motif) and SAMP motifs provide essential multivalency (PubMed:33060621, 37047451). A critical IDR (aa2157-2653) autonomously drives liquid droplet formation (PubMed:38279052). Phosphorylation at specific sites (S1501/S1505/S1504/S1507 in 20R3; S1857/S1861/S1863 in 20R5) inhibits phase separation, narrowing or abolishing droplet formation (PubMed:37047451). Disease-associated truncations (R1450*, R876*) retain phase separation capacity but disrupt functional organization (PubMed:38279052).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: APC co-phase separates with Axin through multivalent interactions, significantly enhancing condensate stability and reducing Axin's critical concentration for assembly (PubMed:33060621, 38279052). It recruits β-catenin, GSK3β, and CK1α into destruction complexes for phosphorylation cascades, though kinase recruitment fails in APC-truncated mutants (PubMed:36037369, 38279052). APC also colocalizes within Dvl2 centrosomal condensates alongside Wnt components like Axin1 and LRP6 (PubMed:35867833). Phase separation is salt-sensitive, following the Hofmeister series, with droplet formation optimized at intermediate ionic strengths (186-336 mM) (PubMed:37047451).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: BMI1 (P35226) does not undergo self-driven phase separation under basal conditions and primarily acts as a client protein recruited into partner-driven condensates within the nucleus (PubMed:37756159, 34620850, 33169020). It associates with nuclear bodies and Polycomb bodies, exhibiting enrichment in CBX2-driven condensates (PubMed:37756159, 33169020). Upon light-induced oligomerization, BMI1 forms dynamic liquid-like condensates characterized by rapid fluorescence recovery and fusion behavior (PubMed:34620850). These condensates maintain a liquid state without reported material state transitions under tested conditions (PubMed:34620850, 33169020).
Functional Summary: BMI1 phase separation facilitates epigenetic silencing through PRC1-mediated formation of repressive chromatin compartments. These condensates enable reading of H3K27me3 marks and writing of H2AK119Ub repressive histone modifications, driving chromatin compaction (PubMed:34620850). Pathological hyper-clustering of BMI1 condensates—observed in MLL4-deficient states—increases nuclear stiffness, impairs mesenchymal stem cell differentiation, and contributes to Kabuki syndrome pathogenesis (PubMed:33169020). Dysregulation disrupts nuclear architecture without reported cytotoxicity (PubMed:33169020).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of BMI1 is intrinsically regulated by its RAWUL oligomerization domain, which is essential for de novo condensate formation. Removal of this domain (ΔOD mutation) abolishes phase separation capacity (PubMed:34620850). In contrast, the intrinsically disordered region (IDR) is dispensable for droplet formation but partially mediates self-interaction within condensates (PubMed:34620850). No disease-associated mutations or post-translational modifications directly regulating phase separation were reported (PubMed:37756159, 34620850, 33169020).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: BMI1 phase separation is extrinsically modulated through heterotypic interactions with multiple partners. It is recruited into condensates formed by CBX2 scaffolds and co-assembles with RING1B in Polycomb bodies (PubMed:37756159, 33169020). BMI1 reciprocally recruits PRC1 components PHC1 and RNF2 into its own condensates, demonstrating bidirectional partnership within the complex (PubMed:34620850). Condensate formation is enriched at H3K27me3-marked chromatin regions and exhibits hyper-clustering upon MLL4 loss-of-function (PubMed:33169020).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NF2 (P35240) exhibits context-dependent phase separation behaviors. Wild-type NF2 undergoes self-driven phase separation (PS-self) forming solid-like condensates in the cytoplasm that age into detergent-resistant fibers in vitro and in mammalian cells (PubMed:39116228). However, specific mutants demonstrate distinct behaviors: the c.770-784del mutant forms liquid-like cytoplasmic puncta requiring LATS for co-phase separation (PS-other), while patient-derived FERM domain mutants (L46R/L64P/L141P) form liquid-like condensates induced by activated IRF3 (PubMed:36300003, 34453890). Material states range from liquid to solid, with wild-type NF2 undergoing liquid-to-solid transitions in vitro (PubMed:39116228).
Functional Summary: Phase separation has significant pathophysiological consequences. Cytoplasmic NF2mut-LATS condensates sequester LATS from the plasma membrane, inhibiting Hippo signaling and promoting meningioma tumorigenesis (PubMed:36300003). For FERM mutants, IRF3-induced condensates sequester TBK1/IRF3 and recruit RACK1-PP2A to dephosphorylate TBK1, suppressing cGAS-STING signaling and compromising antiviral defense, DNA damage responses, and antitumor immunity (PubMed:34453890). Pathological condensates in human schwannomas correlate with tumorigenesis, and liquid-to-solid transitions in wild-type NF2 may contribute to cytotoxicity (PubMed:34453890, 39116228).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by NF2's structural domains and mutations. The FERM domain's hydrophobic core stability controls phase behavior, where mutations (L46R/L64P/L141P) cause conformational changes promoting oligomerization (PubMed:34453890). The LATS-binding domain (residues 69-100) is essential for co-phase separation with LATS, while the IDR (308-590) is dispensable (PubMed:36300003). Phosphorylation at S518 by TBK1 stabilizes an open conformation facilitating oligomerization (PubMed:34453890). The c.770-784del mutation in the F3 module disrupts membrane binding, enabling cytoplasmic condensation (PubMed:36300003).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is extrinsically regulated by partner proteins and signaling contexts. LATS acts as essential co-scaffold for c.770-784del mutant condensates, forming heterogeneous cytoplasmic droplets (PubMed:36300003). For FERM mutants, activated IRF3 directly induces phase separation via FERM domain binding, while TBK1 recruitment enables phosphorylation-dependent regulation (PubMed:34453890). The RACK1-PP2A complex is functionally recruited into mutant condensates to deactivate TBK1 (PubMed:34453890). Phase separation requires innate immune activation (MAVS/STING pathways) and is disrupted by 1,6-hexanediol (PubMed:34453890).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Nup62 (P37198) exhibits context-dependent phase separation behavior primarily associated with the nuclear pore complex (PubMed:36690069, 36482422, 34059832). While it does not undergo self-driven phase separation alone in certain conditions (PubMed:36690069), it forms non-spherical assemblies under molecular crowding (PubMed:34059832). Nup62 readily co-phase separates with partners like FUS into amorphous, solid-like assemblies with reduced dynamics (PubMed:36690069, 34059832), and co-aggregates with TDP-43 into amyloid-like fibrils in pathological contexts (PubMed:36482422). RNA promotes its incorporation into liquid-like FUS droplets, demonstrating material state versatility (PubMed:34059832).
Functional Summary: Nup62's aberrant phase transitions disrupt nucleocytoplasmic transport and contribute to neurodegeneration. Cytoplasmic co-phase separation with FUS or co-aggregation with TDP-43 mislocalizes nuclear pore components, impairing transport in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) (PubMed:36690069, 36482422, 34059832). These pathological solid assemblies recruit phospho-TDP-43 and form amyloid-like fibrils (PubMed:36482422). Therapeutic dissolution of aggregates by KPNB1 restores transport and reduces toxicity, highlighting potential treatment strategies (PubMed:36482422).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by Nup62's domain architecture. Its C-terminal domain (CTD, aa 301–522) with coiled-coil structure is essential for FUS binding and co-phase separation (PubMed:36690069). The N-terminal domain (NTD, aa 1–300) contains phenylalanine-glycine (FG) repeats that mediate multivalent interactions for TDP-43 co-aggregation (PubMed:36482422, 34059832). Mutation of NTD phenylalanines (F->A) abolishes modulatory effects on FUS droplets, confirming their functional role (PubMed:36690069).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Nup62's phase behavior is extrinsically modulated by protein partners and molecular conditions. It co-phase separates with FUS to form solid-like assemblies, accelerated by FUS interaction (PubMed:36690069, 34059832). Co-aggregation with TDP-43 occurs via FG-repeat/PrLD interactions, forming pathological hydrogels (PubMed:36482422). RNA promotes Nup62 incorporation into liquid FUS droplets, inhibiting aberrant assembly (PubMed:34059832). The karyopherin KPNB1 dissolves aggregates by disrupting FG interactions (PubMed:36482422). Ionic strength modulates phase separation, with higher salt concentrations reducing assembly formation (PubMed:36690069).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: MATR3 undergoes self-driven phase separation forming liquid-like condensates primarily in the nucleus, with additional cytoplasmic localization observed under mutation conditions (PubMed:35252808, 33097688, 31019288). It forms dynamic, shell-like spherical structures (anisosome-like) in the nucleus, exhibiting rapid FRAP recovery indicative of liquid properties (PubMed:35252808). Disease-associated mutations (S85C, P154S, T622A) induce material state transitions from liquid to gel/solid states characterized by irregular morphology and loss of dynamics (PubMed:35252808). The F115C mutation enables cytoplasmic aggregation and phase separation (PubMed:33097688).
Functional Summary: Aberrant MATR3 phase separation is mechanistically linked to neurodegenerative pathologies. Disease mutations (S85C, P154S, T622A) cause pathological liquid-to-solid transitions that drive proteotoxicity in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) (PubMed:35252808). The F115C mutant contributes to TDP-43 pathology in ALS and frontotemporal lobar degeneration by forming cytoplasmic aggregates that recruit TDP-43 (PubMed:33097688). These pathological transitions lead to cytotoxic fibril formation and are rescued by engineered Hsp104 variants that reverse misfolding (PubMed:35252808).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by MATR3's N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR; aa 1-397) and modulated by RNA recognition motifs (RRMs) (PubMed:35252808, 31019288). The IDR enables multiple foci formation while RRMs prevent coalescence into single large structures (PubMed:35252808). RRM2 deletion promotes phase separation, indicating RNA binding normally suppresses condensation (PubMed:31019288). Disease mutations significantly alter behavior: S85C inhibits droplet formation and stability, P154S/T622A cause liquid-to-solid transitions with impaired mobility, and F115C enables cytoplasmic aggregation (PubMed:35252808, 33097688, 31019288).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: MATR3 phase separation is regulated by RNA availability and protein partners. RNA binding suppresses condensation, with impaired RNA binding (via RRM2 deletion) enhancing phase separation (PubMed:31019288). MATR3 recruits TDP-43 into condensates when TDP-43's RNA-binding capability is compromised (RRM1-disabled constructs) or as isolated prion-like domains (PubMed:31019288). The F115C mutant forms cytoplasmic aggregates that co-phase separate with and recruit TDP-43 (PubMed:33097688).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SOX2 (P48431) exhibits distinct phase separation behaviors across cellular contexts. It undergoes self-driven reentrant phase separation in vitro, forming liquid-like droplets at both low (50 mM) and high (2.15 M) KCl concentrations, with high circularity (>95%) indicating liquid properties (PubMed:33597515). In the nucleus, SOX2 forms heterogeneous distributions characterized by diffuse 'islands' and sparse diffraction-limited foci, displaying phase separation behavior classified as PS-other (PubMed:36309135). It co-condenses with p300 to form transcriptional condensates (PubMed:33651988) but does not associate with predefined membrane-less organelles. SOX2 disrupts condensates of steroid receptors like glucocorticoid receptor (GR) without direct binding (PubMed:36309135).
Functional Summary: SOX2 phase separation functionally modulates transcriptional programs. By disrupting steroid receptor condensates (e.g., GR) and redistributing coactivators like NCoA-2, it alters transcriptional outcomes (PubMed:36309135). Its co-condensation with p300 enables formation of transcriptional clusters, potentially regulating gene activation (PubMed:33651988). Aberrant SOX2 expression in cancer may dysregulate steroid hormone responses through these condensate-modifying activities (PubMed:36309135).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of SOX2 is intrinsically regulated by its Transactivation Domain (TAD, amino acids 121-317), which drives co-condensation with p300 (PubMed:33651988). No other intrinsic domains, mutations, post-translational modifications, or oligomerization features regulating its phase behavior are reported in the provided data.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SOX2 phase separation is modulated by key extrinsic partners and conditions. It co-condenses with p300 scaffold protein through interactions mediated by its TAD domain (PubMed:33651988). SOX2 redistributes coactivator NCoA-2 to its nuclear islands without direct binding and disrupts GR condensates (PubMed:36309135). Ion concentration critically regulates its behavior, with KCl inducing reentrant phase separation (droplet formation at 50 mM and 2.15 M KCl, absence at 500 mM) through hydrophobic and non-ionic interactions (PubMed:33597515).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: C/EBPα (P49715) undergoes self-driven phase separation to form liquid-like condensates in vitro and forms dynamic nuclear foci in vivo, primarily localized in the nucleus (PubMed:37516962, 37903757). It associates with transcriptional condensates and forms nuclear foci that partially colocalize with MED1 during cellular processes like B cell-to-macrophage transdifferentiation and hematopoiesis (PubMed:37516962). The condensates exhibit liquid-like properties including rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), droplet fusion, and spherical morphology. Material state transitions to solid aggregates are not observed, though aromatic residue mutations (e.g., AroLITE) or heterodimerization with C/EBPα-p30 can inhibit phase separation (PubMed:37516962, 37903757, 38969762).
Functional Summary: Phase separation drives chromatin compartment switching and long-range hub formation during cellular differentiation, activating myeloid genes (e.g., CSF1R, PU1) while repressing B cell genes (e.g., EBF1) (PubMed:37516962). Enhanced condensation capacity correlates with genomic binding strength and reprogramming efficiency (PubMed:38969762). In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), liquid-liquid phase separation is essential for differentiation induced by chemotherapeutic agents; pathological inhibition by C/EBPα-p30 contributes to AML progression by disrupting condensate formation and myeloid gene activation (PubMed:37903757). Mutations impairing phase separation (e.g., AroLITE, S16A) disrupt chromatin reorganization and transcriptional rewiring during transdifferentiation (PubMed:37516962, 37903757).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR, residues 1–255), where hydrophobic interactions involving aromatic residues (including specific tyrosines and phenylalanines) are essential (PubMed:37516962). Optimized dispersion of aromatic residues (AroPERFECT) enhances liquid-like dynamics and functional activity, while substitutions (AroLITE) abolish homotypic condensation (PubMed:38969762, 37516962). Homodimerization via the leucine zipper domain (residues 287–322) and phosphorylation at serine 16 (S16) critically promote phase separation, with phosphomimetic mutations (S16E) enhancing condensate formation (PubMed:37903757).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: C/EBPα co-condenses with transcriptional regulators including MED1 (which enhances droplet size), PU1, PPARG2, and IKAROS in heterotypic nuclear foci, demonstrating cooperative assembly in transcriptional hubs (PubMed:37516962). Hyperosmotic stress induced by mannitol triggers phase separation in cells, while heterodimerization with the isoform C/EBPα-p30 inhibits condensation by disrupting homodimerization at high stoichiometric ratios (PubMed:37903757). No extrinsic chemical partners beyond mannitol were identified across studies (PubMed:38969762, 37516962, 37903757).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: VASP undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) to form dynamic liquid-like condensates in vitro, exhibiting fusion, wetting, and rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) (PubMed:37425724, 38405682, 39914390). These condensates are primarily cytoplasmic and associate with focal adhesions where they partition into LIMD1 biomolecular condensates (PubMed:33891898). Actin polymerization within droplets drives morphological transitions from spheres to rings, ellipsoids, and linear bundles; this liquid state can shift toward solid-like behavior under high crowding conditions (10% PEG) that impair deformation (PubMed:38405682).
Functional Summary: VASP phase separation orchestrates actin cytoskeletal remodeling by mediating competition between filament branching (Arp2/3-dependent) and bundling, enabling formation of aster structures that model filopodia emergence from lamellipodia during cell migration (PubMed:37425724, 38405682). This process facilitates force-sensitive recruitment to focal adhesions via LIMD1 condensates, regulating adhesion maturation, cellular traction forces, and stiffness-guided migration (durotaxis) (PubMed:33891898). Liquid-like droplet properties are essential for actin filament reorganization into bundles; impairment of F-actin binding or excessive crowding disrupts bundling capability, highlighting the mechanistic link between condensate fluidity and cytoskeletal function (PubMed:38405682, 39914390).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: VASP phase separation is intrinsically regulated by its tetramerization domain, which enables multivalent interactions essential for condensate formation (PubMed:37425724, 38405682, 39914390). Mutations in functional domains critically modulate behavior: RK236,237EE substitutions in the G-actin binding (GAB) domain reduce actin partitioning but permit partial droplet deformation, while KR275,276EE/K278E/K280E mutations in the F-actin binding (FAB) domain prevent internal filament organization and abolish deformation (PubMed:38405682). The EVH1 domain facilitates co-condensation with partners through multivalent proline-rich interactions (PubMed:39914390).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: VASP condensates recruit actin monomers and filaments, whose polymerization drives droplet deformation and bundle formation (PubMed:37425724, 38405682, 39914390). The Arp2/3 complex modulates actin organization: it inhibits bundling at low actin:VASP ratios but promotes aster formation with core-spoke architecture at high ratios, requiring N-WASP for activation (PubMed:37425724). VASP co-condenses with Lamellipodin via EVH1-mediated interactions, enhancing actin bundling without crowding agents (PubMed:39914390). Additionally, VASP partitions into LIMD1 condensates at focal adhesions under mechanosensitive regulation (PubMed:33891898).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: VCP (p97) does not autonomously undergo phase separation but is recruited to various membrane-less organelles including arsenite-induced stress granules in the cytoplasm, FUS cytoplasmic granules, and nuclear proteasome foci (PubMed:29804830, 35445401, 32025036). It regulates the material properties of these condensates, facilitating stress granule clearance through proteasomal recruitment and modulating FUS granule stability via ATP-dependent mechanisms without undergoing autonomous state transitions (PubMed:29804830, 35445401).
Functional Summary: VCP serves as a critical regulator of proteostasis within condensates: it enables stress granule clearance by recruiting the 26S proteasome to degrade ubiquitylated substrates, prevents aberrant granule persistence linked to ALS/IBMPFD, and acts as a biphasic timer for FUS granule dissolution to inhibit pathological fibrillization (PubMed:29804830, 35445401). In nuclear proteasome foci, it enhances degradation efficiency under hyperosmotic stress (PubMed:32025036). Dysfunction via mutations (R155H) or impaired recruitment accelerates liquid-to-solid transitions in stress granules and FUS condensates, directly contributing to neurodegenerative pathogenesis (PubMed:29804830, 35445401).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The hexameric AAA ATPase domains of VCP, containing 12 ATPase domains, intrinsically enable its regulatory function by hydrolyzing ATP to modulate condensate stability (PubMed:35445401). Pathogenic mutations including R155H impair stress granule clearance capacity, while the A232E mutation in the ATPase domain alters FUS granule dynamics and promotes cytoplasmic mislocalization (PubMed:29804830, 35445401).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: VCP recruitment is mediated by scaffold proteins: ZFAND1 recruits it to arsenite-induced stress granules, FUS enables its colocalization to cytoplasmic granules, and RAD23B/UBE3A facilitate nuclear proteasome focus association (PubMed:29804830, 35445401, 32025036). Its function is modulated by ATP concentrations (optimal at ~1mM) where ATP depletion rigidifies FUS granules, while arsenite stress specifically induces its interactions with degradation machinery (PubMed:35445401, 29804830). Pathological FUS P525L mutation reduces VCP affinity, extending granule persistence (PubMed:35445401).

Protein Name: Eukaryotic translation initiation factor 3 subunit B
Overall Phase Separation Overview: eIF3η is recruited into stress granules in the cytoplasm through partner-dependent mechanisms rather than self-driven phase separation (PubMed:39306064, 30893049, 29262335). It forms puncta co-localizing with the scaffold proteins G3BP1 and G3BP2 under Cr(VI), arsenic, or rG4C2 RNA stress, exhibiting liquid-like material properties within these condensates (PubMed:39306064, 29262335, 30893049). No material state transitions are reported for eIF3η itself.
Functional Summary: eIF3η enrichment in stress granules facilitates stress-induced translational arrest during cellular stress responses (PubMed:29262335). Pathologically, aberrant condensation driven by expanded rG4C2 RNA disrupts RNA granule homeostasis, contributing to C9-ALS/FTD pathogenesis (PubMed:29262335). Its consistent presence in stress granules under diverse stressors (Cr(VI), arsenic, optical induction) confirms its role as a core stress response component (PubMed:39306064, 30893049).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or molecular features driving eIF3η phase separation are specified in the provided data (PubMed:39306064, 30893049, 29262335).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: eIF3η recruitment requires extrinsic scaffolds: It co-localizes with G3BP1 and G3BP2, which are essential for stress granule integrity (PubMed:39306064). Condensation is RNA-dependent, as rG4C2 repeats promote its partitioning into stress granules in a length- and structure-sensitive manner, with optimal assembly at intermediate salt concentrations (PubMed:29262335). eIF3η also co-partitions with multiple stress granule components including PABP, TDP-43, TIA1, eIF4G, FUS, and polyadenylated mRNAs in optically induced G3BP1 scaffolds (PubMed:30893049).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Histone H1 undergoes partner-dependent phase separation, requiring nucleic acids or proteins rather than self-assembly (PubMed:35484234, PubMed:31952807, PubMed:37468629). It forms condensates primarily in the nucleus, associating with replication fork puncta, nucleolus, and heterochromatin (PubMed:35484234, PubMed:31952807). The material state is substrate-dependent: gel-like with ssDNA/RNA, liquid-like with dsDNA/nucleosomes, and viscous liquid-like when co-phase separating with ProTα (PubMed:35484234, PubMed:37468629). ATP induces transitions from dynamically arrested to liquid-like states in polynucleosome condensates (PubMed:31952807).
Functional Summary: H1 phase separation stabilizes replication forks by shielding ssDNA from mechanical stress and organizes genome maintenance machinery into nuclear puncta during replication stress (PubMed:35484234). In heterochromatin, it scaffolds transcriptionally repressive domains whose ATP-dependent dynamics facilitate chromatin remodeling (PubMed:31952807). Co-phase separation with ProTα forms nuclear condensates enabling rapid partner exchange for chromatin organization and transcriptional regulation (PubMed:37468629). Dysregulation, particularly through CTD impairment, is linked to DNA damage response pathologies (PubMed:35484234).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the disordered C-terminal domain (CTD), which is lysine-rich and essential for nucleic acid-mediated condensation (PubMed:35484234, PubMed:31952807). The N-terminal domain (NTD) contributes secondarily, as its truncation reduces phase separation propensity and increases droplet fluidity (PubMed:35484234). The globular domain alone shows minimal phase separation capacity (PubMed:35484234). The high positive charge (+53) of full-length H1 enables electrostatic interactions with negatively charged partners (PubMed:37468629).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Essential scaffolds include ssDNA (inducing gel-like droplets, enhanced by longer lengths/lower GC content), RNA (stronger driver than ssDNA), dsDNA, and nucleosomes (forming liquid-like droplets) (PubMed:35484234). H1 co-phase separates with prothymosin α (ProTα) through charge complementarity, forming viscous coacervates where each H1 molecule interacts with ~8 ProTα molecules (PubMed:37468629). ATP promotes liquid-like behavior in polynucleosome condensates and is required for in vivo droplet formation (PubMed:31952807). Phase separation is salt-sensitive, with higher KCl concentrations suppressing coacervation by screening electrostatic interactions (PubMed:37468629, PubMed:31952807).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: eIF4G (Q04637) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but is recruited as a client protein to biomolecular condensates in the cytoplasm (PubMed:38421168, 38072230, 30893049). It associates with viral inclusion body-associated granules (IBAGs) during respiratory syncytial virus infection, where it concentrates translation machinery (PubMed:38421168, 38072230), and partitions into stress granules under cellular stress conditions (PubMed:30893049, 36151083). Its material state within condensates is not explicitly characterized in the provided data.
Functional Summary: eIF4G condensate recruitment enables compartmentalized translation initiation. In viral contexts, it enhances RSV replication efficiency by concentrating translation machinery within IBAGs for selective viral mRNA translation (PubMed:38421168, 38072230). Within stress granules, it contributes to stress-adaptive mRNA regulation; however, chronic granule persistence is linked to pathological inclusions in neurodegenerative diseases like ALS/FTD (PubMed:30893049). Dysregulation of this recruitment mechanism may thus contribute to both viral pathogenesis and proteinopathic disorders.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The recruitment of eIF4G to condensates is intrinsically regulated by its PABP-interacting domain, which is essential for incorporation into viral mRNA condensates (PubMed:38072230). No mutations or specific domains driving autonomous phase separation were reported; its scaffolding domain for eIF4F complex assembly supports its role as a client protein rather than a primary scaffold (PubMed:38421168, 30893049).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: eIF4G recruitment is extrinsically controlled by scaffold proteins: it partitions into RSV IBAGs via interaction with viral protein M2-1 (PubMed:38421168) and is incorporated into viral mRNA condensates through binding to PABP (PubMed:38072230). Under stress conditions, it is recruited to G3BP1-driven stress granules (PubMed:30893049, 36151083). These partnerships enable its concentration within translationally active compartments without autonomous phase separation behavior.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Q05086 (E6AP/UBE3A) undergoes phase separation exclusively through partner-dependent mechanisms and does not exhibit self-driven assembly (PubMed:37549262, 36827983, 32025036). It forms liquid-like condensates during in vitro ubiquitination assays (PubMed:37549262) and is recruited to partner-driven condensates in both nucleus and cytoplasm. The protein localizes to proteasome foci in the nucleus under stress conditions (PubMed:32025036) and partitions into UBQLN2 biomolecular condensates (PubMed:36827983). Its material state is consistently liquid across observations, with no reported state transitions (PubMed:37549262, 36827983).
Functional Summary: Phase separation of Q05086 promotes its ubiquitin ligase activity during in vitro ubiquitination (PubMed:37549262). Within UBQLN2 condensates, it ubiquitinates substrates like misfolded proteins for proteasomal degradation (PubMed:36827983). In nuclear proteasome foci, it contributes to stress-responsive proteolytic centers that prevent apoptosis by facilitating efficient degradation of misfolded proteins (PubMed:32025036). Its recruitment to condensates enables substrate ubiquitination in spatially organized compartments, though pathological implications were not reported in the provided studies (PubMed:36827983, 32025036).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The HECT domain is the primary intrinsic feature associated with Q05086 phase separation behavior, though it requires extrinsic partners for actual condensation (PubMed:37549262). No autonomous phase separation occurs due to the absence of intrinsic drivers like low-complexity domains or mutation-sensitive regions (PubMed:36827983, 32025036). The AZUL domain (studied as AZUL-mEGFP) enables recruitment to partner condensates but lacks self-assembly capability (PubMed:36827983).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Q05086 phase separation is extrinsically regulated by multiple partners: polyubiquitin chains directly drive its LLPS during ubiquitination (PubMed:37549262), UBQLN2 scaffolds its recruitment via UBA domain interactions (PubMed:36827983), and K48-linked ubiquitin chains enhance condensate formation through partner modulation (PubMed:32025036, 36827983). It co-localizes with RAD23B and p97 in nuclear proteasome foci (PubMed:32025036), and its partitioning is dependent on UBQLN2 condensates (PubMed:36827983).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SHP2 (PTPN11) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) primarily through its pathogenic variants (e.g., G503R, E76K, R498L), forming dynamic liquid-like condensates in both cytoplasm and nucleus (PubMed:37126322, 33002410). These condensates localize to plasma membrane-associated structures when complexed with receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) and PLCγ1 (PubMed:35231400). Wild-type SHP2 exhibits phase separation only under specific stimuli or in open conformations, while disease mutants spontaneously form condensates at lower critical concentrations (PubMed:33002410). The material state remains predominantly liquid, though ternary complexes show slower dynamics (PubMed:33002410, 35231400).
Functional Summary: SHP2 condensates serve dual physiological-pathological roles: In ternary complexes with RTKs and PLCγ1, they form signaling hubs that enhance kinase/phospholipase activities while suppressing SHP2 phosphatase function, facilitating calcium release and PKCβII/AKT activation (PubMed:35231400). Pathologically, mutant condensates constitutively hyperactivate Ras/Raf/MAPK signaling, driving epileptogenesis in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy and contributing to RASopathies/cancers (PubMed:37126322, 33002410). Mutant SHP2 recruits/activates wild-type protein within condensates, amplifying pathological signaling despite catalytic impairments (PubMed:33002410).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by two key domains: 1) The catalytic PTP domain (residues 221-528) drives self-assembly via electrostatic surfaces, particularly a positively charged patch (R362/K364) essential for multivalency (PubMed:33002410); and 2) Tandem SH2 domains (residues 1-221) mediate partner-dependent LLPS through phosphotyrosine interactions (PubMed:35231400). Pathogenic mutations (G503R, E76K, R498L, Y279C) promote constitutive phase separation by stabilizing open conformations (PubMed:37126322, 33002410). Key residue mutations (R32A/R138A in SH2 domains) disrupt phase separation capacity (PubMed:35231400).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SHP2 phase separation is extrinsically modulated by multiple partners: It co-phase separates with phosphorylated RTKs including FGFR2, EGFR, Her2, Her4, and VEGFR1 via SH2 domain interactions, forming membrane-localized condensates (PubMed:35231400). PLCγ1 stabilizes ternary complexes, altering material properties (PubMed:35231400). Disease mutants recruit wild-type SHP2 into condensates, amplifying signaling (PubMed:33002410). Small molecule ET070 inhibits LLPS by stabilizing closed conformations, while phosphorylation of RTK partners (e.g., FGFR2 Y769) is essential for complex assembly (PubMed:33002410, 35231400).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NCOA4 undergoes both self-driven phase separation in response to iron, forming solid-like cytoplasmic condensates, and heterotypic phase separation with FTH1, forming liquid-like cytoplasmic condensates (PubMed:35318808, 36066504, 39988734). These condensates exhibit dynamic properties including fusion/fission events but display limited fluorescence recovery in FRAP assays, consistent with solid-like behavior in iron-induced states (PubMed:35318808). The protein exclusively localizes to cytoplasmic condensates not classified as canonical membrane-less organelles (PubMed:36066504, 35318808, 39988734).
Functional Summary: Phase separation enables iron homeostasis through ferritinophagy: heterotypic NCOA4-FTH1 condensates facilitate ferritin degradation via both macroautophagy and endosomal microautophagy, releasing stored iron during deficiency (PubMed:36066504). Iron-induced self-assembly serves dual regulatory roles—sequestering NCOA4 from ferritin during early iron repletion to prevent toxicity, while delivering ferritin to lysosomes via noncanonical autophagy during prolonged repletion to avert deficiency (PubMed:35318808). Mechanically regulated phase separation controls ferroptosis sensitivity, where impaired condensate formation under low tension reduces iron release and confers cell death resistance (PubMed:39988734). Dysregulation through mutations (I56E/L63R) or domain deletions disrupts ferritin degradation, directly linking phase separation competence to cellular iron handling (PubMed:36066504, 35318808).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by the N-terminal coiled-coil domain (residues 1-182) enabling homodimerization and intrinsically disordered region 2 (IDR2) facilitating FTH1 binding (PubMed:36066504). For iron-induced self-assembly, the central IDR (residues 167-334) mediates iron binding and multivalency, while the C-terminal region (residues 523-614) provides essential scaffolding (PubMed:35318808). Critical mutations I56E and L63R in the coiled-coil domain disrupt homodimerization and abolish condensate formation (PubMed:36066504). Deletion of IDR (ΔIDR) or combined IDR/C-terminal deletion (ΔIDR+ΔC) significantly impairs iron-responsive phase separation (PubMed:35318808).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: NCOA4 phase separation is extrinsically regulated by FTH1, which co-phase separates to form heterotypic condensates essential for ferritin degradation (PubMed:36066504, 39988734). Iron (Fe(III)) ions act as primary scaffolds for self-driven condensation, directly binding the IDR at concentrations ≥5μM (PubMed:35318808). Mechanical tension modulates condensate formation, with high tension (stiff substrates/sparse cells) promoting NCOA4-FTH1 assembly while low tension (soft substrates/dense cells) reduces NCOA4 levels and suppresses phase separation (PubMed:39988734). TAX1BP1 co-localizes with condensates as a degradation adaptor but is dispensable for formation (PubMed:36066504).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: UBAP2L undergoes self-driven phase separation to form liquid-like stress granules in the cytoplasm, independently nucleating condensates under stress-null conditions at high concentrations and in the absence of G3BP1/2 (PubMed:32302570, 31114027, 31956030). It serves as a core structural component of stress granules across diverse stressors (arsenite, heat shock, ER stress), with its RGG motif recruiting mRNPs and ribosomal subunits (PubMed:31114027, 31956030). Material properties remain liquid-like without observed state transitions (PubMed:32302570, 31956030).
Functional Summary: UBAP2L phase separation orchestrates stress granule assembly and disassembly to stall mRNPs during diverse stresses (arsenite, osmotic shock, heat shock), facilitating cellular adaptation by sequestering mRNAs and ribosomal subunits (PubMed:31114027, 31956030). It acts upstream of G3BP1 to enable granule maturation and determines multiphase organization with P-bodies via DDX6 interactions, regulating mRNA availability during stress recovery (PubMed:32302570, 31956030). Delayed disassembly in UBAP2L-depleted cells disrupts mRNA management, implicating its condensation dynamics in stress response fidelity (PubMed:31114027).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by UBAP2L's RGG motif (aa 131–190), which mediates RNA-dependent recruitment of stress granule components and self-association as a valence multiplier, and the DUF domain (aa 495–526) that binds G3BP1/2 (PubMed:32302570, 31114027). Arginine methylation of the RGG motif by PRMT1 inhibits phase separation by blocking interactions with partners, while demethylation promotes condensation (PubMed:31114027). Mutations disrupting these domains—including RGG deletions (Δ131–190), DUF deletions (Δ495–526), or arginine-to-alanine substitutions (R131–190A)—abolish granule formation (PubMed:31114027).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: UBAP2L co-phase separates with G3BP1/2 in essential complexes for stress granule nucleation, requiring DUF-mediated binding (PubMed:32302570, 31114027). It recruits FXR1 to condensates independently of G3BP and partitions into FXR1-driven mRNA-protein networks (PubMed:32302570, 39106863). Interactions with DDX6 link stress granules to P-bodies, enabling hybrid condensate formation (PubMed:32302570). RNA acts as a critical scaffold, with polyadenylated mRNAs (e.g., NORAD) enriching in UBAP2L cores; cycloheximide-sensitive polysome disassembly is required for granule assembly (PubMed:31114027, 31956030). PRMT1 methylation inversely regulates condensation by modifying the RGG motif (PubMed:31114027).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TRF2 undergoes self-driven phase separation in the presence of nucleic acid scaffolds, forming dynamic condensates primarily in the nucleus (PubMed:35724929, 35077681). It associates with telomeric compartments and PML nuclear bodies (APBs) (PubMed:31171703, 35077681). Material states range from liquid-like droplets (exhibiting fusion and rapid FRAP recovery) to hydrogel/gel-like assemblies with reduced mobility, depending on nucleic acid length and complex composition (PubMed:35724929, 35077681). State transitions occur based on scaffold properties, with long telomeric DNA or full shelterin complexes promoting viscous/gel-like states (PubMed:35724929, 35077681).
Functional Summary: TRF2 condensates compartmentalize telomeres to exclude DNA damage response factors (e.g., RPA, MRN), suppressing ATM/ATR pathways and preventing telomeric fusions (PubMed:35077681). In alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT)-positive cancers, SUMOylation-driven APB formation enables telomere maintenance via mitotic DNA synthesis (MiDAS) (PubMed:31171703). hRap1 modulation ensures specificity for telomeric DNA, preventing aberrant phase separation with non-telomeric nucleic acids (PubMed:35724929). Dysregulated phase separation may contribute to telomere instability in disease contexts (PubMed:35077681).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal basic disordered region and C-terminal DNA-binding domain (DBD), which enable multivalent nucleic acid interactions (PubMed:35724929). Dimerization via the TRFH domain provides essential valency (PubMed:35724929, 35077681). SUMOylation at multiple lysine residues regulates APB recruitment and telomere clustering (PubMed:31171703). Deletions in the N-terminal acidic domain (ΔA), hinge region (ΔHinge), or disordered regions (ΔIDR) disrupt phase separation capacity (PubMed:35077681), while the basic domain governs TERRA RNA partitioning (PubMed:35077681).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Essential scaffolds include telomeric dsDNA repeats, ssDNA, ssRNA, and TERRA RNA, with phase separation exhibiting re-entrant behavior dependent on nucleic acid concentration and length (PubMed:35724929, 35077681). hRap1/RAP1 inhibits phase separation by weakening nucleic acid interactions, abolishing droplet formation at equimolar ratios (PubMed:35724929, 35077681). TRF2 drives multicomponent shelterin condensates incorporating POT1, TIN2, and TPP1 (PubMed:35077681). It partitions into polySUMO/polySIM condensates via SUMO-SIM interactions (PubMed:31171703). Phase behavior is salt-sensitive, occurring at 50-150 mM KCl but suppressed at higher concentrations (PubMed:35724929).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Borealin (Q53HL2) undergoes phase separation as an essential scaffold component of the Chromosome Passenger Complex (CPC), requiring partners INCENP and Survivin for condensate formation (PubMed:37945831, 38456462, 31481798). It localizes to nuclear inner centromeres and spindle midzones, forming gel-like condensates that initially exhibit liquid-like properties but rapidly transition to an anisotropic hydrogel state within minutes (PubMed:37945831, 31481798). This phase separation enables CPC accumulation at inner centromeres, with material properties characterized by slow FRAP recovery (t½=99.71 s) and arrested fusion (PubMed:31481798).
Functional Summary: Borealin-mediated CPC phase separation is essential for error correction of kinetochore-microtubule attachments, sister chromatid cohesion, chromosome alignment, and mitotic fidelity (PubMed:37945831, 38456462, 31481798). Disruption via mutations (e.g., K143R or Δ139-160) or MLL1 inhibition causes chromosome misalignment, spindle multipolarity, aneuploidy, and genome instability (PubMed:37945831, 31481798). Pathologically, this process is critical for growth of CPC-high hepatocellular carcinomas, with irreversible gel transitions linked to mitotic defects and cellular viability loss (PubMed:37945831, 31481798).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by two critical regions: 1) a central intrinsically disordered region (IDR, aa 130-160) containing charged residues essential for LLPS, where CDK1 phosphorylation reduces saturation concentration from 10 µM to 8 µM (PubMed:31481798); and 2) N-terminal salt-bridge residues (K26, K37, K63) that form electrostatic interactions with INCENP (PubMed:38456462). Methylation at K143 within the IDR by MLL1 lowers saturation concentration and stabilizes condensates (PubMed:37945831). Disruptive mutations include K143R (abolishes methylation), V142W (blocks methylation), charge-reversal mutations (K26E/K37E/K63E), and alanine substitutions (R139A/K141A etc.) or deletion (Δ139-160) in the IDR (PubMed:37945831, 38456462, 31481798).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Key extrinsic regulators include CPC complex partners INCENP and Survivin, which co-phase separate with Borealin to form the condensate scaffold through complementary salt-bridges (e.g., Borealin K26/K37/K63 with INCENP D27/E36/E42) (PubMed:38456462, 31481798). The MLL1 core complex partitions into condensates and methylates Borealin at K143, enhancing phase separation (PubMed:37945831). Phosphorylated HP1α enriches in droplets and reduces saturation concentration to 3.5 µM, while α-satellite DNA induces phase separation at sub-saturation concentrations (PubMed:31481798). Aurora B is recruited as a client protein to the condensates (PubMed:38456462).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: MAVS undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro and in vivo, forming dynamic liquid-like condensates primarily in the cytoplasm (PubMed:37188808, 34239064). It associates with 'Mitochondrial MAVS signaling platforms' (PubMed:37188808) and is recruited to viral inclusion bodies during respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection (PubMed:36768473). No material state transitions were reported under tested conditions (PubMed:37188808).
Functional Summary: MAVS condensates form antiviral signaling platforms that recruit IRF3 and TBK1/IKKε, enabling interferon production and innate immune defense (PubMed:37188808, 34239064). Dysregulation occurs when viral proteins disrupt these condensates: SARS2-NP inhibits Lys63-linked ubiquitination and aggregation to suppress interferon-β production (PubMed:34239064), while RSV N protein sequesters MAVS in inclusion bodies to attenuate immune responses (PubMed:36768473). These disruptions enhance viral pathogenesis by enabling immune evasion (PubMed:34239064, 36768473).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the SIM motif within its CARD domain, enabling SUMO-SIM interactions essential for self-association (PubMed:37188808). SUMOylation at Lys461 and Lys500 enhances LLPS by promoting droplet formation, size, fusion, and recovery dynamics (PubMed:37188808). The SIM3A mutation (valine/isoleucine to alanine substitutions) impairs self-association and condensate formation (PubMed:37188808).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: MAVS phase separation is modulated by viral partners: the RSV N protein recruits MAVS into viral inclusion bodies to suppress interferon signaling (PubMed:36768473), while SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein (SARS2-NP) disrupts MAVS condensates to inhibit antiviral responses (PubMed:34239064). The RIG-I N-terminal domain (RIG-IN) enhances LLPS by lowering the saturation concentration for droplet formation (PubMed:37188808). MAVS recruits IRF3 to condensates via SIM-mediated interactions, optimizing immune signaling kinetics (PubMed:37188808).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PABPN1 (Q86U42) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in the nucleus, forming dynamic liquid-like condensates primarily within nuclear speckles (PubMed:37422193, 38381607, 38811444). Its phase behavior is modulated by polyalanine tract length: wild-type (10A) and shorter variants form reversible liquid droplets, while expanded variants (24A/31A) undergo pathological liquid-to-solid transitions into insoluble aggregates with reduced mobility (PubMed:37422193). This protein associates with nuclear speckles and forms distinct subcompartments enriched with SON and U2 snRNA (PubMed:38381607). LLPS is RNA-dependent for physiological condensation but becomes RNA-independent in aggregation-prone states (PubMed:37422193, 38811444).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, PABPN1 LLPS represses proximal alternative polyadenylation (APA) sites to regulate 3' UTR length and mRNA processing (PubMed:38811444). Pathologically, polyalanine expansion-induced aggregation sequesters CFIm25, disrupting alternative polyadenylation (e.g., reduced distal PAS usage in PAK1) and contributing to oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy (OPMD) (PubMed:37422193). SNRNP70-mediated liquid-to-solid transitions exacerbate this dysregulation (PubMed:36073763). In colorectal cancer, SNRPD2-disrupted LLPS promotes shortened CTNNBIP1 3' UTRs, driving proliferation and migration (PubMed:38811444). SON-associated subcompartments suggest additional roles in splicing regulation through selective client enrichment (PubMed:38381607).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by three key domains: (1) The polyalanine tract length directly controls material state, where expansions beyond 17 alanines (24A/31A) drive aggregation (PubMed:37422193); (2) The RNA recognition motif (RRM) domain (residues 215-217) is essential for RNA binding and initial condensation, with mutations (F215A/Y217A) abolishing droplet formation (PubMed:37422193); (3) The glutamic acid-proline-rich (EP) domain (residues 51-118) is critical for LLPS competence, as deletions (ΔEP) or glutamic-to-alanine mutations (EtoA) significantly impair droplet formation (PubMed:38811444).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Extrinsic regulation involves both cooperative and disruptive interactions: Poly(A) RNA acts as a primary scaffold, lowering saturation concentration and enabling cytoplasmic condensation upon exogenous delivery (PubMed:37422193). SNRNP70 co-phase separates with PABPN1 through its LC1 domain, driving pathological liquid-to-solid transitions (PubMed:36073763). Conversely, SNRPD2 disrupts LLPS by binding the EP domain, attenuating condensate formation (PubMed:38811444). PABPN1 selectively enriches within SON+ nuclear speckle subcompartments alongside SRSF1 and U1-70K, exhibiting viscoelastic properties (PubMed:38381607). Additionally, aggregates sequester CFIm25 via RNA-mediated association, impairing mRNA processing (PubMed:37422193).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SERBP1 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) both in vitro and in vivo, forming biomolecular condensates (PubMed:34270902, 34631798, 39937575). It localizes to the cytoplasm and nucleus, associating with stress granules and nucleoli under basal and stress conditions (PubMed:39937575). In Alzheimer's disease, it accumulates in pathological Tau aggregates and stress granules (PubMed:39937575). Condensates exhibit liquid-like properties including reversibility with temperature changes (PubMed:34270902), dynamic recovery in FRAP assays (PubMed:34631798), and sensitivity to ionic conditions (PubMed:34631798), though pathological contexts show evidence of increased condensation and aggregation (PubMed:39937575).
Functional Summary: SERBP1 phase separation facilitates physiological roles in translation regulation, ribosome biogenesis, and stress response through stress granule and nucleolar recruitment (PubMed:39937575). In Alzheimer's disease, pathological condensation within Tau aggregates and stress granules sequesters small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) and essential factors, impairing ribosome biogenesis and translation (PubMed:39937575). This dysfunction is exacerbated by PARP1 hyperactivity and PARylation, forming a pathogenic feedback loop that contributes to cellular degeneration (PubMed:39937575).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by large intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) containing arginine-glycine-glycine (RGG) and arginine-glycine (RG) motifs that mediate electrostatic interactions and nucleic acid binding (PubMed:39937575, 34270902, 34631798). Both RGG boxes within residues 149-400 are essential for efficient salt-independent condensation, with the N-terminal RGG box enabling RNA-modulated phase separation (PubMed:34631798). PARylation by PARP1 post-translationally regulates interaction networks and condensate properties (PubMed:39937575), while oligomerization observed in Alzheimer's disease brain lysates contributes to pathological aggregation (PubMed:39937575).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RNA critically modulates SERBP1 phase separation, enabling condensate formation at lower protein concentrations and altering droplet dynamics (PubMed:34631798, 39937575). Single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) with parallel G-quadruplex structure promotes co-phase separation (PubMed:34270902). Key protein partners include PARP1, which scaffolds condensate assembly through PARylation-enhanced interactions (PubMed:39937575); G3BP1 as a stress granule co-component (PubMed:39937575); and Tau within pathological aggregates (PubMed:39937575). Phase behavior is regulated by environmental factors: salt concentration (inhibited ≥150 mM NaCl) (PubMed:34631798), temperature (reversible at 37°C/4°C) (PubMed:34270902), cellular stress (e.g., arsenite/H₂O₂) (PubMed:39937575), and the G-quadruplex binder pyridostatin (PDS) which dissolves condensates (PubMed:34270902).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: LSM14A (Q8ND56) functions as a scaffold protein essential for P-body assembly and integrity in the cytoplasm, requiring partner proteins for phase separation rather than self-assembly (PubMed:37370689). It primarily associates with P-bodies and also partitions into MX2 condensates, which are dynamic, fusion-competent liquid-like biomolecular condensates (PubMed:37370689, 39389033). No material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: LSM14A-mediated P-body formation represses translation of oncogenic RAS mRNAs (KRAS/NRAS); P-body dissolution upon LSM14A depletion elevates RAS protein levels, driving MEK inhibitor resistance in cancer (PubMed:37370689). As a component of MX2 condensates, LSM14A contributes to antiviral defense by facilitating HIV-1 capsid trapping and HSV-1 genome disassembly, preventing viral nuclear entry (PubMed:39389033).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic drivers (e.g., domains, mutations, or PTMs) regulating LSM14A phase separation were identified in the provided studies; experiments focused solely on full-length protein behavior (PubMed:37370689, 39389033).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: LSM14A forms a core scaffold complex with DDX6 and EIF4ENIF1 (4E-T) in P-bodies, where co-depletion of these partners dissolves condensates (PubMed:37370689). It also associates as a client protein with MX2 condensates, which require scaffold partners NUP35, TNPO1, and SAMD4A for assembly and antiviral function (PubMed:39389033).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: ATXN2L undergoes self-driven phase separation via its C-terminal low-complexity domain (LCD), forming liquid-like condensates in the cytoplasm (PubMed:37369203). It also scaffolds neuronal RNP granules and stress granules, exhibiting scaffold-like properties with slow dynamics in vivo (PubMed:39419034, 38253057). Pathological polyQ expansions (>Q22) disrupt liquid-like behavior of client proteins, reducing mobility and increasing condensate viscosity (PubMed:39419034).
Functional Summary: ATXN2L maintains circadian translation amplitude, where depletion shortens free-running periods and reduces translation indexes by CT12 (PubMed:37369203). It enables axonal mRNA localization and translation, with polyQ expansions disrupting β-actin and Nefl mRNA transport, contributing to ALS pathogenesis (PubMed:39419034). In stress response, ATXN2L-mediated YBX1 recruitment to stress granules enhances radioresistance, while ATXN2L knockdown increases radiosensitivity (PubMed:38253057).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the C-terminal LCD (aa 875-1075), which is sufficient for in vitro droplet formation (PubMed:37369203). Pathological polyglutamine tract expansions beyond Q22 aberrantly sequester client proteins like TDP-43, fundamentally altering condensate dynamics and material properties (PubMed:39419034). The protein's LSm, LSmAD, and PAM2 motifs further contribute to its scaffolding function in RNP granules (PubMed:39419034).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: ATXN2L scaffolds TDP-43 in neuronal RNP granules, with polyQ expansions increasing co-localization and reducing TDP-43 mobility by over 50% (PubMed:39419034). It interacts with YBX1 to enhance stress granule recruitment and radioresistance, particularly following ionizing radiation (PubMed:38253057). ATXN2L also binds β-actin mRNA, with 75% of translating β-actin mRNA co-localizing in condensates, though polyQ expansions suppress this translational activity by over 60% (PubMed:39419034).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TopBP1 undergoes phase separation either by self-assembly (PubMed:33503405) or in complex with partners like pre-rRNA (PubMed:37582658), forming liquid-like condensates primarily in the nucleus. It associates with DNA damage foci, XY bodies in male germ cells, and stalled replication forks (PubMed:37582658, 38578830, 33503405). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties including droplet fusion, rapid FRAP recovery (~80% within 20 seconds), and reversibility upon stimulus removal, with no pathological liquid-to-solid transitions reported (PubMed:37582658, 33503405).
Functional Summary: TopBP1 condensates serve as reaction hubs for ATR-Chk1 signaling, concentrating ATR to phosphorylate Chk1 at interfacial regions and enforcing S-phase/G2/M checkpoints (PubMed:37582658, 38578830, 33503405). This coordinates DNA repair during replication stress, slows fork progression, and supports homologous recombination (PubMed:37582658, 33503405). Dysregulation—such as AAD mutations (M3R: R1113A/R1116A/R1118A)—uncouples condensation from Chk1 activation, causing checkpoint failure despite intact condensate formation (PubMed:38578830).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the ATR activation domain (AAD; residues 884-1522) and BRCT domains, where BRCT4-5 mediates RNA-dependent assembly (PubMed:37582658) and BRCT6-8 enables self-assembly (PubMed:33503405). Phosphorylation at S1138 by ATR creates a positive feedback loop enhancing condensation (PubMed:33503405). Critical residues W1145 and F1071 in the AAD are essential, as mutations (W1145R, F1071A) impair self-driven condensate formation (PubMed:33503405).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Key extrinsic regulators include pre-rRNA, which scaffolds TopBP1 condensation via direct binding to BRCT4-5 (KD ≈ 300 nM; PubMed:37582658), and ribosomal proteins (RPL7A, RPS3, FBL) that co-partition RNA-dependently (PubMed:37582658). DNA damage inducers like camptothecin trigger endogenous condensation (PubMed:38578830), while blue light activates optogenetic assembly (PubMed:38578830, 33503405). DNA fragments permeate condensates and promote nano-cluster organization (PubMed:33503405). FANCJ partitions within condensates and recruits BRCA1; mutations (S1273A, R1280Q) disrupt this recruitment (PubMed:38578830).

MLO Types: Nuclear pore complex; Nuclear speckle; Nucleolus; Stress granule
Overall Phase Separation Overview: Dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs) derived from C9ORF72 undergo self-driven phase separation (PubMed:28306503, 32730793) and modulate partner phase behavior (PubMed:35325178, 27768896, 39146246). They form liquid-like condensates in the nucleus and cytoplasm (PubMed:35325178, 28306503), associating with nucleoli (for poly-PR repeats ≥12), nuclear speckles (repeats <11), and stress granules (PubMed:35325178, 27768896). Material states range from reversible liquid droplets to irreversible solid aggregates during partner interactions (PubMed:35325178, 39146246).
Functional Summary: Pathological implications include: nuclear poly-PR disruption of NPM1-mediated ribosome biogenesis causing nucleolar toxicity (PubMed:35325178); cytoplasmic poly-GR/poly-PR induction of aberrant stress granules disrupting RNA metabolism (PubMed:27768896, 28306503); and PRMT1 sequestration leading to hypomethylation of RBPs (e.g., hnRNPA3) that promotes aggregation in C9-ALS/FTD (PubMed:39146246). Phase-separation-enabling repeat lengths (≥25 poly-PR) align with clinical toxicity thresholds (PubMed:32730793).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by dipeptide repeat length and composition: ≥9 repeats enable condensate formation, ≥12 drive nucleolar partitioning (PubMed:35325178), and critical thresholds (poly-PR25, poly-GA50) determine in vitro phase separation propensity (PubMed:32730793). The arginine-rich nature of poly-GR/poly-PR is fundamental for self-assembly and partner interactions (PubMed:28306503, 27768896).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Key extrinsic regulators include: 1) CRY2 scaffold enabling light-controlled reversible poly-PR condensation (PubMed:35325178); 2) RNA-binding proteins (hnRNPA1, TIA1) whose stress granule dynamics are disrupted by poly-GR/poly-PR (PubMed:27768896); and 3) PRMT1, which undergoes concentration- and length-dependent condensation into insoluble aggregates with poly-GR/poly-PR (PubMed:39146246), with poly-GR additionally impairing enzymatic activity as a substrate sink (PubMed:39146246).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: RBM14 undergoes self-driven phase separation via its prion-like domain (PLD) to form hydrogel-like structures with amyloid-like properties in vitro (PubMed:26283796). In cells, it forms biomolecular condensates in the nucleus and cytoplasm that dissolve upon 1,6-hexanediol treatment, indicating liquid-like properties (PubMed:37806532, 29932899). It consistently associates with paraspeckles across all studies (PubMed:37806532, 26283796, 29932899), with no observed material state transitions reported.
Functional Summary: RBM14 phase separation is essential for paraspeckle assembly, which regulates gene expression through nuclear RNA retention and transcription factor sequestration (PubMed:26283796, 29932899). In prostate cancer, it sustains androgen-responsive gene transcription (e.g., PSA) under androgen deprivation via condensate formation, promoting castration-resistant progression; disruption suppresses oncogenic expression (PubMed:37806532). Perturbations in RBM14 phase separation may link to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) pathobiology (PubMed:26283796).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by RBM14's prion-like domain (PLD, residues 350-669), which forms hydrogels dependent on tyrosine residues within [S/G]YG and Y[G/N/A/S]AQ repeat motifs; mutation of these tyrosines to serine disrupts hydrogel formation, paraspeckle targeting, and protein interactions (PubMed:26283796). An intrinsically disordered region (IDR) also contributes to condensate formation, with a dominant-negative splice variant (DN-Rbm14, residues 1-149) inhibiting this process (PubMed:37806532).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RBM14 co-phase separates with the scaffold protein NONO in paraspeckles, with their interaction being RNA-independent, mediated by the PLD, and disrupted by tyrosine mutations (PubMed:26283796, 29932899). It binds NEAT1_2 subdomains through NONO/SFPQ complexes, with interactions sensitive to 1,6-hexanediol (PubMed:29932899).
