While wild-type NELFE tentacle doesn't partition into MED1IDR condensates, an engineered 'blocky' variant with charge patterning gains partitioning capability (PubMed:36603581).
Functional Summary: Phase separation of the NELF complex containing NELFE drives stress-induced transcriptional downregulation by stabilizing promoter-proximally paused RNA Polymerase II at housekeeping genes, which is essential for cell survival under stress (PubMed:33548202). These condensates represent nuclear counterparts to cytosolic stress granules that coordinate global stress responses (PubMed:33548202). Artificially engineered partitioning of the 'blocky' NELFE variant into MED1IDR condensates mislocalizes the NELF complex, repressing transcription and demonstrating functional consequences of aberrant compartmentalization (PubMed:36603581).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of NELFE is intrinsically regulated by its intrinsically disordered tentacle domain (residues 139-380), which is necessary and sufficient for NELF complex condensation through heterotypic interactions with NELFA's IDR (PubMed:33548202). Deletion of this domain (Δ139-380) abolishes phase separation (PubMed:33548202). Charge patterning within the tentacle domain is a critical determinant: engineered 'blocky' variants with alternating charge blocks gain partitioning capability into MED1IDR condensates, unlike the wild-type sequence (PubMed:36603581).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: NELFE co-phase separates exclusively as part of the heterotetrameric NELF complex with partners NELFA, NELFB, and NELFC (PubMed:33548202). Complex condensation is regulated antagonistically by post-translational modifications: SUMOylation mediated by ZNF451/UBC9 promotes condensation, while phosphorylation by P-TEFb (CDK9) inhibits it by weakening intermolecular interactions and increasing mobility (PubMed:33548202). NELF condensates enrich S5-phosphorylated RNA Polymerase II CTD with distal non-consensus repeats and are dissolved by 1,6-hexanediol treatment (PubMed:33548202). The engineered 'blocky' NELFE variant partitions into MED1IDR condensates as a client (PubMed:36603581).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: XRCC1 (P18887) does not undergo self-driven phase separation (class: PS-other) but partitions into condensates through partner-dependent mechanisms. It forms inhomogeneous multiphase assemblies primarily driven by poly(ADP-ribose) (PAR), localizing into PARP1 condensates where it exhibits enhanced enrichment upon PARylation (PubMed:39496836, 36361989). XRCC1 co-phase separates with FUS in PAR-containing systems and forms distinct multiphase structures with DNA ligase III (LIG3) (PubMed:39496836, 36361989).
Functional Summary: XRCC1 condensates organize DNA repair machinery, enhancing DNA ligation efficiency through multiphase assemblies with LIG3 (PubMed:39496836). PAR-dependent coassemblies with FUS propose a role in damage-site organization, potentially facilitating DNA repair complex formation (PubMed:36361989).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or structural features driving XRCC1 phase separation are reported in the provided studies (PubMed:39496836, 36361989).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: XRCC1 phase separation is extrinsically regulated by nucleic acids and protein partners. PAR chains are essential for inducing its microphase separation and co-assembly with FUS (PubMed:36361989). PARP1 acts as a scaffold for XRCC1 partitioning, with PARylation enhancing enrichment ~2-fold (PubMed:39496836). XRCC1 forms functional multiphase condensates with LIG3 and co-localizes with FUS in shared droplets under PAR-rich conditions (PubMed:39496836, 36361989).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Nucleolin (NCL) undergoes phase separation primarily within the nucleolus, where it functions as a structural component (PubMed:36150385, 34515347, 39108718). Its phase separation behavior is classified as PS-other, requiring partners rather than self-assembly (PubMed:34515347, 36150385). Nucleolin partitions into nuclear condensates through domain-specific mechanisms, with its glycine-arginine rich (GAR) domain contributing to localization while RNA recognition motifs (RRMs) dominate phase separation stability (PubMed:34515347). It forms liquid-like condensates, evidenced by rapid FRAP recovery when its intrinsically disordered region (IDR) functionally rescues defects in other nucleolar proteins (PubMed:39108718). These condensates undergo dissolution upon ssRNA accumulation (PubMed:36150385).
Functional Summary: Nucleolin phase separation is essential for nucleolar integrity and function. Dissolution of its condensates by ssRNA accumulation impairs nucleolar organization (PubMed:36150385). Through heterotypic interactions, it contributes to mitotic organization via recruitment to Ki-67 condensates in the perichromosomal layer (PubMed:37813838). Critically, its phase separation capability maintains ribosome biogenesis and prevents proteotoxic stress, as demonstrated by rescue of protein synthesis deficits, reduced p53 activation, and improved cell survival when its IDR compensates for FBL defects in neural progenitor cells (PubMed:39108718). Impairment of these phase separation functions links to ribosomopathy-like defects including protein synthesis deficiency and developmental delays (PubMed:39108718).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of nucleolin is intrinsically regulated by its glycine-arginine rich (GAR) domain, an intrinsically disordered region (IDR) essential for nucleolar partitioning (PubMed:34515347). Deletion of this domain (ΔGAR) significantly reduces nucleolar localization while maintaining nuclear presence (PubMed:34515347). The RNA recognition motifs (RRMs) play a dominant role in maintaining phase separation stability under stress conditions (PubMed:34515347). The functional importance of the GAR domain as a phase separation driver is confirmed by its ability to replace the IDR of FBL and rescue nucleolar phase separation defects in mutant cells (PubMed:39108718).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Nucleolin phase separation is modulated by RNA and protein partners. Single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) dissolves nucleolar condensates, as demonstrated by microinjection reducing nucleolin intensity by ~50% (PubMed:36150385). Nucleolin co-assembles with Ki-67 in phosphorylation-dependent condensates, forming liquid-like foci observable in optoDroplet systems (PubMed:37813838). This co-assembly occurs alongside nucleophosmin (NPM1) within heterotypic condensates (PubMed:37813838). Nucleolin's IDR serves as a functional phase separation motif that rescues defects in FBL when swapped, indicating cooperative interactions with nucleolar components (PubMed:39108718).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TRIM21 (P19474) exhibits dual phase separation-related behaviors. It undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro and forms dynamic liquid-like cytoplasmic puncta in human cells, primarily driven by its coiled-coil domain (PubMed:37879251). Alternatively, under oxidative stress, it associates with membrane-less organelles (MLOs) like stress granules (SGs) in the cytoplasm without undergoing phase separation itself, instead regulating G3BP1 condensation through ubiquitination (PubMed:36692217).
Functional Summary: TRIM21 phase separation promotes autophagosome nucleation and autophagy activation, leading to reduced p62 levels, increased LC3-II conversion, and inhibition of cell proliferation (PubMed:37879251). Alternatively, through G3BP1 ubiquitination, TRIM21 regulates stress granule homeostasis, preventing pathological SG accumulation linked to neurodegenerative diseases like ALS-FTD and supporting cell survival (PubMed:36692217).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The coiled-coil (CC) domain (residues 80-220) is the primary intrinsic driver of TRIM21 phase separation, containing predicted low-complexity disordered regions essential for condensate formation. Deletion of this domain (ΔCC) completely abolishes phase separation capability (PubMed:37879251).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TRIM21 interacts with G3BP1 under oxidative stress, inhibiting its phase separation via K63-linked ubiquitination (PubMed:36692217). During autophagy-related phase separation, TRIM21 co-localizes with LC3B in cytoplasmic puncta, though LC3B's direct role in modulating phase separation remains unspecified (PubMed:37879251).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TFE3 undergoes self-driven phase separation to form liquid-like condensates in the nucleus (PubMed:35293953, 33290695). These condensates exhibit low fusion propensity and are associated with transcriptional condensates (PubMed:35293953). Under cellular stress, TFE3 forms nuclear puncta (PubMed:33290695). No material state transitions were reported in these studies.
Functional Summary: TFE3 phase separation is associated with transcriptional condensates, suggesting a role in transcriptional regulation (PubMed:35293953). However, specific functional consequences were not detailed in the provided studies (PubMed:35293953, 33290695).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of TFE3 is driven by its full-length protein structure, as both studies utilized full-length constructs and observed self-assembly without identifying specific domains, mutations, or post-translational modifications as regulators (PubMed:35293953, 33290695).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TFE3 phase separation is unaffected by the protein partner IPMK, as co-addition in vitro did not inhibit droplet formation and cellular depletion did not alter puncta formation (PubMed:33290695). The compounds Ro-3306 and vanillic acid, which modulate related proteins, show no effect on TFE3 condensate properties (PubMed:35293953).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TBP (P20226) undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self), forming liquid-like condensates primarily in the nucleus, where it associates with transcriptional condensates (PubMed:32386547). In vitro, phase separation requires molecular crowding agents like dextran to form liquid droplets, otherwise forming fiber-like aggregates (PubMed:34916619). Pathological glutamine repeat expansion (53Q) inhibits its phase separation capacity (PubMed:32386547).
Functional Summary: TBP phase separation compartmentalizes Pol II CTD within transcriptional condensates, facilitating efficient transcription (PubMed:34916619). Dysregulation, particularly inhibition of phase separation by pathological glutamine repeat expansion (53Q), disrupts transcriptional condensate formation and is linked to spinocerebellar ataxia type 17 (SCA17) (PubMed:32386547).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by TBP's intrinsically disordered region (IDR) (PubMed:32386547). Pathological mutations, specifically the glutamine repeat expansion (53Q) within the IDR, disrupt phase separation (PubMed:32386547). The protein's high intrinsic disorder content (51% IDR) further supports phase separation propensity (PubMed:34916619).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TBP co-phase separates with the scaffold protein PSPC1, forming larger condensates that enhance incorporation of Pol II C-terminal domain (CTD) (PubMed:34916619). Phase separation is critically dependent on extrinsic crowding agents (e.g., 10% dextran) to achieve liquid-like states in vitro (PubMed:34916619).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PTBP1 (P26599) undergoes RNA-dependent liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro, classified as partner-driven phase separation (PS-other) (PubMed:34916619, 29425497). It forms droplets that incorporate RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain (Pol II CTD) and requires RNA scaffolds for assembly. Phase separation is enhanced by macromolecular crowding agents (BSA, PEG) and fusion with intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) (PubMed:29425497). Subcellular locations and membrane-less organelle associations are not specified in the provided data.
Functional Summary: PTBP1 phase separation enhances RNA polymerase II engagement with DNA templates, promoting transcriptional regulation in vitro (PubMed:34916619). This behavior provides a model system for studying ribonucleoprotein (RNP) granule assembly mechanisms driven by specific protein-RNA interactions (PubMed:29425497). The crowding-enhanced phase separation demonstrates how cellular environments modulate biomolecular condensate formation (PubMed:29425497).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is driven by PTBP1's RNA-binding domains that facilitate specific RNA interactions (PubMed:29425497). The full-length protein contains substantial intrinsically disordered regions (41% IDR), which contribute to its phase separation propensity (PubMed:34916619). Fusion experiments demonstrate that heterologous IDRs from FUS or Pub1 significantly lower the concentration threshold required for phase separation (PubMed:29425497).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RNA is an essential scaffold for PTBP1 phase separation, with both total RNA and poly-pyrimidine RNA serving as critical partners in droplet formation (PubMed:34916619, 29425497). Macromolecular crowding agents (BSA, PEG, Ficoll) dramatically enhance phase separation efficiency (PubMed:29425497). PTBP1 also interacts functionally with Pol II CTD, with its droplets incorporating this domain to enhance DNA binding (PubMed:34916619).

Gene Names: APEX1 APE APE1 APEX APX HAP1 REF1
Overall Phase Separation Overview: APE1 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in the nucleus, forming liquid-like condensates specifically in the nucleolus of cancer cells, which recruit ATR, TopBP1, and ETAA1 to activate DNA damage response pathways (PubMed:36200829). It also associates with stress granules in the cytoplasm under oxidative stress, though it does not autonomously phase separate in this context (PubMed:38436697). No material state transitions are reported.
Functional Summary: APE1 nucleolar condensates activate the ATR-Chk1 pathway, suppressing rRNA transcription, inducing S/G₂ cell-cycle arrest, elevating DNA damage, and reducing cancer cell viability (PubMed:36200829). In stress granules, it promotes cell survival under oxidative stress and chemoresistance in ovarian cancer via redox-dependent regulation (PubMed:38436697). By scaffolding KAT6A phase separation, APE1 facilitates PARP1 sequestration from DNA damage sites, driving PARP inhibitor resistance; disrupting this process restores drug sensitivity (PubMed:38973255).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: APE1's intrinsic phase separation is driven by its N-terminal NT33 motif (residues 1-33) and a W119 residue within its putative ATR activation domain (AA104-134) (PubMed:36200829). The ΔNT33 deletion abolishes LLPS, while the W119R mutation disrupts nucleolar condensation. The K6R/K7R mutation impairs nuclear localization, a prerequisite for condensation (PubMed:36200829). Additionally, its redox domain (C65) regulates stress granule promotion without autonomous phase separation (PubMed:38436697).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: APE1 nucleolar condensates recruit ATR, TopBP1, and ETAA1 to activate DNA damage response pathways, while co-localizing with NPM1 (PubMed:36200829). In stress granules, APE1 scaffolds YBX1 phosphorylation by PLK1 to enhance YBX1 phase separation and co-localizes with G3BP1 under oxidative stress (PubMed:38436697). APE1 also acts as an essential scaffold for KAT6A phase separation, facilitating KAT6A-PARP1 interaction and condensate formation in PARP inhibitor-resistant cells (PubMed:38973255). DNA/RNA can bypass NT33 dependence in vitro (PubMed:36200829).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TEAD1 (P28347) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but co-phase separates with partner proteins, primarily in the nucleus (PubMed:37788668, 36732631, 31792379, 38784009). It associates with transcriptional condensates and nuclear membrane-less organelles where it exhibits liquid-like material properties, including rapid FRAP recovery and droplet fusion (PubMed:36732631, 31792379). However, under specific conditions, these condensates display viscous properties and resistance to dissolution by aliphatic alcohols (PubMed:38784009).
Functional Summary: TEAD1 condensates function as transcriptional hubs, concentrating transcription machinery (RNA Pol II, BRD4) to activate proliferation genes including Ctgf and Cyr61 (PubMed:31792379, 38784009). In ARID1A condensates, TEAD1 enables chromatin remodeling and enhancer accessibility (PubMed:37788668). Pathologically, TEAD1 recruitment into YAP fusion condensates drives ependymoma tumorigenesis by activating oncogenic pathways (HIPPO, MYC) while excluding repressive complexes like PRC2 (PubMed:36732631). Condensate dissolution via TEAD1 inhibitors reduces transcriptional output (PubMed:38784009).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No specific intrinsic domains or mutations driving TEAD1 phase separation are reported. TEAD1 lacks autonomous phase separation capability, requiring partners for condensation even at concentrations up to 20 μM (PubMed:38784009).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TEAD1 phase separation is extrinsically regulated by scaffold proteins including YAP, which enables co-phase separation in vitro and stabilizes nuclear condensates (PubMed:38784009). It is recruited into ARID1A-containing condensates where it functions as a client for genomic targeting (PubMed:37788668). Under hyperosmotic stress, TEAD1 co-localizes with YAP/TAZ condensates within seconds (PubMed:31792379). In oncogenic contexts, TEAD1 concentrates within YAP fusion condensates alongside transcriptional co-activators like BRD4 and MED1 (PubMed:36732631).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: CLIP1 (P30622) undergoes self-driven phase separation to form liquid-like condensates both in vitro and in vivo within the cytoplasm (PubMed:37603768, 34890409). These condensates associate with microtubule plus-end networks (+TIP networks) and form cytoplasmic patches/droplets exhibiting dynamic properties including fusion, fission, and rapid molecular exchange (PubMed:37603768, 34890409). In vitro condensates show higher viscosity with slower fusion kinetics compared to in vivo droplets, and tubulin enrichment creates anisotropic core-shell structures (PubMed:37603768). No pathological material state transitions are reported, though cellular trailing foci dissolve dynamically (PubMed:37603768).
Functional Summary: Phase separation enables spatial concentration of tubulin at microtubule tips, accelerating growth rates to 3.5-3.6 µm/min and reducing catastrophe events, thereby regulating microtubule dynamics (PubMed:37603768). It forms a dynamic 'polymerization chaperone' scaffold that stabilizes microtubule ends and organizes +TIP networks (PubMed:34890409). Aberrant phase separation is suggested to have pathological relevance analogous to Tau proteinopathies in neurodegeneration, though specific disease mechanisms remain to be fully elucidated (PubMed:34890409).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the C-terminal region, specifically the coiled-coil and zinc-knuckle domains that enable dimerization and are essential for robust condensation (PubMed:37603768). Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) in the N-terminal serine-rich domain and C-terminal region adjacent to zinc knuckles also contribute, with the second zinc-knuckle motif and free C-terminus being critical for functionality (PubMed:34890409). Dimerization via the coiled-coil domain is required for phase separation competence, as monomeric constructs (H1 mutant) fail to form droplets while dimeric forms (H2 mutant) exhibit weak LLPS (PubMed:37603768). C-terminal modifications (e.g., mEmerald/GSSG tags) abolish phase separation, while native C-terminus restoration rescues condensate formation (PubMed:34890409).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: CLIP1 exhibits synergistic co-condensation with EB proteins including EB3 and EB1, where EB3 acts as an essential co-condenser that increases dense-phase partitioning and forms homogeneous droplets (PubMed:37603768, 34890409). This interaction requires EB3's C-terminal tyrosine residue, as EB3-ΔY mutation abolishes co-condensation (PubMed:37603768). Tubulin is enriched at the droplet interface (40× concentration) and functions as a client protein recruited independently of microtubule polymerization (PubMed:37603768, 34890409). Multiple +TIP network components including p150, LIS1, CLASP1/2, and mDia2 partition into condensates, while stress granule markers (YB1), RNP granule components (hnRNPA1/Staufen1), and RNA are excluded (PubMed:34890409).

MLO Types: Cytoplasmic Nucleoporin Granule; Nuclear body; Nuclear pore complex
Overall Phase Separation Overview: NUP214 undergoes partner-dependent phase separation in distinct subcellular compartments. In the nucleus, it forms phase-separated nuclear bodies that co-localize with HOX-B clusters, requiring CRM1 as an essential scaffold (PubMed:37516964). In the cytoplasm, it forms liquid-like cytoplasmic nucleoporin granules (CNGs) exhibiting fusion, fission, and 1,6-hexanediol reversibility, occurring upon downregulation of FXR proteins (PubMed:32706158). These condensates associate with nuclear bodies and CNGs respectively, with no reported material state transitions.
Functional Summary: Phase separation has context-dependent physiological and pathological consequences. Nuclear condensates recruit MLL1 to HOX clusters, driving aberrant gene activation in leukemia (PubMed:37516964). Cytoplasmic granules cause nuclear envelope defects, impair protein export, sequester CRM1, disrupt cell cycle progression (S-phase accumulation), and contribute to fragile X syndrome pathology when FXR regulation fails (PubMed:32706158).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by FG repeat domains mediating multivalent hydrophobic interactions. For nuclear bodies, FG repeats in the NUP214 moiety are essential for phase separation (PubMed:37516964). Similarly, cytoplasmic granule formation relies on FG repeats within FG-nucleoporins including NUP214 for condensate cohesion (PubMed:32706158). No disease-associated mutations or PTMs regulating this behavior were reported.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is extrinsically regulated by specific protein partners and cellular conditions. Nuclear body formation absolutely requires CRM1 as a scaffold protein, with inhibition disrupting condensate stability (PubMed:37516964). Cytoplasmic granule formation is triggered by downregulation of FXR1/FXR2/FMRP proteins and involves dynein-mediated transport machinery (PubMed:32706158). NUP214 recruits MLL1 to nuclear condensates as a client protein, while cytoplasmic granules sequester CRM1 when mislocalized.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: BRCA1 does not undergo self-driven phase separation (class: PS-other) but exhibits context-dependent behavior in the nucleus. It is depleted from chromocenters under normal conditions, though DNA-binding domain fusions reverse this to enrichment (PubMed:36092926). Additionally, it partitions as a client into TopBP1 biomolecular condensates associated with DNA damage foci (PubMed:38578830). Material states and transitions are not specified.
Functional Summary: BRCA1's distribution modulates DNA accessibility in heterochromatin, supporting homologous recombination repair (PubMed:36092926). Its partitioning into TopBP1 condensates at DNA damage foci positions it for DNA repair processes like homologous recombination, particularly during replication stress or damage responses facilitated by FANCJ-mediated recruitment (PubMed:38578830).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features driving BRCA1 phase separation were identified in the provided studies. Both papers explicitly report no specified key drivers for BRCA1's behavior (PubMed:36092926, 38578830).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: BRCA1 partitioning is extrinsically regulated by partners. It requires FANCJ as a mediator for recruitment into TopBP1 biomolecular condensates, with defective FANCJ-TopBP1 interaction (e.g., S1273A/R1280Q mutants) reducing partitioning (PubMed:38578830). It also co-partitions with TopBP1 scaffold condensates at DNA damage sites (PubMed:38578830). No additional chemical or ionic regulators were reported.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Coilin (P38432) undergoes phase separation as a scaffolding component essential for Cajal body (CB) formation, concentrating regulatory RNAs and RNPs in the nucleus (PubMed:39602297, 36224177). It exhibits dynamic, liquid-like properties with rapid exchange kinetics (~1 minute residence time) in CBs (PubMed:39602297). While primarily nuclear, coilin forms fibrillar structures in the cytoplasm that transition to punctate nuclear condensates via Nopp140-mediated remodeling (PubMed:36224177). The protein is excluded from nucleoli and requires its N-terminal domain (NTD) for multivalent interactions driving CB assembly (PubMed:39602297, 36224177).
Functional Summary: Coilin phase separation enables CB assembly, optimizing snRNP/snoRNP maturation, histone mRNA processing, and genomic locus organization (PubMed:39602297, 36224177). Disruption (e.g., via R8A/D79A mutations) impairs CB formation, causing RNA processing defects (PubMed:36224177). Pathological DMA dysregulation in coilin-SMN interactions contributes to spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), while broader CB dysfunction links to diseases with RNA processing defects (PubMed:34115980, 34161763, 39602297).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal domain (NTD; residues 1-90), which mediates higher-order multimerization essential for condensation (PubMed:36224177). Specific residues are critical: R8 and D79 enable self-association and fibril formation, while R36 facilitates Nopp140 binding (PubMed:36224177). Central IDR and C-terminal regions lack autonomous condensation capacity (PubMed:36224177). Methylation may regulate interactions, though not experimentally confirmed (PubMed:39602297).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Nopp140 (NOLC1) extrinsically regulates coilin by remodeling cytoplasmic fibrils into nuclear puncta and enabling CB assembly; its depletion eliminates condensates (PubMed:36224177). Coilin partitions into SMN Tudor-domain condensates via dimethylarginine (DMA)-modified interactions, facilitating Cajal body-gem docking (PubMed:34115980). Within CBs, coilin co-concentrates with snRNP proteins (e.g., SNRPD3) and RNAs (snRNAs/snoRNAs) (PubMed:39602297). TOR signaling indirectly modulates coilin condensates through SMN phosphorylation (PubMed:34161763).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Eps15 undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self), forming liquid-like condensates in vitro (PubMed:33820972, 39914390). It localizes to the cytoplasm and forms dynamic membrane domains through co-assembly with Fcho1/2 proteins, though it is not associated with known membrane-less organelles (PubMed:33820972). Under strong blue light, Eps15 condensates undergo a liquid-to-solid transition characterized by loss of fusion, slowed fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), and spherical morphology (PubMed:33820972).
Functional Summary: Liquid-like Eps15-Fcho1/2 assemblies catalyze clathrin-mediated endocytosis by enabling dynamic protein rearrangement during vesicle budding (PubMed:33820972). Solid-like assemblies formed under strong light stall vesicle budding due to restricted molecular exchange, impairing cellular function (PubMed:33820972). Eps15 condensates show no actin-binding or -bundling capabilities, indicating functional specificity distinct from cytoskeletal regulation (PubMed:39914390).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by multivalent interactions involving N-terminal EH domains, a coiled-coil (CC) domain essential for dimerization/oligomerization, and a disordered C-terminal region containing DPF motifs (PubMed:33820972, 39914390). Deletion of the CC domain (ΔCC), EH domains (Δ3xEH), or C-terminal disordered region (ΔCTD) abolishes phase separation, while DPF→APA point mutations significantly reduce but do not eliminate condensate formation (PubMed:33820972).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Eps15 requires scaffold proteins Fcho1 and Fcho2 for co-phase separation on phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate [PtdIns(4,5)P₂]-containing membranes, forming dynamic protein-rich domains with rapid FRAP recovery (t₁/₂=19 s) (PubMed:33820972). Material state is modulated by light intensity: low light promotes liquid-like properties (fusion in seconds; FRAP t₁/₂=26 s), while strong blue light (50 µW) induces a solid-like state with stalled dynamics (PubMed:33820972).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: WASP (P42768) undergoes phase separation in distinct cellular contexts, displaying compartment-specific behaviors. In the nucleus, it forms liquid-like condensates via optogenetic tools that associate with nuclear speckles, clustering with SRSF2, RNA polymerase II, and nascent RNA; these droplets exhibit liquid properties including fusion and rapid FRAP recovery, and dissolve upon 1,6-hexanediol treatment (PubMed:35752626). In the cytoplasm, WASP is recruited into LAT biomolecular condensates at the immunological synapse via Nck, where it binds F-actin through its basic region (PubMed:31268421). No material state transitions were reported across studies.
Functional Summary: Phase separation enables context-dependent physiological functions. Nuclear condensates organize splicing machinery (SRSF2, Pol II, nascent RNA), with WASP deficiency causing aberrant splicing via dysregulated SRSF2 mobility (PubMed:35752626). Cytoplasmic condensation at the immunological synapse enhances actin clutch efficiency, enabling directional movement of LAT condensates across actin networks for T cell activation; this requires dynamic compositional changes including Nck dissociation during radial traversal (PubMed:31268421).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by distinct structural determinants in each compartment. Nuclear condensation requires the full-length protein, as isolated N- or C-terminal intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) are insufficient despite predicted multivalency (PScore≥4) (PubMed:35752626). Cytoplasmic function depends critically on the basic region (aa 186-200), where charge density governs actin binding affinity: doubled basic residues enhance binding while neutral mutations abolish it (PubMed:31268421).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Extrinsic partners drive compartment-specific condensation. In the nucleus, WASP co-condenses with the splicing factor SRSF2 (direct binding, Kd ~μM), RNA polymerase II, and nascent RNA within transcriptional hubs (PubMed:35752626). In the cytoplasm, Nck recruits WASP into LAT condensates, enabling actin binding proportional to basic charge density; this interaction facilitates co-movement with actin networks (PubMed:31268421).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: RAD52 undergoes partner-driven phase separation (PS-other) to form liquid-like condensates in the nucleus (PubMed:31171703, 39038850). These condensates associate with PML nuclear bodies (APBs) and telomeres, particularly in the Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres (ALT) pathway (PubMed:31171703, 39038850). RAD52 exhibits liquid material properties with observable droplet fusion dynamics when targeted to telomeres or multimerized (PubMed:39038850).
Functional Summary: RAD52 phase separation enables break-induced replication (MiDAS) for telomere elongation in ALT-positive cancers, driving telomeric DNA synthesis and genomic rearrangements (PubMed:31171703). It facilitates telomere clustering, enrichment of DNA repair factors (SUMO, BLM, Rad51AP1, RPA), and collaboration with BLM for SUMO-dependent DNA synthesis in PML-deficient environments (PubMed:39038850). RAD52 partitioning into RPA condensates is essential for RAD52-mediated telomere maintenance and genome stability in ALT pathways (PubMed:36894693).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of RAD52 is intrinsically facilitated by its N-terminal domain (NTD/HCR), which is essential for function (PubMed:31171703). Multimerization through synthetic domains (e.g., HOtag3 hexamers) induces condensate formation, indicating intrinsic multivalency drives self-assembly (PubMed:39038850).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RAD52 phase separation is extrinsically modulated by multiple partners: it partitions into RPA condensates at telomeres, enhanced under replication stress (PubMed:36894693); co-enriches SUMO within its condensates in a SUMOylation-dependent manner (PubMed:39038850); recruits BLM and Rad51AP1 to telomeric condensates for collaborative DNA synthesis (PubMed:39038850); and requires telomeric targeting via TRF1 scaffolding for site-specific condensation (PubMed:39038850).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NEDD4 (P46934) exhibits distinct phase separation behaviors mediated by different domains: its HECT domain undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro when incubated with ubiquitination reagents including polyubiquitin chains, forming liquid-like droplets (PubMed:37549262). Independently, its WW domain drives self-assembly into liquid-like cytoplasmic condensates under serum starvation conditions, characterized by droplet fusion and rapid dynamics (PubMed:36640330). These condensates are not associated with predefined membrane-less organelles. No material state transitions (e.g., liquid-to-solid) were reported in either context.
Functional Summary: Phase separation regulates diverse physiological functions: HECT domain LLPS enhances NEDD4's ubiquitin ligase activity (PubMed:37549262), while WW domain condensates serve as signaling hubs for the Hippo pathway. They compartmentalize YAP1 and NLK to facilitate YAP1 phosphorylation at Ser128, driving nuclear translocation and ectoderm lineage differentiation in stem cells (PubMed:36640330). Dysregulation—such as hCINAP depletion—enhances condensation and impairs endoderm differentiation, highlighting its role in cell fate determination (PubMed:36640330).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by two key domains: the HECT domain is essential for LLPS during ubiquitination reactions (PubMed:37549262), while the WW domain (residues 608–982) autonomously drives self-assembly, with WW1 and WW3 motifs being critical for condensate formation and WW4 required for client recruitment (PubMed:36640330). Catalytic activity (tested via C1286S mutation) does not influence LLPS, but deletions in WW1/WW3 abolish condensation, and WW4 deletion impairs client binding without disrupting phase separation (PubMed:36640330).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Extrinsic regulators include polyubiquitin chains, which promote HECT domain LLPS during ubiquitination (PubMed:37549262). For WW domain condensates, YAP1 and NLK are recruited as clients, with NLK phosphorylating YAP1 within droplets, while hCINAP acts as a potent inhibitor by binding the WW domain to dissolve condensates (PubMed:36640330). Functional modulation is demonstrated by serum starvation (inducing condensation) and serum recovery or 1,6-hexanediol (dissolving droplets) (PubMed:36640330).

Protein Name: Nuclear receptor subfamily 2 group C member 2
Overall Phase Separation Overview: TAK1 (P49116) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but is recruited into biomolecular condensates formed by partner proteins, exclusively in the cytoplasm (PubMed:33895773, 39333690). It associates with SARS-CoV-2 N protein-induced liquid condensates and stress granules during viral infection (PubMed:33895773), and with PrPC condensates in hepatocellular carcinoma tissues (PubMed:39333690). The material state of these host condensates is liquid-like, with no observed state transitions for TAK1 itself (PubMed:33895773).
Functional Summary: TAK1 recruitment into SARS-CoV-2 N condensates hyper-activates NF-κB signaling, driving excessive pro-inflammatory cytokine production (e.g., IL-6, TNF, CXCL10) in COVID-19 (PubMed:33895773). In hepatocellular carcinoma, TAK1 recruitment into PrPC condensates activates NF-κB to promote tumorigenesis (PubMed:39333690).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or structural features driving TAK1 phase separation were identified in the provided studies (PubMed:33895773, 39333690).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TAK1 recruitment requires extrinsic partners: It partitions into SARS-CoV-2 N protein condensates in an RNA-dependent manner (PubMed:33895773), and into PrPC condensates whose formation depends on the α3 helix and disulfide bonds in PrPC's C-terminal domain (PubMed:39333690).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: GSK3β (P49841) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), forming liquid-like droplets in vitro and in cellular optoDroplet systems (PubMed:35790738). It also partitions into multiple cytoplasmic membrane-less organelles, including Dvl2-mediated signalosomes (PubMed:36398662), centrosomal condensates (PubMed:36037369), and Axin/APC destruction complexes (PubMed:38279052). These condensates consistently exhibit liquid-like material properties, with no observed state transitions reported across studies (PubMed:35790738, 36398662, 36037369, 38279052).
Functional Summary: Phase-separated GSK3β plays context-dependent roles in Wnt signaling: Within centrosomal and destruction complex condensates, it phosphorylates β-catenin to promote degradation, suppressing Wnt pathway activation (PubMed:36037369, 38279052). Conversely, sequestration in Dvl2 condensates inhibits β-catenin phosphorylation, activating Wnt signaling (PubMed:36398662). Pathological exclusion from destruction complexes in APC-mutant cells disrupts β-catenin degradation, driving constitutive Wnt activation in colorectal cancer (PubMed:38279052).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The intrinsic drivers of GSK3β phase separation remain uncharacterized in available data, though full-length protein constructs demonstrate self-assembly capability in both cellular optoDroplet systems and in vitro reconstitution assays (PubMed:35790738). No specific domains, post-translational modifications, or mutations regulating its autonomous condensation were identified across studies (PubMed:35790738, 38279052).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: GSK3β recruitment into condensates is extrinsically regulated by multiple partners: It partitions into Dvl2 condensates as a sequestered client following WWP2-mediated K63-linked ubiquitylation of Dvl2 (PubMed:36398662); incorporates into centrosomal condensates scaffolded by Axin1 and APC (PubMed:36037369); and is selectively recruited into destruction complex condensates dependent on wild-type APC, with exclusion observed in APC-mutant contexts (PubMed:38279052).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: MRE11 (P49959) does not undergo autonomous phase separation (class: PS-other) but partitions into biomolecular condensates within the nucleus (PubMed:36092926, 35551189). It exhibits variable association with chromocenters—displaying depleted, homogeneous, or enriched distributions across cells—and forms nuclear foci (PubMed:36092926). MRE11 is recruited into liquid-like condensates formed by MRNIP at DNA damage foci, where it participates in DNA repair mechanisms (PubMed:35551189). No material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: MRE11's condensate partitioning regulates DNA damage response. Its heterogeneous distribution in chromocenters modulates accessibility for DNA break sensing in heterochromatin (PubMed:36092926). Within MRNIP condensates at damage sites, MRE11 enables accelerated ATM activation, DNA end resection, and homologous recombination repair, promoting genome stability and radioresistance in cancer contexts (PubMed:35551189).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features driving autonomous phase separation of MRE11 were identified in the provided studies (PubMed:36092926, 35551189). All experiments utilized full-length constructs (MRE11-YFP or MRE11-mCherry), with no reported modifications affecting condensate partitioning.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: MRE11 partitioning is extrinsically regulated by MRNIP, which undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation and recruits MRE11 (as part of the MRN complex) into DNA damage-associated condensates (PubMed:35551189). This recruitment is independent of PARP-mediated PARylation, as inhibition did not alter MRE11's heterogeneous distribution in chromocenters (PubMed:36092926). DNA substrates are incorporated into these condensates, facilitating repair functions.

Protein Name: SWI/SNF-related matrix-associated actin-dependent regulator of chromatin subfamily A member 4
Overall Phase Separation Overview: BRG1 exhibits weak self-driven phase separation in vitro requiring high concentrations or crowders, but does not form condensates in cells under normal conditions (PubMed:34018649, 38326345). It primarily engages in heterotypic co-condensation via partner interactions, localizing to the nucleus (PubMed:34018649, 38326345, 35585082). BRG1 associates with ectopic oncogenic condensates (e.g., FUS-DDIT3, SS18-SSX1 complexes) where it exhibits liquid-like material properties (PubMed:34018649, 35585082). No material state transitions are reported.
Functional Summary: BRG1 recruitment into oncogenic condensates drives pathological chromatin remodeling: 1) In FUS-DDIT3 complexes, it enables aberrant transcriptional activation at ectopic genomic sites, potentially sequestering SWI/SNF from physiological targets (PubMed:34018649); 2) In SS18-SSX1 condensates, it facilitates oncogenic transformation including cell proliferation, migration, and invasion (PubMed:35585082). Dysregulation is linked to FET fusion oncoproteins, where condensate mis-localization disrupts gene regulation networks (PubMed:38326345). During CRISPR activation, BRG1 recruitment by FUS fusions enhances transcriptional activation of reporter and endogenous genes (PubMed:39174527).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by BRG1's prion-like domain (PLD, residues 1-340), which enables heterotypic interactions but lacks strong self-driving capability (PubMed:34018649). The wild-type PLD only forms condensates under macromolecular crowding conditions like 20% Ficoll (PubMed:38326345). Tyrosine-enriched mutants (Aro+ with 17 proline-to-tyrosine substitutions forming nuclear condensates; Aro++ with 41 substitutions forming cytoplasmic aggregates) demonstrate that tyrosine content critically determines phase separation capacity in cellular environments (PubMed:38326345).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: BRG1 recruitment is extrinsically modulated through heterotypic interactions: 1) Co-condensation with FUS-DDIT3 via PLD-PLD interactions, enriched on dsDNA surfaces (partition coefficient 27±7) (PubMed:34018649); 2) Recruitment into SS18-SSX1 condensates dependent on SS18's SNH domain (PubMed:35585082); 3) Weak partitioning into FUS condensates (k=1.8-5.5) enhanced by tyrosine mutations (PubMed:38326345); 4) Essential recruitment to genomic loci by FUS and TARDBP fusion proteins during transcriptional activation (PubMed:39174527). Macromolecular crowding agents (e.g., Ficoll) significantly promote phase separation (PubMed:38326345).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: HCFC1 (P51610) associates with transcriptional condensates in the nucleus through co-phase separation mechanisms rather than self-driven assembly (class: PS-other) (PubMed:35537448, 37851801). It incorporates into liquid-like biomolecular condensates (BMCs) during transcriptional activation, though its intrinsic phase separation propensity is low when tested in fusion constructs (29% droplet formation in cells) (PubMed:35537448, 37851801). No material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: As a component of transcriptional condensates, HCFC1 is essential for efficient transcriptional elongation in biomolecular condensates (PubMed:37851801). Artificially reinforced phase separation of HCFC1 fusion constructs represses transcriptional activation, indicating that multivalent interactions—rather than droplet formation—drive its functional role (PubMed:35537448).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features driving HCFC1 phase separation were identified in the provided studies (PubMed:35537448, 37851801).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: HCFC1 co-assembles with BRD4, which enhances its droplet formation in fusion constructs (PubMed:35537448). It functionally partners with RNA polymerase II (POLR2A) in transcriptional condensates during elongation and co-phase separates with NONO, SFPQ, FUS, PARP1, LEO1, and OGT via collective weak multivalent interactions in nuclear extracts (PubMed:35537448, 37851801).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TRF1 undergoes self-driven phase separation in vitro forming liquid-like droplets, but its in vivo condensation requires multivalent interactions with telomeric DNA or partner recruitment (PubMed:35077681, 32579423). It primarily localizes to the nucleus where it associates with ALT telomere-associated PML nuclear bodies (APBs) and telomeric heterochromatin (PubMed:32579423, 34072343, 35077681). TRF1 condensates exhibit liquid-like properties including fusion and FRAP recovery (PubMed:32579423, 35077681), but can undergo pathological liquid-to-solid transitions in mutants (TRF1ΔA) (PubMed:35077681).
Functional Summary: TRF1 phase separation drives telomere clustering in ALT cancer cells, providing repair templates for homology-directed telomere synthesis (PubMed:32579423, 39038850). Within shelterin condensates, it protects telomeric ends by selectively recruiting repair factors while limiting DNA damage response activation (PubMed:35077681). In APBs, TRF1-PML-V interactions stabilize condensates essential for telomere lengthening (PubMed:34072343). Pathological liquid-to-solid transitions in mutants cause cytotoxic aggregation (PubMed:35077681), while SUMO-TRF1 condensates in PML-null cells enable alternative telomere maintenance through Rad52/BLM-mediated DNA synthesis (PubMed:39038850).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by TRF1's dimerization capability and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), with the acidic domain modulating electrostatic interactions with DNA (PubMed:35077681). Key mutations (ΔHinge, ΔIDR, A75P) impair oligomerization and reduce condensation efficiency (PubMed:35077681). SUMOylation is critical for nucleating APB condensation via SUMO-SIM interactions (PubMed:32579423).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TRF1 requires SUMOylated proteins (SUMO1/2/3) and SIM-containing partners for APB condensation (PubMed:32579423). It scaffolds PML isoforms (PML-I, PML-III, PML-V) in nuclear bodies (PubMed:34072343) and integrates with shelterin components (TIN2, TPP1, POT1) to form telomeric condensates (PubMed:35077681). Telomeric DNA inhibits phase separation in vitro but enables in vivo condensation (PubMed:35077681). In PML knockout cells, TRF1 scaffolds SUMO condensates recruiting DNA repair proteins (Rad52, BLM, Rad51AP1, RPA) (PubMed:39038850).

Protein Name: UV excision repair protein RAD23 homolog B
Overall Phase Separation Overview: RAD23B undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in the nucleus, forming proteasome-containing foci known as SIPAN (Starvation-Induced Proteasome Assemblies in the Nucleus) during amino acid starvation (PubMed:34848715) and under hyperosmotic stress (PubMed:32025036). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties including droplet fusion and rapid component exchange, with no reported material state transitions (PubMed:34848715, 32025036).
Functional Summary: RAD23B-scaffolded condensates serve as proteolytic hubs for ubiquitinated substrate degradation during cellular stress (PubMed:34848715, 32025036). Under amino acid starvation, they are critical for p53/NOXA-mediated apoptosis (PubMed:34848715), while under hyperosmotic stress they prevent apoptosis by enabling efficient misfolded protein clearance (PubMed:32025036). Depletion disrupts stress-induced proteasome focus formation and compromises cell survival pathways (PubMed:34848715, 32025036).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by RAD23B's ubiquitin-like (UBL) and ubiquitin-associated (UBA) domains through multivalent interactions (PubMed:34848715, 32025036). The UBA domains specifically enable chain-length-dependent LLPS with K48-linked ubiquitin chains requiring ≥4 ubiquitin moieties (PubMed:32025036). Critical mutations disrupting LLPS include ΔUBL, ΔUBA1, ΔUBA2 (PubMed:34848715) and UBA domain point mutations L225A/L401A (PubMed:32025036).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RAD23B requires K48-linked polyubiquitin chains as essential scaffolds for LLPS, with chains ≥4 ubiquitins enabling multivalent interactions (PubMed:34848715, 32025036). It co-phase separates with proteasome components to form functional condensate cores (PubMed:34848715). Additional partners include UBE3A and p97, which localize to these foci and modulate degradation efficiency, with UBE3A depletion reducing focus formation by ~30% (PubMed:32025036).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PSMD4 undergoes partner-dependent phase separation in the nucleus, forming distinct membrane-less organelles under specific stress conditions. During amino acid deprivation, it forms liquid-like SIPAN (Starvation-Induced Proteasome Assemblies in the Nucleus) condensates (PubMed:34848715). Under hyperosmotic stress, it forms reversible nuclear proteasome-containing foci (PubMed:34572142). The material state is consistently liquid-like, with rapid dissolution kinetics observed in SIPAN and reversibility in osmotic stress-induced foci. No material state transitions are reported in either context (PubMed:34848715, 34572142).
Functional Summary: PSMD4 condensates serve as catalytic hubs for ubiquitinated substrate degradation during amino acid deprivation via SIPAN, with sustained formation correlating to apoptosis (PubMed:34848715). The functional role of hyperosmotic stress-induced proteasome foci remains unspecified, though their reversible formation suggests adaptive stress response mechanisms (PubMed:34572142).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic regulators (domains, mutations, PTMs, or structural features) driving PSMD4 phase separation were identified in the provided data (PubMed:34848715, 34572142).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: PSMD4 phase separation requires extrinsic partners: Under amino acid deprivation, it co-assembles with proteasome subunits and the essential scaffold RAD23B, with SIPAN formation dependent on RAD23B and blocked by ubiquitination inhibition (PubMed:34848715). Under hyperosmotic stress, it forms foci through co-phase separation with proteasome subunits PSMB2 and PSMA3 (PubMed:34572142). Both condensate types show environmental specificity—SIPAN is insensitive to osmotic stress but induced by proteasome inhibitors, while hyperosmotic stress-induced foci form independently of signaling cascades (PubMed:34848715, 34572142).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SUMO3 (P55854) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but participates in biomolecular condensates as a key regulatory component through SUMO-SIM interactions (PubMed:32579423, 31171703, 31416913, 35442725, 37059091). It localizes to both the nucleus and cytoplasm, associating with PML nuclear bodies, P bodies, Epac1 nuclear condensates, and SLX4 condensates (PubMed:32579423, 31171703, 31416913, 35442725, 37059091). Within these structures, SUMO3 contributes to liquid-like material states characterized by dynamic exchange and fusion capabilities, though it does not independently form condensates (PubMed:32579423, 35442725, 37059091).
Functional Summary: SUMO3-containing condensates functionally regulate diverse cellular processes: in telomere maintenance, they facilitate ALT cancer cell telomere clustering and repair template organization (PubMed:32579423, 31171703); in neuronal function, they enable CPEB3-mediated mRNA repression in P bodies for synaptic plasticity and memory persistence (PubMed:31416913); in cellular signaling, they promote global SUMOylation within Epac1 condensates, driving macrophage foam cell formation in atherosclerosis (PubMed:35442725); and in DNA repair, they compartmentalize SUMO/RNF4 pathways within SLX4 condensates for TOP1-DNA crosslink removal and DNA damage response (PubMed:37059091).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: SUMO3's phase separation behavior is intrinsically regulated by its capacity for multivalent interactions when engineered as polySUMO repeats, enabling condensate formation through SUMO-SIM scaffolding (PubMed:31171703). Its role as a SUMO modifier facilitates incorporation into condensates via conjugation to target proteins, though no specific domains or mutations directly driving self-assembly are reported (PubMed:32579423, 31416913, 35442725, 37059091).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SUMO3's condensate integration is extrinsically regulated through interactions with partner proteins: it serves as an essential co-factor for SIM-mediated TRF1 condensation in PML bodies (PubMed:32579423), drives CPEB3 phase separation when conjugated during P-body formation (PubMed:31416913), enriches in Epac1 nuclear condensates to promote SUMOylation machinery compartmentalization (PubMed:35442725), and provides SUMO ligands for SIM interactions within SLX4 condensates to enhance DNA repair processes (PubMed:37059091). Additionally, SUMO3 forms functional condensates with PIASx-derived polySIM scaffolds (PubMed:31171703).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SUMO2 (P61956) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but is recruited to membraneless organelles (MLOs) formed by partner proteins (PubMed:35235714, 35442725). It localizes to both the nucleus and cytoplasm and associates with PML nuclear bodies (PubMed:35235714), Epac1 nuclear condensates (PubMed:35442725), and other MLOs through SUMO-SIM interactions. Recruitment requires conjugation via its C-terminal glycine residue (PubMed:35235714). The material state within condensates remains unspecified across all studies, with no reported phase transitions.
Functional Summary: SUMO2 recruitment to MLOs enables diverse functions: 1) In PML bodies, it regulates nuclear processes and lysosomal targeting during mitophagy (PubMed:35235714); 2) For TRF1, it facilitates telomere clustering and DNA repair in ALT cancer cells (PubMed:32579423); 3) With CPEB3, it drives mRNA repression in P-bodies essential for synaptic plasticity and memory (PubMed:31416913); 4) In Epac1 condensates, it enhances global SUMOylation to promote atherosclerosis (PubMed:35442725); 5) Within SLX4 condensates, it compartmentalizes DNA repair pathways for TOP1-DPC resolution (PubMed:37059091); and 6) In CHAF1A bodies, it supports HIV-1 latency through epigenetic silencing (PubMed:33739466).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The primary intrinsic regulator of SUMO2's MLO recruitment is its conjugation capacity (sumoylation) mediated by the C-terminal glycine residue (PubMed:35235714). Mutation of the conjugation site (e.g., Gly93 deletion in SUMO2ΔG93) abolishes nuclear puncta formation (PubMed:35235714). No other intrinsic domains, mutations, or features driving SUMO2 phase separation were identified in the provided data.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SUMO2 recruitment is extrinsically regulated by scaffold proteins that form condensates: 1) PML nucleates SUMO2 enrichment in PML nuclear bodies (PubMed:35235714); 2) TRF1 recruits SUMO2 as an essential co-factor for DNA damage-induced APB condensation via SUMO-SIM interactions (PubMed:32579423); 3) CPEB3 incorporates SUMO2 into P-bodies through SUMOylation-dependent partitioning (PubMed:31416913); 4) Epac1 activation by cAMP enriches SUMO2 in nuclear condensates with SUMOylation machinery (PubMed:35442725); 5) SLX4 concentrates SUMO2 in chromatin-bound condensates to enhance SUMO-SIM valency (PubMed:37059091); and 6) CHAF1A recruits SUMO2 to nuclear bodies via SIM domain interactions for epigenetic silencing (PubMed:33739466).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: WDR5 (P61964) does not autonomously undergo phase separation but is recruited as a client protein to cytoplasmic viral inclusion bodies (IBs) formed during measles virus infection (PubMed:39194235, 31375591). These IBs, which exhibit liquid-like properties in small puncta, allow dynamic exchange of WDR5 but transition to a gel-like state in larger puncta where WDR5 becomes immobilized (PubMed:31375591). WDR5 localizes to both the nucleus and cytoplasm but specifically partitions into viral IBs in the cytoplasm during infection (PubMed:39194235, 31375591).
Functional Summary: WDR5 enrichment in viral IBs suppresses the PKR-mediated integrated stress response by sequestering immunostimulatory RNA, thereby preventing translational shutdown and enhancing viral replication (PubMed:39194235). This function requires RNA-binding activity, as F266A mutants fail to suppress PKR despite normal IB localization (PubMed:39194235). The transition to gel-like IB states may limit WDR5's functional availability during infection (PubMed:31375591).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Recruitment to inclusion bodies is mediated by WDR5's WBM interaction surface, with residue L240 being critical for efficient localization and binding to the viral phosphoprotein (P) (PubMed:39194235). Mutations such as L240K disrupt this interaction, while RNA-binding activity (dependent on residue F266) is dispensable for localization but essential for functional suppression of PKR activation within IBs (PubMed:39194235).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: WDR5 is recruited to viral IBs through direct interaction with the measles virus phosphoprotein (P), which serves as a scaffold for IB formation via phase separation with the viral nucleoprotein (N) (PubMed:39194235). Within IBs, WDR5 binds viral/host RNA to mask immunostimulatory motifs (PubMed:39194235). The material state of these condensates regulates WDR5 dynamics, with liquid-like small puncta permitting rapid exchange (>90% FRAP recovery) and gel-like large puncta restricting mobility (<50% recovery) (PubMed:31375591).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: RPL7A (P62424) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but is recruited into biomolecular condensates formed by partner proteins. It localizes to both the nucleus and cytoplasm, associating with DNA damage foci in the nucleus where it co-localizes with TopBP1 (PubMed:37582658) and is recruited into cytoplasmic STAU1 condensates (PubMed:38913026). The material state of these condensates is liquid-like, consistent with the properties of TopBP1-pre-rRNA and STAU1 condensates, though no direct state transitions for RPL7A itself are reported (PubMed:37582658, 38913026).
Functional Summary: RPL7A regulates Cajal body abundance, as its depletion increases their number (PubMed:39602297). At DNA damage foci, it contributes to TopBP1-mediated ATR activation, DNA repair, and cell cycle checkpoint control as part of the pre-rRNP complex (PubMed:37582658). In STAU1 condensates, it facilitates MTOR mRNA translation; dysregulation of this process promotes mTOR hyperactivation, autophagy-lysosome dysfunction, and pathological protein aggregation in neurodegenerative models (PubMed:38913026).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features driving RPL7A phase separation are reported in the provided data (PubMed:39602297, 37582658, 38913026). All available evidence indicates its recruitment into condensates is extrinsically regulated by partner proteins and RNAs.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RPL7A is recruited into TopBP1 condensates in an RNA-dependent manner, requiring pre-rRNA as a scaffold for co-localization at DNA damage foci (PubMed:37582658). In the cytoplasm, it partitions into STAU1 condensates alongside MTOR mRNA and PABPC1, where it functions as a component of the translation machinery (PubMed:38913026). Its recruitment to both condensates is abolished by RNase treatment, confirming RNA-dependent interactions (PubMed:37582658, 38913026).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Rab11a (P62491) scaffolds liquid-like viral inclusions through heterotypic co-phase separation with influenza vRNPs in the cytoplasm during viral infection (PubMed:37013374, 30967547). These membraneless organelles form near ER exit sites and exhibit liquid properties including fusion/fission events, dynamic material exchange, and sensitivity to hypotonic shock/1,6-hexanediol (PubMed:30967547). While Rab11a itself maintains liquid characteristics, the inclusions it scaffolds can undergo pathological liquid-to-solid transitions when treated with nucleozin, resulting in hardened aggregates (PubMed:37013374).
Functional Summary: Rab11a-mediated phase separation concentrates vRNPs into dynamic liquid inclusions that facilitate selective viral genome assembly and enable co-packaging of vRNPs from different strains (reassortment) (PubMed:37013374, 30967547). Disruption via dominant-negative Rab11a reduces viral titers, confirming its essential role in viral production (PubMed:30967547). Pathological liquid-to-solid transitions induced by nucleozin disrupt replication, demonstrating material properties as antiviral targets, though these inclusions don't affect immune evasion pathways (PubMed:37013374, 30967547).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Rab11a phase separation is intrinsically regulated by its GTP-bound state, as evidenced by the GDP-locked dominant-negative mutant (S25N) which prevents redistribution into inclusions and subsequent phase separation (PubMed:37013374, 30967547). Full-length Rab11a is required for its scaffolding function, with overexpression enlarging inclusions without altering their material state (PubMed:37013374).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Rab11a co-phase separates with viral ribonucleoprotein particles (vRNPs) containing NP protein (P03466) and influenza vRNA to form viral inclusions, requiring direct Rab11a-vRNP interactions (PubMed:37013374, 30967547). Inclusion integrity depends on continuous ER-Golgi vesicular cycling, as disruption by Brefeldin A causes disassembly (PubMed:30967547). The small molecule nucleozin induces hardening of inclusions by stabilizing vRNP interactions, though Rab11a itself isn't directly hardened (PubMed:37013374).

Protein Name: CCHC-type zinc finger nucleic acid binding protein
Overall Phase Separation Overview: CNBP exhibits context-dependent phase separation behavior, forming dynamic liquid condensates in the nucleus through co-assembly with SMARCC2, essential for repressing SWI/SNF complex activity in neuroblastoma (PubMed:37186134). In contrast, during SARS-CoV-2 infection, CNBP does not undergo phase separation itself but disrupts viral nucleocapsid protein-RNA condensate formation in the cytoplasm (PubMed:37963251). Its subcellular localization spans both nucleus and cytoplasm, with material properties limited to liquid states in physiological contexts, without observed state transitions (PubMed:37186134, 37963251).
Functional Summary: CNBP phase separation with SMARCC2 represses the SWI/SNF complex, activating alternative transcriptional programs that drive 18S rRNA processing, ribosome biogenesis, and neuroblastoma progression, including extracellular vesicle-mediated M2 macrophage polarization (PubMed:37186134). Conversely, in antiviral defense, CNBP-mediated disruption of SARS-CoV-2 N-RNA condensates inhibits viral replication and virion assembly through an interferon-independent mechanism (PubMed:37963251).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The RGG domain (amino acids 22-42) within CNBP's intrinsically disordered region intrinsically drives its phase separation capabilities. This domain is essential for self-assembly into nuclear condensates with SMARCC2, as deletion abolishes LLPS (PubMed:37186134). The same RGG domain and an adjacent linker region (GFTSDRG motif) enable competitive viral RNA binding that disrupts SARS-CoV-2 N protein phase separation, with deletion mutants confirming domain necessity (PubMed:37963251).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: CNBP's phase behavior is extrinsically regulated by specific partners: it co-phase separates with SMARCC2 in nuclear condensates, requiring this interaction for LLPS (PubMed:37186134). KPNB1 facilitates nuclear translocation of CNBP, enabling SMARCC2 co-condensation (PubMed:37186134). During viral infection, CNBP competitively binds SARS-CoV-2 genomic RNA (5'UTR/3'UTR), disrupting phase separation of the viral N protein and inhibiting condensate formation (PubMed:37963251).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SUMO1 (P63165) undergoes self-driven phase separation (PS-self) to form liquid-like droplets in vitro that transition to solid aggregates over time (PubMed:37782899). It localizes primarily to the nucleus (PubMed:39038850) and associates with multiple membrane-less organelles including APBs (PML nuclear bodies) (PubMed:32579423), telomeric condensates in ALT cancer cells (PubMed:39038850), N2NLCpolyG inclusions in neuronal disease (PubMed:34694469), and CAF-1 nuclear bodies (PubMed:33739466). The condensates exhibit liquid properties in physiological contexts (e.g., fusion dynamics in APBs and telomeric foci) but undergo pathological liquid-to-solid transitions in neurodegenerative inclusions and in vitro systems (PubMed:34694469, 37782899).
Functional Summary: SUMO1 condensates enable telomere clustering and DNA repair protein enrichment for break-induced replication in ALT cancer cells, with inhibition selectively killing ALT-positive cells (PubMed:39038850, 32579423). Pathologically, it contributes to solid aggregates in Neuronal Intranuclear Inclusion Disease inclusions, driving neurodegeneration (PubMed:34694469). In HIV-1 latency, SUMO1 enrichment in CAF-1 bodies facilitates epigenetic silencing (PubMed:33739466). Its in vitro liquid-to-solid transition models disease-relevant aggregation, challenging paradigms of disorder-exclusive phase separation (PubMed:37782899).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by SUMO1's structured domain (residues 18-97), which autonomously forms condensates without requiring disordered regions (PubMed:37782899). The N-terminal disordered tail (residues 1-17) is dispensable, and its deletion (ΔN-SUMO1) accelerates droplet kinetics and dense-phase partitioning (PubMed:37782899). Multivalent SUMO-SIM interactions are essential, as mutations in the SIM-binding site (FKIK→FAAA) or prevention of SUMOylation (di-Gly→di-Val) abolish condensate formation in cellular contexts (PubMed:39038850).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SUMO1 phase separation is regulated by extrinsic partners across systems: TRF1 scaffolds its recruitment to telomeres for condensate formation (PubMed:39038850, 32579423), while CHAF1A recruits it to nuclear bodies via SUMO-SIM interactions (PubMed:33739466). In pathological contexts, it is recruited to N2NLCpolyG inclusions (PubMed:34694469). SUMO1 also co-enriches with DNA repair factors (Rad52, BLM, Rad51AP1, RPA) in telomeric condensates, dependent on SUMOylation and SIM interactions (PubMed:39038850).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Ubc9 (P63279) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but co-partitions into various biomolecular condensates in both the cytoplasm and nucleus (PubMed:28377462, 35442725). In the cytoplasm, it associates with stress granules and aggresomes, often adopting a solid-like aggregated state (PubMed:28377462). In the nucleus, it is recruited into Epac1-dependent condensates that promote SUMOylation (PubMed:35442725) and heterochromatin condensates formed by HP1α (PubMed:39192031). Ubc9 can promote liquid-to-solid transitions in partner condensates, such as those formed by FUS (PubMed:28377462).
Functional Summary: The co-partitioning of Ubc9 into stress granules promotes aberrant material states, leading to stress granule dysfunction and persistence, which may contribute to proteinopathies (PubMed:28377462). In the nucleus, Ubc9's recruitment into Epac1 condensates facilitates the concentration of SUMOylation machinery, enhancing cellular SUMOylation processes that are critical for stress responses and atherosclerosis development (PubMed:35442725). Additionally, Ubc9-mediated SUMOylation of HP1α is essential for heterochromatin formation and maintenance, thereby repressing repetitive elements and preserving genome stability (PubMed:39192031).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The intrinsic propensity of Ubc9 to accumulate in condensates is primarily driven by a temperature-sensitive mutation that causes misfolding, which enhances its recruitment to stress granules and promotes aberrant transitions (PubMed:28377462). No specific domains or post-translational modifications of Ubc9 were identified as intrinsic drivers of its phase separation behavior in the provided data.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Ubc9's partitioning into condensates is modulated by multiple extrinsic partners. It co-localizes with stress granule markers G3BP1 and G3BP2 in cytoplasmic stress granules (PubMed:28377462). In the nucleus, it is recruited into Epac1 condensates in a cAMP-dependent manner, where it colocalizes with SUMOylation machinery components (PubMed:35442725). Ubc9 also interacts with IRTKS to catalyze SUMOylation of HP1α, thereby enhancing HP1α phase separation in heterochromatin condensates (PubMed:39192031). Notably, misfolded Ubc9 (Ubc9TS) accumulates in FUS condensates and triggers a liquid-to-solid transition (PubMed:28377462).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PHC1 undergoes self-driven phase separation (PS-self) forming liquid condensates in vitro at concentrations above 50 nM, independent of its SAM domain polymerization capability, as demonstrated by the L307R mutant retaining condensation ability (PubMed:37756159). In cellular environments, PHC1 requires light-induced oligomerization for phase separation, forming dynamic liquid-like condensates in the nucleus that exhibit fusion and rapid fluorescence recovery, with the SAM oligomerization domain being essential for this process (PubMed:34620850). It associates with nuclear bodies, specifically Polycomb condensates (PubMed:37756159, 34620850). No material state transitions were reported under tested conditions.
Functional Summary: As a core component of Polycomb repressive complexes, PHC1 phase separation contributes to epigenetic silencing through formation of multicomponent condensates that write repressive H2AK119Ub histone marks and compact chromatin (PubMed:34620850). It regulates client partitioning in CBX2-scaffolded condensates essential for Polycomb-mediated gene silencing (PubMed:37756159).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by the sterile alpha motif (SAM) domain with context-dependent requirements: SAM-mediated polymerization is dispensable for in vitro condensation, as evidenced by the polymerization-defective L307R mutant forming droplets similar to wild-type (PubMed:37756159). However, in cellular environments, the SAM oligomerization domain is essential for phase separation, as deletion (ΔOD) completely abolishes condensate formation (PubMed:34620850).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: PHC1 exhibits mutual modulation with CBX2, displaying re-entrant phase behavior in multi-component systems and inhibiting partitioning of other clients like RING1B and MEL18 (PubMed:37756159). It recruits BMI1 and RNF2 into its condensates, demonstrating heterotypic interactions within PRC1 complexes (PubMed:34620850). PHC1 itself partitions into CBX2-scaffolded condensates and is recruited into RNF2 condensates (PubMed:37756159, 34620850).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SMAD3 exhibits both autonomous and partner-dependent phase separation behaviors. It undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro, forming liquid-like droplets (PubMed:31563432). However, in cellular contexts, SMAD3 primarily co-phase separates with partners like Smad2/Smad4 to form liquid condensates in the nucleus (PubMed:38769521, 39234824). It associates with transcriptional condensates at super-enhancers and Mediator condensates (PubMed:31563432), with no reported material state transitions.
Functional Summary: SMAD3 phase separation enables precise transcriptional regulation with significant disease implications. In METTL3 condensates, it promotes m6A methylation-mediated degradation of tumor-suppressor ITIH1 mRNA, driving hepatocellular carcinoma progression (PubMed:39234824). Within Smad2/3/4 complexes, phase separation activates TAT transcription, inducing caspase-9-mediated apoptosis and suppressing hepatocellular carcinoma (PubMed:38769521). At super-enhancers, SMAD3 condensates facilitate cell-type-specific responses to TGF-β signaling, regulating key genes like Nanog (PubMed:31563432).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by SMAD3's intrinsically disordered region (IDR), which facilitates homotypic interactions and autonomous droplet formation (PubMed:31563432). However, conflicting evidence suggests SMAD3 lacks intrinsic disorder domains and requires oligomerization with Smad2/Smad4 for phase separation in complex contexts (PubMed:38769521). No disease-associated mutations or specific PTMs directly modulating phase separation were reported.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SMAD3's phase separation is extrinsically regulated by multiple partners and signaling pathways. It serves as an essential scaffold for METTL3 condensate formation, which is promoted by TGF-β and inhibited by Galunisertib (PubMed:39234824). SMAD3 co-phase separates with Smad2 and Smad4 to form ternary transcriptional complexes (PubMed:38769521) and partitions into MED1-containing Mediator condensates (PubMed:31563432). TGF-β signaling consistently promotes SMAD3's phase separation across contexts (PubMed:38769521, 39234824).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TFAM undergoes self-driven phase separation (PubMed:34711968, 33619770), forming condensates primarily in the cytoplasm within mitochondrial nucleoids (PubMed:34711968, 33619770). These condensates exhibit complex material properties: while demonstrating liquid-like fusion behavior in vitro and in vivo, they possess viscoelastic or gel-like characteristics evidenced by slow FRAP recovery (t½ ~30s in vitro; τ≈350s for TFAM in TFAM-DNA complexes) and non-spherical morphologies (PubMed:34711968, 33619770). The phase separation occurs spontaneously via weak multivalent interactions and is concentration-dependent, with no reported material state transitions under tested conditions (PubMed:33619770).
Functional Summary: TFAM phase separation organizes mitochondrial nucleoids to package mtDNA and concentrate transcription machinery (POLRMT, TFB2M, TEFM, MTERF1) and substrates (NTPs), enhancing mitochondrial transcription efficiency (PubMed:34711968). This process protects mtDNA from reactive oxygen species by reducing exposed surface area (PubMed:33619770). Aberrant phase separation—manifested as enlarged nucleoids in Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) fibroblasts—remains transcriptionally active but is linked to mitochondrial dysfunction in aging (PubMed:33619770). TFAM knockdown disrupts nucleoid formation and impairs transcription, confirming its functional necessity (PubMed:34711968).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by TFAM's disordered linker domain, which is essential for droplet formation as truncations lacking this domain (e.g., TFAM43-122, TFAM152-246) abolish phase separation (PubMed:34711968). The C-tail contributes to wetting behavior but is dispensable for phase separation (PubMed:33619770). Oligomerization through the HMGA domain is critical, as dimerization-disrupting mutations (no-dimer mutant: p.K95A/Y99F/E106A/E112A/R116A) increase saturation concentrations and reduce droplet size (PubMed:33619770). Mutations in the linker region (L6 mutant: p.K136A/H137A/K139A/R140A/K146A/K147A) cause abnormal non-spherical morphologies, while HMGA domain removal (ΔHMGA) elevates concentration requirements for phase separation (PubMed:33619770).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) acts as a critical scaffold that nucleates droplet formation, reduces saturation concentration, and alters material properties—partitioning heterogeneously with immobile fractions in condensates (PubMed:34711968, 33619770). High salt concentrations (≥300 mM NaCl) dissolve droplets, indicating electrostatic interaction dependence (PubMed:33619770). TFAM condensates recruit client proteins including transcription machinery components POLRMT, TFB2M (Q9H5Q4), TEFM (Q96QE5), and MTERF1 (Q99551), which localize to droplet peripheries (ρ=0.3 colocalization for TFB2M) (PubMed:34711968, 33619770).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: ENL (Q03111) undergoes self-driven phase separation to form liquid-like condensates in the nucleus (PubMed:36272410, 32270036). At near-endogenous expression levels, cancer-associated hotspot mutations (T1-T8) in its YEATS domain drive aberrant formation of functional submicron condensates at native genomic targets like the HOXA locus, which exhibit slower dynamics and chromatin association (PubMed:36272410). Overexpression induces large, transcriptionally non-functional liquid droplets (PubMed:36272410). In the super elongation complex (SEC), ENL forms dynamic nuclear droplets that compartmentalize elongation factors; these display liquid-like properties when complexed with AFF4 but transition toward solid-like states without AFF4 (PubMed:32270036). ENL associates with transcriptional condensates and SEC droplets (PubMed:36272410, 32270036).
Functional Summary: Physiologically, ENL condensates enable rapid transcriptional activation of immediate early genes (e.g., FOS) and developmental loci (e.g., HOXA) by concentrating elongation machinery like Pol II S2P and CDK9 (PubMed:36272410, 32270036). Pathologically, cancer-associated mutations drive oncogenesis via hyperactivation of target genes through aberrant condensate formation at native chromatin sites (PubMed:36272410). Dysregulation – via overexpression (causing non-functional droplets), mutation-enhanced phase separation, or MLL fusions – directly promotes leukemogenesis (PubMed:36272410, 32270036). Disrupting condensates (via revertant mutations, domain deletions, or partner dissociation) abolishes oncogenic transcription (PubMed:36272410).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by: 1) Mutated YEATS domain (β8 extension/PP-bulge removal enabling homotypic interactions), 2) IDR1 (aa 201-343; positive charge density initiating condensation), and 3) IDR2 (aa 344-450; negative charge/serine residues regulating growth) (PubMed:36272410). Cancer-associated mutations (T1-T8) enhance phase separation propensity, while revertants (H116P/N111P) suppress it by abolishing structural changes (PubMed:36272410).
