Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic molecular features (domains, mutations, PTMs, or oligomerization states) driving or regulating MDC1 phase separation were identified in the provided study (PubMed:31267591).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulatory partners, biomolecules, or chemical modulators of MDC1 phase separation were reported in the provided data (PubMed:31267591).

Protein Name: KN motif and ankyrin repeat domain-containing protein 1
Overall Phase Separation Overview: KANK1 (Q14678) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) via its N-terminal disordered regions, forming dynamic liquid droplets in vitro and belt-like condensates at focal adhesions in the cytoplasm (PubMed:37874676). This LLPS is concentration-dependent and enhanced by the coiled-coil domain, with no reported material state transitions to solid or gel states (PubMed:37874676).
Functional Summary: KANK1 phase separation enables its accumulation at focal adhesion (FA) belts, where it regulates FA morphology by limiting size and promoting rounder shapes, recruits liprin-β and microtubules to FAs, and attenuates actin stress fiber formation (PubMed:37874676). Disruption of LLPS (e.g., via ΔL1 or ΔCC mutations) causes mislocalization to FA centers, increasing FA size by 40–60% and disrupting cytoskeletal remodeling in response to mechanical force (PubMed:37874676).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of KANK1 is intrinsically driven by its intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs): the KN motif (residues 30–66) and L1 loop region (residues 69–257), which are essential for LLPS (PubMed:37874676). The coiled-coil domain (CC, residues 258–534) promotes phase separation and stabilizes condensates by increasing viscosity, as evidenced by slower FRAP recovery kinetics (PubMed:37874676). Deletion of the L1 region (ΔL1) abolishes LLPS, while replacement with FUS's low-complexity domain (DL1-FUS) restores phase separation capability (PubMed:37874676).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators, partners, or environmental modulators (e.g., ions, chemicals) of KANK1 phase separation were reported in the provided study (PubMed:37874676).

Protein Name: Ribosomal RNA processing protein 1 homolog B
Overall Phase Separation Overview: HP1α (Q14684) undergoes partner-dependent phase separation (class: PS-other), forming liquid-like condensates primarily associated with heterochromatin (PubMed:30425322, 32698189, 39192031). Its phase separation requires H3K9me3-modified nucleosome arrays and occurs in nuclear compartments, though specific subcellular locations are not explicitly detailed in all studies (PubMed:30425322, 39738032). HP1α associates with heterochromatin condensates and perinucleolar heterochromatin, exhibiting miscibility with proteins like NPM1 and DDX18 in context-dependent manners (PubMed:39738032, 39192031). The material state remains liquid-like across observed conditions, with no reported state transitions (PubMed:30425322, 39192031).
Functional Summary: HP1α phase separation is functionally critical for heterochromatin organization and gene regulation: 1) It maintains heterochromatin integrity by compacting chromatin and silencing repetitive elements through condensate formation with MeCP2 and IRTKS (PubMed:32698189, 39192031); 2) In nucleolar contexts, its miscibility with NPM1 promotes perinucleolar heterochromatin (PNH) formation, which—when unrestricted by DDX18—drives differentiation in human embryonic stem cells (PubMed:39738032); 3) IRTKS-mediated SUMOylation of HP1α stabilizes heterochromatin condensates; disruption causes heterochromatin loss, derepression of repetitive DNA, cGAS-STING pathway activation, and cellular senescence (PubMed:39192031).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features driving HP1α phase separation are explicitly detailed in the provided data. The key_drivers sections across all studies report 'Not specified' for domains, PTMs, splicing, oligomerization, repeat features, and mutations related to HP1α's phase separation behavior (PubMed:30425322, 32698189, 39192031, 39738032). Phase separation is primarily regulated through extrinsic interactions with partners and modified nucleosomes.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: HP1α phase separation is extrinsically regulated by multiple partners: 1) It requires H3K9me3-modified nucleosome arrays for liquid droplet formation, with no phase separation occurring with unmodified arrays (PubMed:30425322); 2) It co-phase separates with NPM1, forming homogeneous mixtures (PubMed:39738032); 3) It is enriched in MeCP2 condensates, facilitating heterochromatin compaction (PubMed:32698189); 4) It forms shared condensates with IRTKS (BAIAP2L1), with mutual enhancement of phase separation (PubMed:39192031); 5) SUMOylation by Ubc9 (recruited by IRTKS) stabilizes HP1α and enables larger droplet formation (PubMed:39192031). HP1α also exhibits context-dependent miscibility: miscible with DDX18 alone but excluded from ternary DDX18-NPM1 condensates (PubMed:39738032).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: MEF2D undergoes phase separation, forming dynamic liquid-like nuclear condensates (termed transcriptional clusters) and solid-like cytoplasmic aggregates (described as higher-order assemblies) in both nucleus and cytoplasm (PubMed:36898987). The nuclear condensates exhibit liquid properties including spherical morphology, rapid FRAP recovery, and fusion capability, while cytoplasmic aggregates show solid characteristics with minimal FRAP recovery and stable morphology (PubMed:36898987). Transitions between material states occur, with nuclear liquid condensates maturing into cytoplasmic solid aggregates, regulated by β-domain dynamics (PubMed:36898987).
Functional Summary: MEF2D phase separation facilitates muscle cell differentiation by concentrating myogenic regulators (including MyoD) and transcriptional machinery within higher-order assemblies, potentiating expression of muscle-specific genes (PubMed:36898987). Rigid β-domain variants enhance transcriptional activity (135-178% of wild-type) and accelerate early myotube formation, while the var4 variant promotes differentiation independently of MyoD/desmin upregulation (PubMed:36898987). Notably, the observed solid aggregates are functional rather than pathological, with no disease-linked solidification reported (PubMed:36898987).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by MEF2D's disordered transactivation domain (TAD), particularly the β-domain (residues 286-292) which serves as an ordered interaction hub (PubMed:36898987). Mutations within this domain critically alter material states: rigid variants (e.g., var8 W31 mutation) promote solid aggregates through enhanced hydrophobic/aromatic interactions, while mobile variants (e.g., var4 N30 mutation) enable context-dependent liquid/solid switching via polar/charge interactions (PubMed:36898987). Variant var3 (K292) predominantly forms liquid condensates, whereas var8 induces solid-prone assemblies (PubMed:36898987).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: MEF2D co-phase separates with the transcription factor MyoD (UniProt: P15172), which enhances transcriptional synergy and stabilizes assemblies through physical interaction (PubMed:36898987). Disruption of MyoD via mutagenesis impairs synergistic gene activation with MEF2D, confirming its functional partnership in condensate formation (PubMed:36898987).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: KPNB1 does not undergo intrinsic phase separation (PubMed:36482422) but regulates biomolecular condensates through its nuclear transport activity. It localizes to both the nucleus and cytoplasm (PubMed:36482422) and associates with pathological TDP-43 inclusions (PubMed:36482422). As a soluble chaperone, it dissolves aberrant aggregates without undergoing material state transitions itself (PubMed:36482422). KPNB1 facilitates nuclear translocation of phase-separating proteins like CNBP and phospho-HDAC6, enabling their condensate formation in target compartments (PubMed:37186134, 39198689).
Functional Summary: KPNB1's condensate regulation has dual physiological and pathological impacts: It restores nucleocytoplasmic transport and reduces neurodegeneration by dissolving pathological TDP-43 inclusions in ALS/FTD models (PubMed:36482422). Paradoxically, its nuclear transport function enables oncogenic condensates—facilitating CNBP/SMARCC2 assemblies that drive ribosome biogenesis and neuroblastoma progression (PubMed:37186134), and promoting phospho-HDAC6 transcriptional condensates that establish aberrant chromatin architecture in triple-negative breast cancer (PubMed:39198689).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: KPNB1 lacks intrinsic phase separation drivers but contains a critical HEAT 1-8 domain that binds FG-Nups via a Nup-Interacting Site (NIS) (PubMed:36482422). Mutations in this domain (I178A/F217A/Y255A/I263R) abolish its disaggregation activity while preserving structural integrity (PubMed:36482422). This domain mediates KPNB1's chaperone function by disrupting pathological phase transitions in client proteins like TDP-43 and Nup62 (PubMed:36482422).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: KPNB1 interacts with multiple partners to regulate condensate dynamics: It is recruited to pathological aggregates by Nup62 (PubMed:36482422) and dissolves TDP-43/Nup62 co-aggregates through FG-motif interactions (PubMed:36482422). As a nuclear transport factor, KPNB1 enables phase separation of client proteins—facilitating CNBP translocation to form neuroblastoma-driving condensates with SMARCC2 (PubMed:37186134) and mediating phospho-HDAC6 nuclear import for transcriptional condensate formation in triple-negative breast cancer (PubMed:39198689).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NOLC1 (Q14978) undergoes self-driven phase separation in the nucleus, exhibiting autonomous condensation capacity that enables Cajal body and nucleolus association (PubMed:36224177). It forms liquid-like condensates and remodels coilin assemblies from fibrillar to punctate states (PubMed:36224177).
Functional Summary: NOLC1 phase separation is essential for Cajal body assembly, facilitating snRNP maturation, telomerase concentration, and splicing fidelity; its dysregulation is linked to diseases such as spinal muscular atrophy (PubMed:36224177). Depletion abolishes coilin condensation and disrupts Cajal body maintenance (PubMed:36224177).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of NOLC1 is intrinsically driven by its intrinsically disordered region (IDR), which is sufficient for condensation as demonstrated by light-induced droplet formation of the IDR-Cry2 construct (PubMed:36224177).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: NOLC1 directly interacts with coilin, serving as a scaffold for coilin recruitment and structural remodeling in Cajal bodies, with their interaction mediated by the R36 residue in coilin as confirmed by FRET and co-IP assays (PubMed:36224177).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SLMAP (Q14BN4) undergoes self-driven phase separation to form constitutive, ER-localized liquid-like condensates in the cytoplasm (PubMed:36318920). These condensates exhibit liquid properties including fusion and rapid FRAP recovery, with no observed material state transitions reported.
Functional Summary: SLMAP condensates enrich MST and SIKE to facilitate STRIPAK complex-mediated dephosphorylation and inactivation of MST, thereby inhibiting the Hippo pathway (PubMed:36318920). In tri-scaffold condensates with AMOT/KIBRA, KIBRA-mediated SIKE exclusion inactivates SLMAP's inhibitory function, promoting Hippo pathway activation during stress responses (PubMed:36318920). Phase separation deficiency (ΔCC mutation) impairs SLMAP's regulatory function and elevates MST activity (PubMed:36318920).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of SLMAP is intrinsically driven by its coiled-coil domains (amino acids 160-762), with deletion of these domains (ΔCC mutation) abolishing phase separation capacity (PubMed:36318920).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SLMAP co-phase separates with KIBRA to form biphasic condensates where KIBRA competes with SIKE for SLMAP binding, exhibiting immiscible phases in vitro and adjacent condensates in cells (PubMed:36318920). SLMAP additionally forms tri-scaffold condensates with AMOT and KIBRA during osmotic stress, with AMOT enhancing KIBRA-SLMAP interactions (PubMed:36318920).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SUZ12 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in the nucleus, forming dynamic condensates (PubMed:37537343). It co-phase separates with FUBP3 to form liquid-like droplets and associates with CAF-1 nuclear bodies, maintaining a liquid material state without observed transitions (PubMed:37537343, 33739466).
Functional Summary: SUZ12 condensates regulate PRC2-mediated H3K27me3 methylation to repress tumor-suppressor genes (e.g., GATA2, EYA4), promoting neuroblastoma progression (PubMed:37537343). In HIV-1 latency, recruitment to CAF-1 bodies enables epigenetic silencing of the viral LTR through H3K27me3 maintenance, where disruption reactivates latent virus (PubMed:33739466).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of SUZ12 is intrinsically driven by its intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), which are essential for LLPS (PubMed:37537343).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SUZ12 requires FUBP3 for co-condensation, forming shared liquid droplets via IDR-mediated interactions (PubMed:37537343). It is also recruited to CHAF1A-mediated CAF-1 nuclear bodies, where it co-localizes with epigenetic modifiers to modulate H3K27me3 marks on the HIV-1 LTR (PubMed:33739466).

Protein Name: 116 kDa U5 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein component
Overall Phase Separation Overview: EFTUD2 (Q15029) is a component of the U4•U6/U5 tri-snRNP complex that concentrates in Cajal bodies (CBs) within the nucleus (PubMed:39602297). It does not undergo self-driven phase separation but associates with CBs as part of spliceosomal machinery, with depletion experiments showing increased CB formation, suggesting regulatory roles in condensate dynamics (PubMed:39602297). Material state properties were not specified.
Functional Summary: As part of spliceosomal machinery assembled in Cajal bodies, EFTUD2 contributes to snRNP maturation (PubMed:39602297). Its depletion increases CB abundance, indicating potential accumulation of immature snRNPs in condensates and implicating EFTUD2 in maintaining CB homeostasis for efficient spliceosome assembly (PubMed:39602297).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic regulators (domains, mutations, PTMs, or specific regions) driving phase separation were identified for EFTUD2 in the provided data; studies exclusively examined full-length protein behavior (PubMed:39602297).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: EFTUD2's condensate association is extrinsically regulated through its integration into the U4•U6/U5 tri-snRNP complex, a critical spliceosomal component whose assembly in CBs facilitates EFTUD2 enrichment (PubMed:39602297).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: RNPS1 (Q15287) undergoes phase separation primarily in the nucleus. It forms chromatin-excluding condensates in vivo, with dynamic properties evidenced by increased partition coefficient during cellular deformation (PubMed:39557835). Additionally, RNPS1 is recruited as a client protein into CLK2-driven liquid-like condensates that reorganize nuclear speckles, co-localizing with markers like SC35 and SON (PubMed:39119950). Material states are characterized as liquid-like in CLK2-associated contexts, but no state transitions were reported for RNPS1-specific condensates.
Functional Summary: When sequestered into CLK2 condensates, RNPS1 contributes to the reorganization of nuclear speckles and promotes intron retention. This process leads to nuclear transcript sequestration, cellular senescence, tumor growth inhibition, and impaired stemness maintenance in glioma stem cells (PubMed:39119950). No functional implications were reported for RNPS1's chromatin-excluding condensates observed during cellular deformation (PubMed:39557835).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or post-translational modifications regulating RNPS1 phase separation were identified in the provided studies. Both papers exclusively used full-length RNPS1 constructs without domain manipulation or mutational analysis (PubMed:39119950, 39557835).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RNPS1's phase separation is extrinsically regulated by CLK2, which recruits RNPS1 as a client into its condensates through protein-protein interactions. This recruitment occurs during CLK2-driven reorganization of nuclear speckles, demonstrated via co-IP/MS and co-localization assays (PubMed:39119950). No other extrinsic partners (proteins, RNA, ions, or chemicals) were reported to directly modulate RNPS1 phase separation.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Her4 undergoes partner-driven phase separation (class PS-other) as demonstrated in vitro, where its phosphorylated intracellular domain (pHer4Kinase-Tail) forms droplets with effector proteins (PubMed:35231400). The subcellular location, membrane-less organelle associations, material state properties, and state transitions were not specified in the provided data.
Functional Summary: Droplet formation with SHP2 and SHC may regulate receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK)-containing signaling complexes, though specific physiological or pathological roles were not detailed in the provided data (PubMed:35231400).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation involves the Her4 intracellular domain (residues 718-1305), but no specific intrinsic domains, post-translational modifications, mutations, or oligomerization features driving this behavior were identified in the provided study (PubMed:35231400).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Her4 phase separation is extrinsically regulated by the phosphatase SHP2 and adaptor protein SHC, with which it forms heterotypic droplets in vitro (PubMed:35231400). Phosphorylation of Her4's kinase-tail domain is required for this interaction.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SAFB undergoes phase separation to form liquid-like nuclear granules (nuclear stress bodies) in response to heat stress (43°C), with formation inhibited by 2,5-hexanediol and SB366791 (PubMed:34067147). These granules dissolve during recovery and are involved in regulating HSP27 upregulation.
Functional Summary: SAFB granule formation confers thermal resistance by upregulating HSP27 during recovery from heat stress, while inhibition of granule formation enhances apoptosis and reduces cell viability under heat stress conditions (PubMed:34067147).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic regulators of SAFB phase separation were reported in the provided context (PubMed:34067147).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SAFB phase separation is induced by heat stress (43°C) and inhibited by chemical compounds 2,5-hexanediol (a disruptor of hydrophobic interactions) and TRPV1 antagonist SB366791 (PubMed:34067147).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Sec23a (Q15436) undergoes phase separation in the absence of Sar1 GTPase, forming unique COPII condensates in the cytoplasm that exhibit dual liquid-like and gel-like material properties. These condensates display rapid molecular exchange (t½ recovery ~3-4s via FRAP), fusion competence, and partial dissolution/coalescence cycles, classified as hydrogel structures. They distinctly associate with cargo packaging machinery and are sensitive to 1,6-hexanediol. Sec23a is also recruited to SEC16A-driven condensates at ER exit sites (ERES) (PubMed:37300835, 37643612).
Functional Summary: Sec23a phase separation enables Sar1-independent cargo export from the ER by promoting membrane deformation and non-canonical transport carrier biogenesis. However, persistent condensates delay Golgi trafficking due to impaired disassembly, reversible by 1,6-hexanediol treatment. Recruitment to SEC16A condensates organizes COPII machinery at ER exit sites for efficient secretory trafficking. Disruption of this recruitment – via SEC16A tyrosine mutations or impaired phosphorylation dynamics – abrogates ERES formation and blocks cargo export (PubMed:37300835, 37643612).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of Sec23a is intrinsically driven by disordered domains, particularly the flexible 'L loop' region, and low-complexity regions within the Sec23-Sec24 heterodimer. These domains facilitate multivalent interactions essential for scaffold formation in COPII condensates (PubMed:37300835).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Sec23a requires co-scaffolding partners including Sec24a, Sec31a, and TFG for stable COPII condensate formation. Its recruitment and local concentration are enhanced by multivalent interactions with Sec16a and Tango1. Crucially, Sec23a partitions into SEC16A-driven condensates at ER exit sites, where its incorporation is regulated by SEC16A phosphorylation states mediated by DYRK3 kinase and phosphatases. Phosphorylation of SEC16A promotes condensate dissolution, while dephosphorylation stabilizes recruitment (PubMed:37300835, 37643612).

Protein Name: Nuclear receptor subfamily 0 group B member 2
Overall Phase Separation Overview: NR0B2 undergoes phase separation driven by extrinsic factors, as evidenced by in vitro droplet formation experiments (PubMed:39591966). While specific subcellular locations and material states remain unspecified, the protein's phase separation behavior is fundamentally linked to sorbitol-mediated biomolecular condensation.
Functional Summary: NR0B2 phase separation is functionally implicated in breast cancer pathology, where matrix stiffening promotes condensation via sorbitol accumulation (PubMed:39591966). Pharmacological or genetic manipulation of sorbitol concentration directly modulates condensate formation in this mechano-dependent disease context (PubMed:39591966).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic regulators (domains, mutations, PTMs, or structural features) of NR0B2 phase separation were identified or reported in the provided study (PubMed:39591966).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation of NR0B2 is extrinsically regulated by sorbitol, which acts as a natural crowding agent to promote biomolecular condensation (PubMed:39591966). This process is mechanistically linked to extracellular matrix stiffening, which controls glucose-to-sorbitol metabolism, with condensate formation being sensitive to physiological sorbitol concentrations but not glucose levels (PubMed:39591966).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: STIL (Q15468) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but co-phase separates with Plk4 to form liquid-like condensates in the cytoplasm, specifically at centrosomes (PubMed:31672968, 33323015). These co-condensates transition from hollow Plk4 spheres to inside-filled structures upon STIL binding, enabling recruitment of downstream components like Sas6 (PubMed:33323015).
Functional Summary: STIL-Plk4 co-phase separation enables centriole biogenesis by forming procentriole assembly bodies that recruit Sas6 and stabilize the condensate structure (PubMed:31672968, 33323015). This process is critical for proper centrosome duplication, with aberrant phase separation potentially contributing to centriole overduplication and genomic instability (PubMed:31672968).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The coiled-coil (CC) domain of STIL is intrinsically involved in co-phase separation, though full-length STIL (not the CC domain alone) is required for functional integration into Plk4 condensates (PubMed:31672968, 33323015). Regions beyond the CC domain cooperate with Plk4 to generate mature condensates (PubMed:33323015).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: STIL strictly requires Plk4 as its primary phase separation partner, forming co-condensates that convert hollow Plk4 spheres into inside-filled structures (PubMed:31672968, 33323015). These co-condensates recruit Sas6 to enable procentriole assembly (PubMed:31672968, 33323015).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NCoA2 (Q15596) forms large nuclear clusters colocalizing with PML nuclear bodies and is recruited to glucocorticoid receptor (GR) condensates upon receptor activation (PubMed:36309135). Its distribution is modulated by extrinsic factors like SOX2, which partitions NCoA2 into diffuse regions overlapping with SOX2 islands (PubMed:36309135). The material state and transitions remain unspecified.
Functional Summary: NCoA2 is critical for GR condensate assembly and transcriptional activation of target genes (PubMed:36309135). SOX2-induced redistribution impairs NCoA2 dynamics and GR interactions, contributing to GR dysfunction and altered transcriptional outcomes relevant to hormone response pathways (PubMed:36309135).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or molecular features driving phase separation were identified in this study (PubMed:36309135). Experimental analysis focused solely on full-length GFP-tagged NCoA2 without domain-specific perturbations.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: NCoA2 recruitment to GR condensates requires glucocorticoid receptor activation, with FCCS confirming direct GR-NCoA2 interactions essential for condensate formation (PubMed:36309135). SOX2 redistributes NCoA2 to heterogeneous nuclear regions without direct binding, altering its compartmentalization and dynamics as evidenced by FCS showing partial immobilization (~40% molecules) and reduced mobility (PubMed:36309135).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: GMAP210 undergoes phase separation (classified as PS-other) to form spherical cytoplasmic condensates that exhibit partial fluidity and detach from the Golgi apparatus over time (PubMed:32668013). It is associated with Golgin condensates and exists in a liquid-like state, with no observed material state transitions.
Functional Summary: The phase separation of GMAP210 has a potential role in defining the cis-Golgi compartment through self-assembly, as observed by the formation of spherical condensates that initially concentrate at the Golgi rims before detaching into the cytoplasm (PubMed:32668013).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of GMAP210 is intrinsically driven by its coiled-coil domains, which facilitate intermolecular interactions leading to condensation (PubMed:32668013).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators or partner proteins modulating GMAP210 phase separation are reported in the provided data (PubMed:32668013).

Protein Name: Probable JmjC domain-containing histone demethylation protein 2C
Overall Phase Separation Overview: JMJD1C undergoes self-driven phase separation to form dynamic, liquid-like nuclear condensates in vitro and in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cells, as evidenced by rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), droplet fusion, and spherical morphology (PubMed:39450904). These condensates are not associated with known membrane-less organelles (e.g., stress granules or nucleoli) and exhibit concentration-dependent formation that is enhanced by molecular crowding agents like PEG (PubMed:39450904). No material state transitions (e.g., liquid-to-solid) were reported (PubMed:39450904).
Functional Summary: JMJD1C phase separation facilitates chromatin looping between enhancers and promoters to activate RUNX1-dependent leukemic genes (e.g., EGR1, TOX2), essential for AML cell survival by co-regulating proliferation and metabolic pathways (PubMed:39450904). This function hinges on the dual capability of the N-terminus—phase separation and direct RUNX1 binding—to mediate chromatin interactions; disruption of this region impairs AML growth (PubMed:39450904).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal disordered region (residues 1-757), with the C-terminal subregion (550-757) partially retaining this capability (PubMed:39450904). The full 1-757 region is essential for homotypic interactions and efficient condensation, while truncation (1-647) abolishes phase separation entirely (PubMed:39450904).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: JMJD1C condensates recruit the transcription factor RUNX1 and DNA containing RUNX1 binding motifs via direct interaction (PubMed:39450904). RUNX1 enables DNA incorporation exclusively when motifs are present, facilitating chromatin interactions (PubMed:39450904). Phase separation is enhanced by molecular crowding agents like PEG in vitro (PubMed:39450904).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Twist1 (Q15672) undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) to form liquid-like nuclear condensates at miR-9 super-enhancers (PubMed:36669583). Its phase separation behavior is concentration-dependent, sensitive to salt concentrations, and enhanced by crowding agents like PEG8000. These dynamic condensates exhibit rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), droplet fusion, and spherical morphology, with dissolution occurring upon treatment with 1,6-hexanediol or metformin (PubMed:36669583).
Functional Summary: Twist1 phase separation at miR-9 super-enhancers activates oncogenic transcription, driving epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), migration, invasion, and tumor growth in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) (PubMed:36669583). Disruption of condensates by metformin or 1,6-hexanediol suppresses miR-9 expression and inhibits HCC progression. The coactivator p300 is essential for maintaining condensate integrity, as its knockout impairs nuclear translocation of Twist1 and reduces chromatin accessibility at target enhancers (PubMed:36669583).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of Twist1 is intrinsically driven by its N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR, residues 1-120), which facilitates multivalent IDR-IDR interactions through electrostatic and hydrophobic forces (PubMed:36669583). Charge-disrupting mutations (D/E or R/K to alanine) within this IDR significantly inhibit droplet formation, demonstrating the critical role of charged residues in mediating phase separation (PubMed:36669583).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Twist1 co-phase separates with the transcription factor YY1, with mutual enhancement via IDR-IDR interactions, and requires the coactivator p300 for condensate stabilization and nuclear translocation (PubMed:36669583). Phase separation is promoted by molecular crowding agents (e.g., PEG8000) but inhibited by 1,6-hexanediol and metformin. The process is energy-dependent, as evidenced by reduced FRAP recovery after ATP depletion, and shows sensitivity to ionic conditions (PubMed:36669583).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: HuR (ELAVL1) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but associates with multiple membrane-less organelles, primarily localizing to both the nucleus and cytoplasm (PubMed:36151083, 33650968). It forms mesh-like condensates when fused to multivalent domains such as TIS11B or FUS (PubMed:33650968). HuR is consistently observed in stress granules (both conventional and energy deficiency-induced) as a core component (PubMed:36151083) and in P-bodies (PubMed:39776340, 40056914). The material state of its condensates is not explicitly characterized, though mesh-like organization is reported in fusion constructs (PubMed:33650968).
Functional Summary: HuR's phase separation behavior has significant physiological and pathological implications. In stress granules, it contributes to mRNA regulation during cellular stress, with dysregulation linked to neurodegeneration in C9-ALS patient neurons (PubMed:36151083). In P-bodies, HuR enables mRNA stabilization by Syncrip; disruption of this process due to Syncrip mutations causes neurodevelopmental disorders through dysregulated Notch signaling (PubMed:39776340). HuR's inhibition of Ago2 phase separation regulates miRNA-mediated repression, with amyloid beta oligomers compromising this function in Alzheimer's disease contexts (PubMed:40056914).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation capability is intrinsically mediated by HuR's RNA recognition motifs (RRM1 and RRM2), which are sufficient to drive mesh-like condensate formation when combined with heterologous multivalent domains (PubMed:33650968). No specific mutations, post-translational modifications, or oligomerization features regulating HuR phase separation are reported in the provided data.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: HuR's condensate association is extrinsically regulated by multiple partners and conditions. It co-localizes with G3BP1 in stress granules alongside mRNA, PABP, eIF4G, RPS6, and TDP-43 (PubMed:36151083). In P-bodies, HuR is recruited to Syncrip condensates where it stabilizes target mRNAs (PubMed:39776340). HuR inhibits Ago2 phase separation by sequestering miRNAs, thereby regulating P-body targeting (PubMed:40056914). Mesh-like condensate formation requires target mRNAs with high NED values (PubMed:33650968). Energy stress (ATP reduction) promotes HuR inclusion in stress granules (PubMed:36151083).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: CEBPE (Q15744) was investigated for liquid-liquid phase separation in HEK 293T cells using live-cell imaging, but no LLPS behavior was observed as evidenced by the absence of puncta formation. The study specifically examined the full-length protein and concluded no phase separation occurred under the tested conditions (PubMed:37903757).
Functional Summary: No functional implications related to phase separation were established for CEBPE, as the experimental results demonstrated no LLPS behavior in cellular contexts (PubMed:37903757).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, motifs, mutations, or structural features driving phase separation were identified for CEBPE, as no LLPS was detected in the experimental analysis of the full-length protein (PubMed:37903757).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators, binding partners, or environmental conditions influencing phase separation were reported for CEBPE, consistent with the absence of observed LLPS behavior in the study (PubMed:37903757).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SRC-1 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in the nucleus, forming dynamic, liquid-like condensates both in vitro and in cells (PubMed:33850322). It associates with transcriptional condensates through co-localization with YAP/TEAD4 and forms distinct condensates with ERα upon estrogen stimulation (PubMed:33850322). No material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: SRC-1 phase separation facilitates oncogenic transcription in non-small cell lung cancer by forming condensates enriched with H3K27ac and RNA Pol II-S5P that upregulate genes like CTGF and ANKRD1 (PubMed:33850322). Disruption of LLPS by EVG suppresses cancer proliferation, migration, and transcriptional activity, demonstrating its role in tumorigenesis (PubMed:33850322).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of SRC-1 is intrinsically driven by its second intrinsic disordered region (IDR-2, residues 967–1362), which contains prion-like domains and is sufficient for liquid-like droplet formation in physiological conditions (PubMed:33850322). Other domains contribute to condensate maintenance but IDR-2 serves as the primary driver (PubMed:33850322).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SRC-1 co-phase separates with YAP and TEAD4 to form transcriptional condensates, and with ERα upon estrogen activation (PubMed:33850322). Its phase separation is disrupted by the chemical elvitegravir (EVG), which binds SRC-1, alters multivalency, and dissolves condensates without affecting YAP/TEAD4 assemblies (PubMed:33850322).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Smad2 (Q15796) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but requires partners to co-phase separate, exhibiting liquid-like behavior as part of the Smad2/3/4 complex (PubMed:38769521). This complex formation occurs in the nucleus and is concentration-dependent. The material state remains liquid without observed transitions (PubMed:38769521).
Functional Summary: The co-phase separation of Smad2 within the Smad2/3/4 complex enables transcriptional activation of the TAT gene, triggering caspase-9-mediated apoptosis and suppressing hepatocellular carcinoma progression (PubMed:38769521). This mechanism links liquid condensate formation to tumor suppression pathways without observed pathological transitions (PubMed:38769521).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Smad2 lacks intrinsic phase separation drivers, with no identified disordered domains, PrLD regions, or repeat features (PubMed:38769521). Its phase separation entirely depends on oligomerization with Smad3 and Smad4 partners (PubMed:38769521). Phosphorylation by TβRI may contribute to activation but was not directly tested for phase separation modulation (PubMed:38769521).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Smad2 co-phase separates exclusively with Smad3 and Smad4, forming ternary complex droplets in vitro (PubMed:38769521). This process is strictly dependent on both partners, with Smad4 acting as the primary scaffold driver (PubMed:38769521). No ions, chemicals, or additional regulators were identified for Smad2-specific behavior (PubMed:38769521).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: EZH2 does not undergo self-driven phase separation but is recruited into phase-separated nuclear bodies formed by other proteins, exclusively in the nucleus (PubMed:35642598). It associates with nuclear bodies formed by CBX4 and co-localizes with CHAF1A nuclear bodies (PubMed:33739466, 35642598). Within CBX4 condensates, EZH2 exhibits liquid-like dynamics but does not independently form condensates (PubMed:35642598). No material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: EZH2's phase separation enables SUMOylation-dependent enhancement of H3K27me3 catalytic activity within nuclear bodies, reinforcing heterochromatin formation on HIV-1 LTR to maintain viral latency (PubMed:35642598). This mechanism contributes to epigenetic silencing in HIV-1 latency models and primary CD4+ T cells, with disruption of condensates reactivating latent virus (PubMed:33739466, 35642598).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The recruitment and functionality of EZH2 within condensates are intrinsically regulated by its N-terminal region (residues 1-68), which is essential for SUMOylation (PubMed:35642598). This post-translational modification is critical for its retention and enzymatic activity within phase-separated environments.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: EZH2 is extrinsically recruited into phase-separated nuclear bodies by scaffold proteins CBX4 and CHAF1A (PubMed:33739466, 35642598). Within CBX4 condensates, SUMO4 mediates EZH2 SUMOylation, enhancing its methyltransferase activity (PubMed:35642598). Recruitment requires intact phase separation capability of CBX4, as LLPS-deficient CBX4 mutants abolish EZH2 incorporation (PubMed:35642598).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: H-Ras (Q16046) undergoes phase separation behavior classified as 'other', partitioning into liquid-ordered domains and forming clusters upon heptanol treatment in live-cell systems (PubMed:35490741).
Functional Summary: The phase separation behavior of H-Ras, particularly its partitioning into liquid-ordered domains, is essential for cellular signal transduction processes (PubMed:35490741).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The partitioning of H-Ras into liquid-ordered domains is intrinsically driven by palmitoylated cysteine residues within its membrane anchor region (PubMed:35490741).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Heptanol, a chemical compound, induces clustering of H-Ras as demonstrated through TIRF imaging experiments in SH-SY5Y cells (PubMed:35490741).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: β-synuclein (SNCB) does not undergo spontaneous liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) but partitions into α-synuclein condensates in the cytoplasm (PubMed:39384788). It promotes α-synuclein LLPS while inhibiting its liquid-to-solid phase transition (LSPS), maintaining dynamic liquid-like properties in partner condensates (PubMed:39384788). Disease-associated mutants (V70M, P123H) disrupt this regulation, accelerating pathological solidification (PubMed:39384788).
Functional Summary: By maintaining α-synuclein in a dynamic liquid state, β-synuclein prevents amyloid toxicity and neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies (PubMed:39384788). Disease-associated mutants disrupt this protective function, exacerbating α-synuclein aggregation, movement defects, and reduced lifespan in C. elegans models—directly linking phase separation dysregulation to in vivo neurotoxicity (PubMed:39384788).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation regulation of β-synuclein is intrinsically governed by its domain architecture, featuring a positively charged N-terminal, hydrophobic NAC domain, and negatively charged C-terminal (PubMed:39384788). Disease-associated mutations (V70M, P123H) and brain-specific splicing isoforms (β-Syn120, β-Syn104) critically alter its function—reducing condensate fluidity and promoting pathological solidification of α-synuclein (PubMed:39384788).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: β-synuclein co-phase separates with α-synuclein as its primary partner, partitioning into α-synuclein condensates within 60 minutes and modulating their dynamics via electrostatic interactions (PubMed:39384788). Wildtype β-synuclein enhances α-synuclein droplet fluidity (72% FRAP recovery) and delays amyloid formation, while mutants (V70M/P123H) reduce fluidity (10-20% FRAP recovery) and accelerate fibrillization (PubMed:39384788).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SRSF7 partitions into nuclear speckles in the nucleus, where it positions associated RNA motifs toward the speckle interior (PubMed:38638569). These speckles exhibit liquid-like properties, but their dynamics are impaired by the arginine-rich dipeptide repeat protein PR, which reduces SRSF7 mobility and increases condensate viscosity (PubMed:27768896).
Functional Summary: SRSF7-mediated RNA organization within nuclear speckles supports coordinated pre-mRNA splicing (PubMed:38638569). Pathological disruption by PR impairs speckle dynamics, contributing to C9-ALS/FTD pathogenesis through cellular toxicity and dysfunction of membrane-less organelles (PubMed:27768896).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The nuclear partitioning of SRSF7 is driven by its RNA-binding domains, which specifically recognize SRSF7 motifs in RNA transcripts to facilitate spatial organization within speckles (PubMed:38638569).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SRSF7 requires SRSF7 motif-containing RNA transcripts as scaffolds to position RNA domains within nuclear speckles (PubMed:38638569). Its dynamics are disrupted through direct interaction with the dipeptide repeat protein PR, which significantly reduces SRSF7 mobility in speckles as demonstrated by impaired FRAP recovery (PubMed:27768896).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TAZ does not undergo autonomous phase separation but partitions into pre-formed biomolecular condensates as a client protein (PubMed:37027309, 38322995, 31792379, 37494632). It localizes to cytoplasmic mitochondrial biomolecular condensates (Mi-BCs) and nuclear transcriptional condensates, exhibiting liquid-like material properties in both contexts (PubMed:38322995, 31792379, 37494632). No material state transitions specific to TAZ were reported.
Functional Summary: As a cardiolipin remodeling enzyme in mitochondrial Mi-BCs, TAZ supports cardiolipin metabolism and cristae maintenance, with deficiency linked to Barth syndrome (PubMed:38322995). Within YAP nuclear condensates, TAZ contributes to chromatin reorganization and transcriptional activation of proliferation genes (e.g., Ctgf, Cyr61), with dysregulation implicated in cancer (PubMed:31792379). In human bone marrow stem cells, TAZ recruitment into YAP condensates under low mechanical stress inhibits osteogenic differentiation (PubMed:37494632).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: TAZ phase separation is intrinsically regulated by post-translational modifications, particularly phosphorylation at Ser89, which enables its recruitment into synthetic coacervates via 14-3-3 binding (PubMed:37027309). No domains, mutations, or intrinsic features directly driving autonomous condensation were identified in the provided data.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TAZ partitioning requires extrinsic scaffolds: Mieap recruits TAZ into mitochondrial biomolecular condensates (Mi-BCs) where it concentrates in the Mieap-depleted phase (PubMed:38322995); 14-3-3 anchors phosphorylated TAZ in synthetic coacervates (PubMed:37027309); and YAP recruits TAZ into nuclear/cytoplasmic condensates under hyperosmotic stress or in low-elasticity hydrogels (PubMed:31792379, 37494632). The chemical verteporfin inhibits YAP/TAZ condensate formation by disrupting YAP-TEAD interactions (PubMed:37494632).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: HIF-1α does not undergo autonomous phase separation but is recruited to TiPARP nuclear bodies in the nucleus (PubMed:32482854). These TiPARP condensates form in an ADP-ribosylation-dependent manner, though the material state of HIF-1α within them remains uncharacterized.
Functional Summary: Recruitment to TiPARP condensates enables HUWE1-mediated ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of HIF-1α, suppressing HIF-1 signaling pathways, inhibiting the Warburg effect (glycolysis), angiogenesis, and tumor growth (PubMed:32482854).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The recruitment of HIF-1α to condensates is intrinsically regulated by its bHLH-PAS1 domain (amino acids 1-400), which mediates essential interactions with TiPARP (PubMed:32482854).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: HIF-1α recruitment requires catalytic activity of the scaffold protein TiPARP and occurs within TiPARP nuclear condensates under hypoxia (PubMed:32482854). Within these condensates, HIF-1α interacts with the E3 ubiquitin ligase HUWE1, facilitating ubiquitination and degradation.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PGS1 functions as a client enzyme incorporated into mitochondrial biomolecular condensates (Mi-BCs) formed by Mieap, exhibiting wetting behavior at the interface between Mieap-rich and enzyme-rich phases without undergoing self-driven phase separation (PubMed:38322995). These multi-phase condensates are localized to mitochondria and display liquid-like properties including fusion and partial recovery in FRAP assays (PubMed:38322995).
Functional Summary: Compartmentalization of PGS1 within Mi-BCs supports its catalytic function in phosphatidylglycerophosphate synthesis during cardiolipin biosynthesis, thereby contributing to mitochondrial cristae maintenance and oxidative phosphorylation (PubMed:38322995). This spatial organization optimizes substrate accessibility for lipid metabolic reactions critical for cellular energy production (PubMed:38322995).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic molecular features (domains, mutations, or post-translational modifications) driving or regulating PGS1 phase separation were identified in the study (PubMed:38322995).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: PGS1 recruitment into condensates is extrinsically regulated by the scaffold protein Mieap, which enables compartmentalization within Mi-BCs through direct co-localization (PubMed:38322995). This positioning facilitates PGS1's enzymatic activity at the phase interface within the mitochondrial inner membrane environment (PubMed:38322995).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: INAVA undergoes stimulus-induced phase separation in the cytoplasm (PubMed:34251416), forming condensates in response to IL-1β, reactive oxygen species (H₂O₂), proteasome inhibitors (MG132, bortezomib), and HSP90 inhibitors (ganetespib, 17AAG) (PubMed:34251416). These condensates are distinct from stress granules, P-bodies, and aggresomes (PubMed:34251416) and exhibit a material state transition: initially liquid-like (with fusion and rapid FRAP recovery) that matures into less dynamic or solid states over time or under continuous proteotoxic stress (PubMed:34251416).
Functional Summary: INAVA condensates compartmentalize ubiquitination machinery (βTrCP2 and ubiquitin) to regulate proteostasis during cellular stress, with the long isoform specifically required for stress-induced ubiquitination (PubMed:34251416). This phase separation functionally competes with INAVA's role in cell-junction maintenance mediated by ARNO recruitment (PubMed:34251416), but is dispensable for IL-1β–TRAF6–NF-κB signaling amplification (PubMed:34251416).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by the N-terminal intrinsically disordered region exclusive to the long isoform of INAVA, which is essential for condensate formation (PubMed:34251416). Alternative splicing generates a short isoform lacking this region that cannot undergo phase separation (PubMed:34251416).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: INAVA condensates co-localize with the E3 ligase βTrCP2 and ubiquitin (PubMed:34251416), while the protein ARNO extrinsically regulates phase separation by competing for INAVA localization—recruiting it to cell junctions and reducing cytosolic condensate formation (PubMed:34251416). Condensate induction is triggered by extrinsic stressors (IL-1β, H₂O₂, proteasome/HSP90 inhibitors), and their resolution is accelerated by inhibition of p38α or mTOR pathways (PubMed:34251416).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: USH1G (Q495M9) undergoes partner-dependent phase separation, requiring MYO7A and USH1C to form liquid-like condensates in the cytoplasm, associated with receptor clusters (PubMed:31644917). When expressed alone, it localizes predominantly to the nucleus and forms puncta at high expression levels, but does not undergo self-driven phase separation (PubMed:31644917). No material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: Phase separation of the MYO7A/USH1C/USH1G complex enables assembly of stereocilia tip-link densities, providing mechanical stability for hearing and balance (PubMed:31644917). Defects in this process are linked to Usher syndrome, though no specific USH1G mutations affecting phase separation were reported (PubMed:31644917).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of USH1G is intrinsically regulated by its binding domains that interact with MYO7A's N-terminal MyTH4-FERM domain and USH1C, enabling multivalent interactions essential for tripartite complex condensation (PubMed:31644917).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: USH1G exclusively co-phase separates with extrinsic partners MYO7A and USH1C to form membraneless condensates in cells, as demonstrated by co-localization in puncta (PubMed:31644917). Condensate formation requires both partners, with MYO7A serving as a critical scaffold for complex assembly (PubMed:31644917).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: VPS26B (Q4G0F5) undergoes phase separation behavior classified as PS-other, forming cytoplasmic puncta that co-localize with P-bodies in vivo, as observed in HeLa cells. The primary subcellular location is the cytoplasm, with specific association to P-body membrane-less organelles. Material state and state transitions were not specified in the study (PubMed:38459060).
Functional Summary: VPS26B phase separation is implicated in P-body assembly, with cytoplasmic puncta formation co-localizing with the P-body marker EDC4, suggesting a role in cellular organization through this membrane-less organelle (PubMed:38459060).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, modifications, mutations, or specific protein regions driving phase separation were identified; experiments studied the full-length endogenous protein without characterizing specific drivers (PubMed:38459060).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators, partner proteins, or environmental modulators of VPS26B phase separation were reported in the study (PubMed:38459060).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: AMOT undergoes self-driven phase separation to form liquid-like condensates in the cytoplasm in response to cell-cell contact or osmotic stress (PubMed:36318920). These condensates, termed 'Hippo-activating condensates', enrich core Hippo pathway components including MST/SAV, LATS/MOB, and YAP, exhibiting liquid material properties with fusion and rapid FRAP recovery without reported state transitions (PubMed:36318920).
Functional Summary: AMOT condensates facilitate Hippo pathway activation by enriching core components (MST/SAV, LATS/MOB, YAP) during cellular stress, enabling phosphorylation cascades that regulate YAP activity (PubMed:36318920). Phase separation deficiency (e.g., via ΔCC mutation) impairs YAP phosphorylation and target gene repression, demonstrating its critical role in Hippo-mediated signaling and cellular homeostasis (PubMed:36318920).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of AMOT is intrinsically driven by its coiled-coil domains (CC, residues 430-751), which are essential for droplet formation (PubMed:36318920). Conversely, the actin-binding domain (AB, residues 157-191) suppresses phase separation by sequestering AMOT to F-actin; mutations disrupting this domain (ΔAB or S175E) enable phase separation even in non-permissive conditions (PubMed:36318920).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: AMOT phase separation is extrinsically regulated by F-actin binding, which suppresses condensate formation in sparse cultures but is relieved during cell-cell contact (PubMed:36318920). AMOT co-phase separates with KIBRA (Q8IX03) via PY-WW domain interactions to form bi-scaffold condensates, and further coalesces with SLMAP (Q14BN4) into tri-scaffold condensates, where AMOT enhances KIBRA-SLMAP interactions (PubMed:36318920).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: CRTC2 undergoes self-driven, cAMP-induced liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) both in vitro and in vivo, forming dynamic liquid-like condensates exclusively in the nucleus (PubMed:35037420). These condensates associate with transcriptional condensates and exhibit properties including rapid FRAP recovery, droplet fusion, and dissolution by 1,6-hexanediol or high salt concentrations. No material state transitions were reported (PubMed:35037420).
Functional Summary: CRTC2 nuclear condensates recruit and concentrate P-TEFb, facilitating its extraction from the inhibitory 7SK snRNP complex to activate transcription elongation of cystogenesis-associated genes (PubMed:35037420). This mechanism is pathologically elevated in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), where aberrant condensates drive cyst formation in renal epithelial cells. Genetic depletion of CRTC2 suppresses cyst growth, confirming its causal role in disease pathogenesis (PubMed:35037420).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR), where arginine residues play a critical role (PubMed:35037420). Arginine-to-alanine (R>A) substitutions within this IDR completely abolish phase separation capacity, as demonstrated through mutagenesis studies and optogenetic assays (PubMed:35037420).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: CRTC2 phase separation is induced by cAMP signaling and modulated by external factors (PubMed:35037420). It co-assembles with the P-TEFb protein complex into condensates, which is essential for functional activation and confirmed through co-localization and co-immunoprecipitation (PubMed:35037420). Formation is inhibited by high salt concentrations and 1,6-hexanediol, indicating sensitivity to ionic conditions and aliphatic alcohols (PubMed:35037420). HEXIM1 indirectly influences CRTC2 condensates by dissolving P-TEFb droplets, which CRTC2 can counteract to restore phase separation (PubMed:35037420).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: GLE1 associates with stress granules as a recruited client component in the cytoplasm, co-localizing within dynamic, liquid-like OptoGranules scaffolded by G3BP1. These granules exhibit fusion behavior and rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), characteristic of liquid condensates (PubMed:30893049).
Functional Summary: As a component of stress granules, GLE1 participates in cellular stress response mechanisms. Chronic persistence of G3BP1-scaffolded granules leads to their evolution into pathological, cytotoxic inclusions containing ubiquitinated proteins and phosphorylated TDP-43, recapitulating features of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) pathology (PubMed:30893049).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic drivers or regulators of GLE1 phase separation were identified in the provided study, as no specific domains, mutations, or modifications were investigated for their role in its condensate behavior (PubMed:30893049).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: GLE1 recruitment into condensates is extrinsically regulated by the scaffold protein G3BP1, which drives stress granule assembly. GLE1 co-partitions with multiple stress granule components including PABP, TDP-43, TIA1, TIAR, eIF4G, eIF3η, ataxin 2, FUS, and polyadenylated mRNAs within the G3BP1-formed OptoGranules (PubMed:30893049).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: USP39 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation to form dynamic, liquid-like condensates exclusively in the nucleolus, specifically within all subcompartments (fibrillar center, dense fibrillar component, granular component) (PubMed:39885503). This behavior is driven by its N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR; residues 1-103) and occurs both in vitro under macromolecular crowding/salt conditions and in vivo within the nucleus (PubMed:39885503). The condensates exhibit rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, fusion events, spherical morphology, and sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol, confirming their liquid material state; no material state transitions were observed under tested conditions (PubMed:39885503).
Functional Summary: USP39 phase separation in the nucleolus promotes lung adenocarcinoma progression by upregulating the oncogenic transcription factor GLI1 (PubMed:39885503). Knockdown of USP39 suppresses GLI1 expression, inhibits cancer cell growth/migration in vitro, and reduces tumor xenograft growth in vivo; these effects are rescued by exogenous USP39 complementation only when both the N-terminal IDR (for phase separation) and C-terminal domains (for catalytic activity) are intact (PubMed:39885503). This establishes USP39 condensates as functional drivers of tumorigenesis, suggesting therapeutic targeting of its phase separation may suppress lung cancer progression (PubMed:39885503).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of USP39 is intrinsically regulated by its N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR; residues 1-103), which is necessary and sufficient for condensate formation (PubMed:39885503). Deletion of the IDR (in constructs USP39-ΔN and USP39-(184–565)) abolishes phase separation and nucleolar localization, resulting in diffuse cellular distribution, while constructs retaining the IDR (full-length USP39, USP39-N(1-103), USP39-ΔC, USP39-ΔUBP) form condensates (PubMed:39885503). No mutations, post-translational modifications, splicing variants, oligomerization domains, or repeat features were identified as regulators (PubMed:39885503).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: USP39 phase separation is modulated by extrinsic physicochemical conditions but no protein partners or co-condensers were reported (PubMed:39885503). In vitro droplet formation requires macromolecular crowding agents (e.g., PEG 4000) and intermediate NaCl concentrations (150–300 mM), with size and frequency increasing at higher protein concentrations (≥3 µM) (PubMed:39885503). Condensate dissolution occurs upon treatment with the aliphatic alcohol 1,6-hexanediol, confirming hypersensitivity to hydrophobic disruptors (PubMed:39885503).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PABPC (Q58A45) does not undergo autonomous phase separation (class: PS-other) but acts as an RNA-dependent chaperone regulating phase separation of partner proteins like ATXN2 (PubMed:37295429). Located in the cytoplasm, it associates with stress granules under arsenite or heat shock stress. Its regulatory role involves modulating condensate wetting and mixing without forming autonomous condensates, and no material state transitions are observed for PABPC itself.
Functional Summary: PABPC's chaperone activity prevents irreversible ATXN2 condensation, enabling adaptive stress granule assembly during cellular stress (PubMed:37295429). Dysregulation—such as loss of PABPC function or RNA-binding capacity—contributes to neurodegeneration via pathological aggregation and sequestration of PABPC in cytotoxic aggregates. This evolutionarily conserved mechanism maintains proteostasis, with RNA-dependent wetting of condensate phases being critical for cellular viability.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The RNA recognition motif (RRM) domains of PABPC are intrinsically essential for its chaperone function, with RNA binding licensing its holdase activity (PubMed:37295429). Mutations in RRM domains—such as the F-PABPC* variant where aromatic residues are replaced by leucine—abolish this regulatory capability, confirming that specific RNA-binding residues govern PABPC's phase separation modulation.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: PABPC interacts with ATXN2 to prevent its aberrant condensation and enable stress granule mixing, with disruption of this interaction (e.g., via ATXN2 ΔPAM2 mutation) leading to pathological aggregation (PubMed:37295429). Cellular mRNA licenses PABPC's holdase activity, as RNA-binding-deficient mutants lose function, while engineered RNA recruitment (e.g., via hnRNPI-PopTag chimera) prevents condensate coalescence. PABPC also bridges immiscible condensate phases, promoting wetting between stress granules and other compartments.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Sgo1 (Q5FBB7) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but partitions into liquid-like condensates formed by the Chromosomal Passenger Complex (CPC) in the nucleus (PubMed:31481798). It modulates the phosphorylation-driven phase separation of HP1α in heterochromatin bodies, which are membrane-less organelles (PubMed:36537242, 28636604).
Functional Summary: Sgo1's enrichment in CPC condensates is essential for proper inner-centromere localization and chromosome segregation during mitosis (PubMed:31481798). By enhancing HP1α phase separation, Sgo1 contributes to heterochromatin domain formation, gene silencing, and chromatin compartmentalization (PubMed:36537242, 28636604).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic features driving Sgo1 phase separation are reported in the provided studies (PubMed:36537242, 28636604, 31481798).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Sgo1 partitions into CPC condensates formed by Survivin, Borealin, and INCENP (PubMed:31481798). It also enhances the phosphorylation-driven liquid-liquid phase separation of HP1α, lowering its saturation concentration (PubMed:36537242, 28636604).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TIP150 (Q5JR59) undergoes self-driven phase separation under crowding conditions but primarily forms liquid-like biomolecular condensates through co-phase separation with EB1 in the cytoplasm (PubMed:38323478, 36536176). It localizes to the spindle apparatus and centrosome, where it organizes microtubule plus-end machinery. While its condensates exhibit liquid-like properties including fusion and dynamic recovery when complexed with EB1, no material state transitions were reported for TIP150 itself (PubMed:38323478).
Functional Summary: Co-phase separation of TIP150 with EB1 and MCAK creates biochemical hubs that ensure accurate kinetochore-microtubule attachments and chromosome segregation during mitosis (PubMed:38323478, 36536176). These condensates concentrate tubulin dimers and plus-end tracking proteins (+TIPs), regulating microtubule dynamics including growth rate and catastrophe frequency. Disruption of co-phase separation causes severe mitotic defects: chromosome misalignment, delayed anaphase onset, reduced kinetochore tension, and impaired MCAK localization (PubMed:38323478). The evolutionary conservation of this mechanism is demonstrated by functional studies in Drosophila embryos (PubMed:38323478).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of TIP150 is intrinsically driven by its C-terminal region (aa 800–1368), which contains an intrinsically disordered EB1-binding domain (EBD) and a coiled-coil MCAK-binding domain essential for co-phase separation (PubMed:38323478). The full-length protein is intrinsically disordered, contributing to its phase separation propensity. These domains enable synergistic interactions that lower the phase separation threshold when complexed with EB1 and MCAK (PubMed:38323478, 36536176).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TIP150 requires EB1 for functional co-phase separation, forming dynamic condensates that serve as scaffolds for microtubule regulators (PubMed:38323478, 36536176). This co-condensation enhances droplet size and dynamics, with faster fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) observed in complexes. Without EB1, TIP150 only forms droplets in the presence of crowding agents like 5% PEG-8000 (PubMed:38323478). TIP150 also interacts with MCAK in the EB1 complex, though MCAK alone cannot induce TIP150 phase separation (PubMed:38323478).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The protein Q5T1M5 (FKBP/Fm) does not undergo self-driven phase separation in its native state but participates in engineered phase separation systems. In the cytoplasm, it forms synthetic liquid-like condensates (ArtiG) through concentration-dependent phase separation, exhibiting spherical morphology, fusion, coalescence, and rapid component exchange (PubMed:31324804). Alternatively, it compartmentalizes into SUMO5-FRB/SIM6 synthetic condensates as a client protein upon rapamycin-induced binding, displaying liquid-like properties and mobility confirmed by FRAP (PubMed:36396954). No material state transitions were reported in either system.
Functional Summary: Engineered phase separation systems serve functional roles: ArtiG condensates act as protein reservoirs buffering cytosolic concentration fluctuations and can recruit specific RNA targets when functionalized (PubMed:31324804). Rapamycin-inducible recruitment validates controllable protein clustering tools for synthetic biology applications (PubMed:36396954).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation behavior is intrinsically regulated by engineered domains: The F36M-FKBP domain enables homodimerization (Kd ~µM), creating multivalent interactions essential for ArtiG condensate formation, where wild-type FKBP fails to phase separate (PubMed:31324804). The FKBP domain facilitates binding to the FRB-rapamycin complex, enabling recruitment into synthetic condensates (PubMed:36396954).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Condensate formation requires extrinsic regulators: Rapamycin induces FKBP recruitment into SUMO5-FRB/SIM6 condensates by mediating FRB binding (PubMed:36396954). ArtiG formation is concentration-dependent, with nucleation occurring at critical cytosolic concentrations (PubMed:31324804).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Wild-type RBM20 localizes to nuclear speckles without cytoplasmic granule formation, while the R636S mutation causes mislocalization from the nucleus to sarcoplasm, forming liquid-like RNP granules (R3Gs) that exhibit fusion events, wetting behavior, and partial FRAP recovery (t½ ~100s) with core-shell substructure (PubMed:33188278). These granules associate with cytoskeletal elements, recruit mRNA, and fuse with stress granules, classified as PS-other behavior (PubMed:33188278).
Functional Summary: Pathological R3G formation disrupts actin cytoskeleton organization, reducing cardiomyocyte striation by 41% and impairing sarcomere biogenesis, leading to dilated cardiomyopathy and heart failure (PubMed:33188278). These granules sequester cell cycle regulators to arrest cardiomyocyte proliferation and fuse with stress granules, disrupting mRNA metabolism (PubMed:33188278).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal low-complexity domain (LCD), with deletion of this domain (ΔN mutant) abolishing granule formation (PubMed:33188278). The pathogenic R636S mutation enables cytoplasmic mislocalization and granule assembly, while deletion constructs (del1-658, del658-1227) confirm the requirement of the N-terminal region containing the LCD for phase separation (PubMed:33188278).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: R3Gs recruit poly-A+ mRNA and partition ACTC1 to their phase boundary, demonstrated through FISH co-localization and co-staining (PubMed:33188278). They fuse with stress granules containing TIA1, TIAR, and G3BP1 upon sodium arsenite-induced stress, with complete absorption of G3BP1 observed (PubMed:33188278).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: UBAP2 (Q5T6F2) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but is recruited by K6-polyubiquitinated PAICS to drive liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), forming purinosome condensates in the cytoplasm (PubMed:37848033). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties, including dynamic fusion events and rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) both in vivo and in vitro (PubMed:37848033). No material state transitions (e.g., liquid-to-solid) were reported.
Functional Summary: UBAP2-mediated phase separation drives purinosome assembly, enhancing de novo purine synthesis (DNPS) flux to support cellular proliferation and tumorigenesis in melanoma (PubMed:37848033). Depletion of UBAP2 impairs cell growth and purinosome formation, which is rescued by wild-type UBAP2 but not ΔUBA or ΔIDR mutants, linking phase separation directly to oncogenic metabolism (PubMed:37848033).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: UBAP2's phase separation is intrinsically regulated by two critical features: its ubiquitin-associated (UBA) domain (aa 46-94) that binds polyubiquitin chains, and multiple intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs: IV:aa 622-736, V-VI:aa 853-966, VII-VIII:aa 982-1119) that provide multivalency (PubMed:37848033). Deletion of either the UBA domain (ΔUBA) or IDRs (ΔIDR) abolishes phase separation in vivo and in vitro, confirming their essential synergistic roles (PubMed:37848033).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: UBAP2's phase separation is extrinsically regulated by K6-polyubiquitinated PAICS, which provides multivalent binding sites for UBAP2's UBA domain to initiate condensate assembly (PubMed:37848033). Additionally, K6-linked tetra-ubiquitin chains (K6-Ub₄) directly induce UBAP2 phase separation in vitro, with specificity over other chain types (e.g., K48-Ub₄ shows no activity) (PubMed:37848033).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: EB1 undergoes self-driven phase separation to form liquid-like condensates in the cytoplasm, primarily associated with spindle apparatus and centrosomes (PubMed:38323478, 36536176). These dynamic condensates serve as scaffolds for microtubule regulators and exhibit reversible fusion and rapid fluorescence recovery. In engineered systems, EB1 forms fiber-like synthetic organelles along microtubules (PubMed:35033560). While wild-type condensates maintain liquid properties, specific mutations (e.g., EB1-hnRNPA1D262V) undergo pathological liquid-to-gel transitions (PubMed:36536176).
Functional Summary: EB1 condensates organize microtubule plus-end machinery by concentrating tubulin, TIP150, and MCAK to regulate microtubule dynamics (growth rate, catastrophe frequency) and ensure accurate chromosome segregation during mitosis (PubMed:38323478, 36536176). Disruption (e.g., via IDR mutations) causes spindle defects, lagging chromosomes, and impaired kinetochore attachments (PubMed:36536176). In synthetic biology, EB1 enables orthogonal translation within engineered organelles (PubMed:35033560). EB1-tau co-condensates facilitate microtubule regulation, while EB1 inhibits pathological tau phase separation and aggregation, suggesting neuroprotective roles (PubMed:32997736, 38445984).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is driven by multivalent interactions among EB1's calponin homology (CH) domain, C-terminal coiled-coil (EBH) dimerization domain, C-terminal tail (CTT), and intrinsically disordered region (IDR, residues 126-183) (PubMed:36536176). Charged lysine/arginine residues within the IDR constitute critical 'molecular grammar', as mutations (e.g., KR6Q: K174Q/R176Q/K178Q/K180Q/K182Q/R183Q) attenuate phase separation by disrupting electrostatic interactions (PubMed:36536176). Acetylation at Lys220 promotes self-phase separation but disrupts co-condensation with partners; the K220Q mutation mimics this effect (PubMed:38323478).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: EB1 co-phase separates with microtubule regulators TIP150 and MCAK, which synergistically lower phase separation thresholds and enhance condensate dynamics (PubMed:38323478, 36536176). In engineered systems, RNA-binding proteins FUS and EWSR1 enhance EB1's phase separation efficiency within synthetic organelles (PubMed:35033560). Tubulin dimers are enriched within condensates, forming reservoirs for microtubule growth (PubMed:36536176). EB1 also co-phase separates with tau's proline-rich domain to form heterotypic microtubule-associated condensates (PubMed:32997736).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: RIF1 (Q5UIP0) undergoes partner-driven phase separation through incorporation into Mitotic Stress Bodies (MSBs) in the nucleus of colon cancer cells during prolonged mitotic arrest or spontaneously in normally dividing cancer cells (PubMed:36606487). These MSBs exhibit liquid-like properties including spherical morphology, sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol, salt, and osmotic stress, and reformation after washout. RIF1 does not independently form condensates but co-localizes with TP53BP1 within these dynamic structures adjacent to centromeres (PubMed:36606487).
Functional Summary: RIF1 incorporation into MSBs contributes to the sequestration of DNA repair machinery components during mitosis, which in cancer cells suppresses aberrant nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) activation, prevents telomere fusion and lethal chromosome breakage, reduces DNA damage (γH2AX foci), and promotes survival following mitotic stress (PubMed:36606487). This mechanism facilitates cancer cell viability after aberrant mitoses but specific pathological implications of RIF1's phase separation were not detailed independently.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features regulating RIF1's phase separation were identified in the provided study (PubMed:36606487). The key_drivers section explicitly states no specifications for domains, PTMs, oligomerization, repeat features, or mutations related to RIF1's condensate behavior.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RIF1 requires TP53BP1 for incorporation into Mitotic Stress Bodies, co-localizing exclusively with this partner within MSBs (PubMed:36606487). No other extrinsic regulators (ions, chemicals, or additional protein partners) influencing RIF1's phase separation were reported in the provided data.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: 14-3-3 (Q6LD62) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but partitions into synthetic coacervates (artificial membraneless organelles) via engineered His-tag/Ni-NTA interactions, exhibiting liquid-like behavior as demonstrated by FRAP recovery (PubMed:37027309). It serves as a scaffold protein within these condensates, achieving a 640-fold local concentration enrichment without transitioning to other material states.
Functional Summary: As a scaffold in synthetic condensates, 14-3-3 enables phosphorylation-dependent recruitment of client proteins like RAF1 and TAZ, modeling enzymatically regulated signaling processes with 161-fold uptake efficiency for phosphorylated RAF1 peptides (PubMed:37027309). This reconstitution demonstrates utility for studying confined biomolecular interactions but shows no direct disease associations.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The partitioning behavior of 14-3-3 is intrinsically regulated by its C-terminal His-tag (14-3-3-His), which mediates specific anchoring to Ni-NTA functionalized coacervates. No domains, PTMs, mutations, or other intrinsic features were identified as drivers of phase separation beyond this engineered modification (PubMed:37027309).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: 14-3-3 partitioning requires the presence of Ni-NTA within synthetic coacervates, which serves as the primary extrinsic anchor for its His-tag (PubMed:37027309). Once partitioned, 14-3-3 recruits phosphorylation-dependent client proteins including RAF1 and TAZ, enhancing condensate functionality through native protein-protein interactions.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: MRNIP undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) both in vitro and in vivo, forming liquid-like condensates primarily in the nucleus that associate with DNA damage foci (colocalizing with γ-H2A.X) (PubMed:35551189). These condensates exhibit dynamic properties including FRAP recovery, droplet fusion, and sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol, with no observed material state transitions reported.
Functional Summary: MRNIP condensates accelerate double-strand break sensing by concentrating the MRN complex, promoting ATM activation, DNA end resection, and homologous recombination repair (PubMed:35551189). This mechanism confers radioresistance in colorectal cancer, with condensate disruption impairing DNA repair functionality.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the Intrinsically Disordered Region 1 (IDR1, residues 123-176), which is essential for condensate formation (PubMed:35551189). Deletion of IDR1 abolishes both LLPS and functional activity, while phosphorylation at S100/115 shows no regulatory effect on phase separation behavior.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: MRNIP co-phase separates with the MRN complex components MRE11, RAD50, and NBS1, which concentrate within the condensates and are essential for DNA damage sensing (PubMed:35551189). Linear and circular DNA incorporates into the droplets, evidenced by colocalization with γ-H2A.X at DNA damage sites.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PARIS (Q6NUN9) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), forming dynamic liquid droplets in vitro that transition to amorphous solid aggregates over time or under high concentrations (PubMed:37870275). It localizes to the nucleus in vivo, forming nuclear droplets not classified into predefined membrane-less organelles (PubMed:37870275). This liquid-to-solid transition is accelerated by poly(ADP-ribose) (PAR) binding (PubMed:37870275).
Functional Summary: Pathological solidification of PARIS sequesters PGC-1α into insoluble aggregates, depleting soluble PGC-1α and causing mitochondrial dysfunction (reduced mtDNA) in dopaminergic neurons (PubMed:37870275). This mechanism contributes to neurodegeneration in Parkinson’s disease models, evidenced by SDS-resistant PARIS aggregates in the substantia nigra of aged mice, parkin knockout models, and α-synuclein pre-formed fibril-injected mice (PubMed:37870275).
