Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: MBNL1 phase separation is extrinsically modulated by reciprocal interactions with the protein CUGBP1, with which it colocalizes in SGs and P-bodies, dynamically influencing each other's behavior (PubMed:35642886). Additionally, expanded CUG repeat RNA (CUGexp RNA) reduces MBNL1 localization to P-bodies and alters SG kinetics by delaying granule formation and accelerating dispersal in DM1 models (PubMed:35642886).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: EIF4ENIF1 (4E-T) functions as a scaffold protein essential for P-body assembly and integrity in the cytoplasm (PubMed:37370689). It is classified as a phase separation-related protein (PS-other) and associates specifically with P-bodies as a core scaffold component. The material state of these condensates and any state transitions are not specified in the study.
Functional Summary: EIF4ENIF1-mediated P-body formation represses translation of KRAS and NRAS mRNAs. Dissolution of P-bodies upon EIF4ENIF1 knockdown elevates RAS protein levels, driving resistance to MEK inhibitors in cancer cells (PubMed:37370689).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or molecular features driving or regulating EIF4ENIF1 phase separation were reported in this study (PubMed:37370689).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: EIF4ENIF1 co-assembles with core scaffold partners DDX6 and LSM14A to form P-bodies, with co-invalidation (knockdown) of any of these components leading to P-body dissolution (PubMed:37370689).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TREX1 (Q9NSU2) undergoes partner-dependent phase separation with DNA under non-physiological conditions (low salt/high concentration), forming liquid-like droplets in vitro (PubMed:33606975). It localizes to the cytoplasm and associates with cGAS-DNA membrane-less organelles, where it co-localizes at the periphery of these condensates but does not penetrate their core. The protein maintains a liquid material state during phase separation, with no observed state transitions reported (PubMed:33606975).
Functional Summary: Phase separation of TREX1 directly inhibits its dsDNA degradation activity under non-physiological conditions, while its restriction to the periphery of cGAS-DNA condensates in physiological contexts enables immune sensing by limiting DNA degradation (PubMed:33606975). This spatial regulation protects immunostimulatory DNA within condensate cores, facilitating efficient cytosolic DNA sensing. Dysregulation through mutations like E198K disrupts this compartmentalization, potentially altering immune response pathways (PubMed:33606975).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of TREX1 is intrinsically driven by its exonuclease domain (residues 1-242), which forms dimers and requires dsDNA with exposed 3' ends for recruitment (PubMed:33606975). The disease-associated E198K mutation significantly enhances phase separation propensity by lowering the protein concentration threshold for droplet interaction and enabling permeation into the droplet core, contrasting with wild-type behavior restricted to the periphery (PubMed:33606975).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TREX1 phase separation is extrinsically regulated by nucleic acids and partner proteins. DNA is essential for droplet formation, with both ssDNA and dsDNA acting as scaffolds (PubMed:33606975). The protein co-localizes with cGAS-DNA condensates, where cGAS phase separation restricts TREX1 to the droplet periphery, limiting its enzymatic access and activity (PubMed:33606975).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: DIAPH3 (mDia2) undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) to form cytoplasmic D-granules under stress conditions or overexpression, exhibiting liquid-like properties including fusion and rapid recovery (PubMed:36640348). These stress-induced condensates are distinct from known membrane-less organelles (MLOs) like stress granules and P-bodies. DIAPH3 also partitions into CLIP-170-induced cytoplasmic condensates ('patches') that are similarly distinct from predefined MLOs (PubMed:34890409). The material state transitions from liquid to gel/solid under chronic stress conditions (PubMed:36640348).
Functional Summary: D-granule formation sequesters DIAPH3, inhibiting actin nucleation at filopodia tips and enabling rapid actin cytoskeleton remodeling during stress adaptation (PubMed:36640348). Chronic condensation induces liquid-to-solid transitions linked to cytotoxicity. Recruitment into CLIP-170 condensates suggests involvement in +TIP network superstructures proposed to stabilize microtubule tips, with pathological implications analogous to proteinopathies in neurodegeneration (PubMed:34890409, 36640348).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the LC2 (low-complexity domain 2), which is essential and sufficient for condensation. LC1 and LC3 domains show no phase separation capability. The requirement of a free C-terminus for partitioning into condensates is implied by mutagenesis studies showing abolished recruitment with C-terminal tags (PubMed:36640348, 34890409).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: DIAPH3 partitions into CLIP-170-induced cytoplasmic condensates ('patches'), indicating CLIP-170 acts as an extrinsic regulator that recruits DIAPH3 into biomolecular condensates (PubMed:34890409). No other extrinsic partners or chemical regulators were identified in the provided data.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: RBM12 (Q9NTZ6) does not autonomously undergo liquid-liquid phase separation but is recruited as a client protein into liquid-like condensates formed by WAC in the nucleus (PubMed:39840526). It localizes to nuclear speckles via this recruitment mechanism, requiring WAC for integration and splicing regulation, with no observed material state transitions reported (PubMed:39840526).
Functional Summary: Recruitment into WAC condensates enables RBM12 to interact with U5 snRNP (via SNRNP200/PRPF6) and regulate alternative splicing of mitophagy-related genes like BECN1 (PubMed:39840526). Disruption of the WAC-RBM12 axis alters BECN1 splicing, leading to hyperactivated mitophagy (PubMed:39840526).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The RRM domain of RBM12 is essential for nuclear localization and proper co-phase separation with WAC, as deletion of RRMs (ΔRRM) causes mislocalization and ectopic droplet formation outside the nucleus (PubMed:39840526). Conversely, deletion of the P-rich region (ΔP-rich) does not affect localization or co-phase separation capabilities (PubMed:39840526).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RBM12 recruitment is strictly dependent on the scaffold protein WAC, which undergoes phase separation via its C-terminal coiled-coil domain and facilitates RBM12 integration into nuclear speckles (PubMed:39840526). No other extrinsic partners or regulators were identified.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: ZCCHC3 undergoes robust liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) upon binding cytosolic RNA or DNA, forming dynamic, liquid-like condensates in the cytoplasm characterized by droplet fusion and rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) (PubMed:39983719). These condensates are distinct from stress granules, showing no colocalization with G3BP1 (PubMed:39983719).
Functional Summary: ZCCHC3 condensates regulate innate immunity: RNA-induced assemblies activate RIG-I/MDA5 sensors, driving MAVS oligomerization and interferon responses, while DNA-induced condensates enhance cGAS enzymatic activity to promote STING signaling and antiviral defense (PubMed:39983719). Condensation-deficient mutants (e.g., ZF123) or knockout impair antiviral responses against RNA/DNA viruses like influenza and HSV-1 (PubMed:39983719).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of ZCCHC3 is intrinsically driven by multivalent interactions involving its intrinsically disordered region (IDR), RNA recognition motifs (RRM1, RRM2), and zinc finger domains (ZF1, ZF2, ZF3) (PubMed:39983719). Deletion of the IDR (ΔIDR) disrupts condensate formation, confirming the critical role of multivalency in LLPS (PubMed:39983719).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: ZCCHC3 phase separation is extrinsically triggered by cytosolic RNA or DNA binding, which initiates condensate formation (PubMed:39983719). These condensates enrich immune sensors (RIG-I-like receptors for RNA; cGAS for DNA) and cofactors including ATP and GTP, creating functional platforms for downstream signaling (PubMed:39983719).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: POT1 (Q9NUX5) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but partitions into TRF1/TRF2 droplets within nuclear telomeric compartments (heterochromatin) as part of the shelterin complex (PubMed:35077681). It associates exclusively with telomeric membrane-less organelles and requires partner proteins for incorporation into condensates, though its material state remains unspecified with no reported state transitions.
Functional Summary: POT1 enrichment in telomeric condensates protects single-stranded telomeric overhangs and suppresses ATR DNA damage response pathway activation (PubMed:35077681). As an integral component of phase-separated shelterin complexes, it contributes to telomere compartmentalization that limits DNA damage repair factor access, maintaining genomic stability (PubMed:35077681).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or structural features driving POT1 phase separation were identified in the study (PubMed:35077681).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: POT1 partitions into condensates scaffolded by TRF1 and TRF2, requiring telomeric DNA for complex assembly (PubMed:35077681). It integrates into multicomponent shelterin droplets through interactions with TPP1-TIN2 subcomplexes and exhibits co-phase separation with full shelterin components (TRF1, TRF2, TIN2, TPP1) on 8ds3ss telomeric DNA repeats (PubMed:35077681).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: RBFOX1 undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) to form liquid-like droplets in the nucleus and cytoplasm, associating with stress granules (PubMed:29358748). These condensates exhibit partial liquid-like properties as evidenced by sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol, but aggregate formation in aged cells implies a potential transition to a solid state (PubMed:29358748).
Functional Summary: RBFOX1 phase separation regulates stress response through stress granule formation (PubMed:29358748). Dysregulation, including pathological aggregate accumulation in aged cells, is implicated in neurodegeneration and other RBFOX-associated diseases (PubMed:29358748).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of RBFOX1 is intrinsically driven by its Low Complexity Domains (LCDs) (PubMed:29358748). Alternative splicing generates isoforms with varying LCD content, directly influencing phase separation propensity (PubMed:29358748).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators or partners modulating RBFOX1 phase separation are reported in the provided study (PubMed:29358748).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TRIAD3A undergoes self-driven, ATP-dependent liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro without crowding agents, forming liquid-like droplets that do not transition to other material states (PubMed:39030428). It primarily localizes to autophagosomes, where it scaffolds tau recruitment and facilitates pathological fibril formation in neurodegenerative contexts (PubMed:39009640). These condensates enable rapid liquid-to-solid transitions of client proteins like tau within the droplets, termed 'nested phase separation' (PubMed:39009640, 39030428).
Functional Summary: TRIAD3A condensates concentrate tau for ubiquitination, fibrillization, and autophagic clearance, providing a quality-control mechanism (PubMed:39009640, 39030428). Dysregulation – via mutations (e.g., R694C) or lysosomal dysfunction – causes pathological tau accumulation in autophagosomes, exacerbating tauopathies like Alzheimer's disease (PubMed:39009640, 39030428).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by TRIAD3A's RBR domain, which provides essential E3 ligase activity (PubMed:39030428). Autoubiquitination – the assembly of polyubiquitin chains – serves as a key post-translational modification that promotes LLPS (PubMed:39030428).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: ATP is a critical extrinsic regulator required for droplet formation (PubMed:39030428). TRIAD3A recruits tau (MAPT) into condensates for ubiquitination and fibrillation, with disease-associated tau mutants (e.g., P301L) exhibiting enhanced aggregation (PubMed:39009640, 39030428). It also partners with LC3 to dock condensates onto autophagosomes and utilizes ubiquitin to modify tau within droplets (PubMed:39009640, 39030428).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PARP-1 (Q9NWS1) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but scaffolds FUS condensates in the nucleus via PAR synthesis (PubMed:37804508). It associates with DNA repair compartments and facilitates the formation of reversible, liquid-like condensates during DNA damage response, though no material state transitions are reported for PARP-1 itself.
Functional Summary: PARP-1 catalyzes PAR synthesis to recruit FUS into reversible DNA repair compartments, concentrating repair activities during genotoxic stress (PubMed:37804508). Dysregulation of this process, such as impaired PARylation (e.g., K893I mutation), compromises compartment formation and may contribute to DNA repair deficiencies.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or modifications driving PARP-1 phase separation were identified in the provided data (PubMed:37804508).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: PARP-1 co-phase separates with FUS in a PARylation-dependent manner, exhibiting strong mixing in condensates as demonstrated by microtubule bench assays (PubMed:37804508). This interaction is essential for recruiting FUS to DNA damage sites and forming functional repair compartments.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TXNL4B forms cytoplasmic puncta co-localizing with P-bodies in vivo, indicating association with this membrane-less organelle (PubMed:38459060). The material state and transitions were not specified.
Functional Summary: TXNL4B phase separation is implicated in P-body assembly, as evidenced by co-localization with the P-body marker EDC4 in cellular systems (PubMed:38459060).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic regulators (domains, mutations, PTMs, or other features) driving phase separation were identified; only full-length protein behavior was studied (PubMed:38459060).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators or partner proteins modulating TXNL4B phase separation were reported in the study (PubMed:38459060).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: DACT1 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation to form cytoplasmic biomolecular condensates (200 nm–2 μm punctate bodies) that do not colocalize with known membrane-less organelles such as stress granules or P-bodies (PubMed:33723425). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties including fusion events and partial fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), with a dense protein refractive index of 1.36–1.38 (PubMed:33723425). Phase separation occurs specifically in the cytoplasm, is induced by TGF-β signaling, and no material state transitions (e.g., liquid-to-solid) were reported under tested conditions (PubMed:33723425).
Functional Summary: DACT1 phase separation represses Wnt signaling by compartmentalizing CK2 within cytoplasmic condensates, limiting CK2 availability for Wnt pathway activation (PubMed:33723425). This TGF-β-induced mechanism promotes breast and prostate cancer bone metastasis, with clinical data linking high DACT1 expression to increased bone metastasis risk (PubMed:33723425). Functional rescue experiments confirmed that phase separation capability (via engineered Fus domains) is sufficient to restore Wnt repression and metastatic outgrowth (PubMed:33723425).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of DACT1 is intrinsically driven by its disordered regions DR7 and DR8, with deletion of either domain (ΔDR7 or ΔDR8) abolishing condensate formation (PubMed:33723425). The DR8 region alone is sufficient to form punctate bodies, though primarily in the nucleus rather than the cytoplasm (PubMed:33723425).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: DACT1 phase separation is induced by TGF-β signaling (PubMed:33723425). Its primary extrinsic partner is CK2 (P68400), which is sequestered into DACT1 condensates, leading to inhibition of Wnt signaling (PubMed:33723425). This sequestration specifically affects the cytoplasmic pool of CK2 while sparing nuclear CK2 (PubMed:33723425).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TAB2 does not undergo self-driven phase separation (class: PS-other) but is recruited into cytoplasmic biomolecular condensates formed by PrPC (PubMed:39333690). These condensates exhibit liquid-like properties, evidenced by rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) and dissolution with 1,6-hexanediol treatment (PubMed:39333690). No material state transitions were reported for TAB2 under studied conditions.
Functional Summary: Recruitment of TAB2 into PrPC condensates facilitates NF-κB pathway activation, leading to IL-8 upregulation that promotes proliferation, migration, and metastasis in hepatocellular carcinoma, with pathological significance confirmed in patient tissues (PubMed:39333690).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features driving TAB2 phase separation were identified in the provided data (PubMed:39333690).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TAB2 is recruited into and fully co-localizes within PrPC-formed condensates, where it functions as a core component essential for TAK1 activation and NF-κB signaling (PubMed:39333690).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: FAM120A associates with stress granules in the cytoplasm, as demonstrated by co-localization with the stress granule marker G3BP1 in U-2 OS cells. This behavior was observed in vivo using endogenous protein constructs, though the material state and transitions remain unspecified (PubMed:26777405).
Functional Summary: As a novel component of stress granules, FAM120A is implicated in stress granule functionality, though specific physiological or pathological roles related to its phase separation were not detailed in the provided study (PubMed:26777405).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic regulators (domains, mutations, PTMs, or specific protein regions) driving FAM120A phase separation were identified in the provided study (PubMed:26777405).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: FAM120A co-localizes with the stress granule marker G3BP1, indicating potential recruitment to or co-assembly within stress granules. However, no extrinsic partners (proteins, ions, or chemicals) modulating its phase separation were reported (PubMed:26777405).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NOP53 (Q9NZM5) undergoes self-driven phase separation (PS-self) to form dynamic, liquid-like condensates in the nucleolus (specifically the granular component, colocalized with NPM1) and nucleoplasmic puncta in vivo, and autonomously forms reversible liquid droplets in vitro (PubMed:36316314). These condensates exhibit characteristic liquid properties including droplet fusion, rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol, and energy dependence (evidenced by slowed FRAP recovery after ATP depletion) (PubMed:36316314). No material state transitions (e.g., liquid-to-solid) were reported (PubMed:36316314).
Functional Summary: Phase separation of NOP53 facilitates its nucleolar localization and functions in ribosome biogenesis and DNA damage response (PubMed:36316314). Silencing NOP53 activates the p53 pathway, inhibits tumor growth, and sensitizes colorectal cancer cells to radiotherapy, with high NOP53 expression correlating with clinical radio-resistance and poor prognosis (PubMed:36316314).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of NOP53 is intrinsically driven by its N-terminal Intrinsically Disordered Region 1 (IDR1, amino acids 1-200), with residues 41-159 being critical for LLPS competency (PubMed:36316314). Disruption of R/M-R motifs via the Rm mutation redirects condensates to the nucleoplasm without inhibiting phase separation, indicating these motifs mediate nucleolar targeting but are dispensable for LLPS (PubMed:36316314).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: NOP53 phase separation is modulated by environmental conditions: enhanced by high pH and macromolecular crowding, inhibited by high salt concentrations, and dependent on cellular energy (ATP) for maintaining droplet dynamics in vivo (PubMed:36316314). No protein partners or chemical regulators were identified (PubMed:36316314).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SENP1 (Q9P0U3) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but is recruited into TOLLIP (Q9H0E2)-formed condensates where it aggregates, as observed both in vitro and in vivo during RNA viral infection (PubMed:40022729). These condensates are located in the cytoplasm, and while SENP1's material state within aggregates remains uncharacterized, no transitions to other states were reported (PubMed:40022729).
Functional Summary: Aggregation of SENP1 within TOLLIP condensates enhances MAVS deSUMOylation, inhibiting RIG-I-like receptor (RLR) signaling and promoting viral infection, as demonstrated by reduced SENP1 puncta and impaired viral resistance in TOLLIP-deficient systems (PubMed:40022729).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features driving SENP1 phase separation were identified; studies utilized full-length SENP1 without domain-specific analyses (PubMed:40022729).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SENP1 recruitment and aggregation are exclusively regulated by TOLLIP (Q9H0E2), which scaffolds condensate formation. Experimental evidence confirms direct interaction via co-immunoprecipitation, co-localization in TOLLIP droplets in vitro, and abolished aggregation in TOLLIP-knockout cells (PubMed:40022729).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: WHRN undergoes partner-dependent phase separation, forming liquid-like condensates through multivalent interactions with USH2A (PubMed:36964137). It localizes to the ankle regions of stereocilia in cochlear hair cells and associates with the ankle link complex membrane-less organelle (PubMed:36964137). These spherical droplets exhibit liquid material properties including fusion events and rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), with no observed material state transitions (PubMed:36964137).
Functional Summary: WHRN-mediated phase separation is essential for ankle link complex assembly during stereocilia development, with the NTD required for precise subcellular targeting to ankle regions (PubMed:36964137). Disruption of LLPS by mutations (A64D, T110A, R223H) directly impairs complex formation and provides molecular pathogenesis insights for sensorineural deafness (PubMed:36964137). ADGRV1-mediated inhibition at high concentrations suggests a regulatory mechanism for complex disassembly (PubMed:36964137).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal domain (NTD) enabling dimerization and the PDZ1 domain facilitating partner binding (PubMed:36964137). Disease-causing mutations disrupt LLPS through distinct mechanisms: A64D impairs NTD-mediated dimerization, T110A weakens USH2A binding affinity (Kd 16µM vs 2.7µM WT), and R223H disrupts condensation without affecting binding interactions (PubMed:36964137).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: WHRN forms core condensates with the scaffold protein USH2A, which serves as an essential platform (PubMed:36964137). ADGRV1 exhibits concentration-dependent modulation: recruited to droplets at low concentrations but inhibiting LLPS at >20µM through competitive binding to the WHRN NTD (PubMed:36964137). PDZD7 acts as a client component recruited into pre-formed condensates without initiating phase separation (PubMed:36964137).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PGC-1α forms nuclear condensates in human skeletal muscle, exhibiting liquid-like material properties and associating with transcriptional condensates. This behavior is consistent with observations in mouse models, though no material state transitions are reported (PubMed:34465622).
Functional Summary: Phase separation enables PGC-1α recruitment to chromatin within transcriptionally active liquid-like condensates, regulating complex transcriptional networks involved in skeletal muscle metabolism. This compartmentalization mechanism is conserved between human and mouse systems (PubMed:34465622).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation and nuclear foci localization are intrinsically regulated by the RNA recognition motif (RRM) and C-terminal domain (CTD). The RRM facilitates RNA binding essential for foci localization, while deletion of the CTD (ΔCTD mutation) abolishes nuclear condensate formation in cellular models (PubMed:34465622).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators or partner proteins were reported for PGC-1α phase separation in the provided data (PubMed:34465622).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: UBA2 (Q9UBT2) does not undergo self-driven phase separation (class: PS-other) but forms nuclear condensates that colocalize with Epac1 nuclear condensates upon Epac1 activation (PubMed:35442725). It is exclusively localized in the nucleus (PubMed:35442725). The material state of UBA2 within these condensates is not specified, and no state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: No functional implications of UBA2 phase separation were reported in the provided data (PubMed:35442725).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features regulating UBA2 phase separation were identified in the provided data (PubMed:35442725).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: UBA2 condensate formation is extrinsically regulated by Epac1 activation, which promotes the formation of colocalizing nuclear condensates containing both proteins (PubMed:35442725).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: ZO2 (Q9UDY2) undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) to form liquid-like, membrane-attached compartments in vitro and in cells, primarily localizing to the cytoplasm (PubMed:31675499). It associates with the ZO protein compartment (tight junction plaque) and exhibits faster dynamics than ZO1 at cellular junctions, with full FRAP recovery in 126 seconds (PubMed:31675499). The condensates display liquid material properties including fusion and rapid component exchange, with no observed state transitions reported (PubMed:31675499).
Functional Summary: ZO2 phase separation cooperates with ZO1 to assemble functional tight junctions by specifically enriching and localizing adhesion receptors, cytoskeletal adapters, and transcription factors within membrane-attached compartments (PubMed:31675499). This process is redundant with ZO1 in sequestering junctional proteins and forming the structural scaffold essential for tissue sealing, with condensate formation occurring near physiological concentrations (~8 µM) in cells (PubMed:31675499).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of ZO2 is intrinsically driven by its conserved PDZ3-SH3-GuK (PSG) supra-domain (residues 509-876), which is essential for condensation (PubMed:31675499). Phosphorylation serves as a key regulatory mechanism, as dephosphorylated ZO2 efficiently phase-separates while phosphorylated forms cannot undergo condensation under tested conditions (PubMed:31675499).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: ZO2 co-assembles with partner proteins ZO1 and ZO3 via trans interactions in vitro (PubMed:31675499). Its condensates specifically enrich tight-junction proteins including Claudin-1, Occludin, Afadin, Cingulin, and Actin through partitioning mechanisms similar to ZO1 (PubMed:31675499).

Protein Name: Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma translocation protein 1
Overall Phase Separation Overview: MALT1 (Q9UDY8) does not undergo phase separation under the conditions studied (PubMed:35727133). It is localized in the cytoplasm and shows no association with membrane-less organelles (PubMed:35727133). No material state or state transitions were observed, as clustering-driven activation occurs without structural ordering or phase separation (PubMed:35727133).
Functional Summary: MALT1 clustering by BCL10 filaments activates NF-κB signaling through TRAF6 ubiquitination, driving p65 nuclear translocation (PubMed:35727133). This process requires proximity-induced activation but does not involve phase separation or structural ordering (PubMed:35727133).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features driving phase separation were identified for MALT1 (PubMed:35727133). Studies examined its Death Domain (DD) and DD-removed fragment (MALT1₁₂₆₋₈₂₄), but neither exhibited phase separation behavior (PubMed:35727133).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: MALT1 is recruited as a client to BCL10 filaments for activation, evidenced by co-immunoprecipitation from condensates (PubMed:35727133). Artificial multimerization via Cry2clust induces downstream signaling without phase separation, while dimerization (VfAU1-LOV) fails to activate (PubMed:35727133).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: LIMD1 undergoes self-driven, force-sensitive liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro and in cells, forming dynamic liquid-like droplets primarily in the cytoplasm at focal adhesions (described as membraneless ensembles) (PubMed:33891898). These condensates exhibit liquid properties including fusion and rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), but undergo time-dependent liquid-to-solid transitions after prolonged incubation (>20 minutes) in vitro, forming hydrogel states (PubMed:33891898).
Functional Summary: LIMD1 phase separation facilitates focal adhesion maturation by enriching late adhesion components, thereby regulating adhesion longevity, assembly/disassembly kinetics, and cell spreading (PubMed:33891898). It critically modulates cellular mechanics—enhancing traction forces and enabling durotaxis (stiffness-guided migration)—as demonstrated by impaired traction and abolished directional migration in LIMD1-knockout or phase separation-deficient mutants (ΔIDR/ΔLIM/+Phos) (PubMed:33891898).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by multivalent interactions between the intrinsically disordered region (IDR) and LIM domains (PubMed:33891898). Phosphorylation potently regulates this process: a phosphorylation-mimetic mutant (+Phos) impairs LLPS while a phosphorylation-deficient mutant (-Phos) enhances it (PubMed:33891898). Truncation of either the IDR (ΔIDR) or LIM domains (ΔLIM) abolishes phase separation capacity, though functionality can be restored by swapping the IDR with FUS-derived sequences (PubMed:33891898).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation is mechanosensitively enhanced by vinculin activation and substrate stiffness through Rho-mediated pathways, while inhibited by actomyosin disruption (e.g., blebbistatin/Y27632) (PubMed:33891898). LIMD1 condensates selectively recruit late focal adhesion client proteins including zyxin, TRIP6, and VASP through multivalent interactions, but exclude others like paxillin (PubMed:33891898).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: BAIAP2L1 (IRTKS) undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro, forming dynamic, liquid-like droplets that exhibit fusion and rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) (PubMed:39192031). This concentration-dependent phase separation occurs in the nucleus, where IRTKS associates with heterochromatin condensates and co-localizes with heterochromatin markers (HP1α, H3K9me3) and Hoechst-dense regions (PubMed:39192031). The material state remains consistently liquid under all tested conditions, with no observed state transitions (PubMed:39192031).
Functional Summary: IRTKS condensates are essential for heterochromatin formation and maintenance: they recruit Ubc9 to SUMOylate HP1α, stabilize heterochromatin structure, concentrate DNA/nucleosomal arrays, and repress repetitive DNA elements (PubMed:39192031). IRTKS deficiency causes heterochromatin loss, leading to genome instability, derepression of repetitive elements, activation of the cGAS-STING pathway and interferon signaling, and induction of cellular senescence and senescence-associated secretory phenotype (PubMed:39192031).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by IRTKS's intrinsically disordered region (IDR, residues 250-511) containing SH3 and WH2 domains (PubMed:39192031). Proline residues within this IDR are critical for phase separation, as evidenced by disrupted condensate formation in proline-to-alanine mutants (PubMed:39192031).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: IRTKS co-phase separates with HP1α in a mutually enhancing manner, forming co-condensates through direct interaction (PubMed:39192031). It incorporates Cy5-labeled DNA, nucleosomal DNA, and reconstituted nucleosomal arrays in a dose-dependent manner (PubMed:39192031). Phase separation is highly sensitive to ionic conditions, being inhibited by high salt concentrations and 1,6-hexanediol (PubMed:39192031).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: NRBP1 (Q9UHY1) does not undergo autonomous phase separation but is recruited into cytoplasmic condensates called TWN bodies via interaction with TSC22D proteins under hyperosmotic stress (PubMed:38980795). It co-localizes with TSC22D2 and WNK1 in these reversible, liquid-like condensates, which form rapidly in response to osmotic stressors like NaCl, KCl, or sorbitol and dissolve upon stress removal (PubMed:38980795).
Functional Summary: NRBP1 incorporation into TWN bodies is essential for cell volume regulation during hyperosmotic stress, specifically in facilitating regulatory volume increase (RVI) via osmotic sensing (PubMed:38980795). Loss of recruitment in TSC22D-deficient cells disrupts RVI, leading to intracellular K+ imbalance and cell volume defects (PubMed:38980795).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The recruitment of NRBP1 into condensates is intrinsically mediated by its C-terminal NbrT domain (amino acids 439-535), which is essential for binding to TSC22D proteins (PubMed:38980795).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: NRBP1 requires TSC22D2 as a scaffold for translocation into TWN bodies, demonstrated through genetic dependency and co-immunoprecipitation (PubMed:38980795). It co-localizes with WNK1 within these condensates, and hyperosmotic stress (induced by sorbitol, NaCl, or KCl) triggers TWN body formation, facilitating NRBP1 incorporation (PubMed:38980795).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: MBD1 associates with condensed heterochromatin structures in the nucleus, where mechanical force application reduces condensation and increases molecular separation (PubMed:36943889). It is recruited into liquid-like CAF-1 nuclear bodies formed by CHAF1A via liquid-liquid phase separation, exhibiting co-localization within these structures (PubMed:33739466).
Functional Summary: Force-induced decondensation of MBD1-bound chromatin may regulate DNA accessibility for transcription and repair processes, linking mechanical cues to epigenetic regulation (PubMed:36943889). When recruited to CAF-1 bodies, MBD1 participates in suppressing HIV-1 latency by maintaining DNA methylation at viral integration sites, establishing an epigenetic barrier to viral reactivation (PubMed:33739466).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features driving phase separation of MBD1 were reported in the provided studies (PubMed:36943889, 33739466).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: MBD1 is recruited to CHAF1A-driven CAF-1 nuclear bodies, where it contributes to DNA methylation maintenance through co-localization within these phase-separated condensates (PubMed:33739466).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: CRLS1 (Q9UJA2) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but is recruited as a client protein into Mieap-induced biomolecular condensates (Mi-BCs) within mitochondria (PubMed:38322995). These multi-phase condensates exhibit liquid-like properties, including fusion and partial FRAP recovery, and compartmentalize cardiolipin metabolic enzymes (PubMed:38322995).
Functional Summary: The incorporation of CRLS1 into Mi-BCs facilitates cardiolipin biosynthesis and remodeling, which is essential for maintaining mitochondrial cristae structure and supporting oxidative phosphorylation (PubMed:38322995). Disruption of this condensate-mediated compartmentalization leads to abnormal cristae morphology and reduced ATP production (PubMed:38322995).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic regulators of phase separation for CRLS1 were reported in the provided context (PubMed:38322995).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: CRLS1 is recruited into Mi-BCs by the scaffold protein Mieap, partitioning into the enzyme-rich phase of these condensates alongside other cardiolipin metabolism enzymes like TAMM41, PGS1, and PTPMT1 (PubMed:38322995).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: HspB8 (Q9UJY1) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but partitions into FUS condensates via its intrinsically disordered region (IDR) in the cytoplasm, particularly within stress granules under heat shock conditions (PubMed:34487489). It modulates the material state of FUS condensates, preventing pathological liquid-to-solid transitions through chaperone activity mediated by its α-crystallin domain (αCD) (PubMed:34487489).
Functional Summary: HspB8 prevents pathological liquid-to-solid transitions of FUS in stress granules, preserving mRNA regulation during cellular stress (PubMed:34487489). Loss-of-function mutations (e.g., K141E) are linked to Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease due to failed chaperone activity, leading to irreversible FUS aggregation and cytotoxicity (PubMed:34487489).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation partitioning is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal IDR (residues 1-71), which utilizes arginine-mediated interactions for condensate targeting (PubMed:34487489). The C-terminal αCD (residues 72-196) provides essential chaperone activity within condensates (PubMed:34487489). Disease-associated mutations impair these mechanisms: K141E in the αCD disrupts chaperone function, while the 10RtoG substitution (arginine-to-glycine in IDR) abolishes partitioning (PubMed:34487489).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: HspB8 partitions into and stabilizes FUS condensates, maintaining their liquid state through specific αCD::FUS-RRM interactions (PubMed:34487489). RNA competes with HspB8 for binding to FUS, reducing their association and potentially modulating chaperone efficacy (PubMed:34487489).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: The protein ALK (Q9UM73) undergoes partner-driven phase separation as part of the EML4-ALK fusion protein to form de novo membraneless cytoplasmic granules, distinct from canonical RNA-protein condensates like P-bodies or stress granules (PubMed:33848463). These granules exhibit heterogeneous biophysical states ranging from liquid-like (with partial FRAP recovery in variant 3) to predominantly solid-like (hexanediol-resistant with low FRAP recovery, porous morphology, and no fusion/fission events), suggesting possible liquid-to-solid maturation through aging though not directly observed (PubMed:33848463).
Functional Summary: Phase separation of the EML4-ALK fusion organizes oncogenic RAS/MAPK signaling by enabling compartmentalized, lipid membrane-independent RAS activation—a mechanism critical for cancer pathogenesis in lung carcinomas (PubMed:33848463). Granule formation correlates with robust ERK phosphorylation and tumor progression, while autophagy-mediated degradation modulates signaling output (PubMed:33848463). Disruption of this process via kinase inhibition or domain deletion impairs oncogenic signaling, highlighting its therapeutic relevance (PubMed:33848463).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of the EML4-ALK fusion is intrinsically regulated by ALK's kinase activity and specific structural domains (PubMed:33848463). The truncated TAPE domain containing the HELP motif and the TD domain are essential for granule formation, while kinase autophosphorylation enables GRB2 scaffolding (PubMed:33848463). A kinase-deficient mutation (K589M, corresponding to p.A2036T) disrupts granule assembly and downstream signaling (PubMed:33848463).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: ALK's phase separation within the EML4-ALK fusion is extrinsically modulated by scaffolding proteins and cellular machinery (PubMed:33848463). GRB2 acts as a critical scaffold—its knockdown disrupts granule formation, while its SH2 domain mutant (R86K) fails to rescue granule assembly (PubMed:33848463). The granules recruit RAS-activating complexes (GRB2/SOS1/GAB1) for lipid membrane-independent signaling, and their turnover is regulated by autophagy pathways (PubMed:33848463).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: N-myc undergoes concentration-dependent liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro and in the nucleus, forming dynamic, transcriptionally active condensates above a saturation concentration of approximately 300-400 nM (PubMed:38811792). These liquid-like condensates exhibit fusion and rapid coalescence, dissolve during mitotic entry, and reassemble during mitotic exit (PubMed:38811792). They are associated with transcriptional condensates and require partner interactions for formation (PubMed:38811792).
Functional Summary: N-myc phase separation selectively regulates transcription by enhancing expression of oncogenes like SERINC2 and ANXA8 while repressing tumor suppressors, promoting cell proliferation (PubMed:38811792). This process modulates only approximately 3% of upregulated and 1% of downregulated genes, indicating targeted transcriptome regulation rather than genome-wide effects (PubMed:38811792). The condensates recruit transcriptional machinery including MED1, Pol II S5p, and nascent RNA, with both TAD and bHLH-LZ domains being essential for this recruitment (PubMed:38811792).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by the transactivation domain (TAD, aa 1–137), which is essential for LLPS as truncation abolishes condensate formation (PubMed:38811792). The basic helix-loop-helix leucine zipper (bHLH-LZ, aa 366–464) domain reduces the saturation concentration for phase separation, with truncation increasing it approximately two-fold (PubMed:38811792). Oligomerization via bHLH-LZ-mediated dimerization contributes to phase separation propensity (PubMed:38811792).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation requires the partner protein MAX, which enhances condensate formation; MAX knockout increases the saturation concentration, an effect rescued by MAX re-expression (PubMed:38811792). E-box DNA acts as a multivalent scaffold that enhances phase separation and lowers the critical concentration, with non-E-box DNA failing to induce condensation (PubMed:38811792).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: CHIP (Q9UNE7) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but is recruited to nuclear p62 condensates formed via liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) (PubMed:34385323). These p62 condensates exhibit liquid-like properties, including rapid FRAP recovery, fusion competence, and sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol, with no observed material state transitions under tested conditions (PubMed:34385323).
Functional Summary: CHIP recruitment to p62 condensates facilitates protein quality control during cellular stress by promoting ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of misfolded proteins (e.g., stress-induced ubiquitin adducts) and nuclear substrates like c-Myc (PubMed:34385323). This process accelerates clearance of damaged proteins, reduces nucleolar accumulation of toxic species, and decreases apoptosis during stress recovery (PubMed:34385323).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features driving self-phase separation of CHIP were identified in the provided data (PubMed:34385323).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: CHIP partitions into nuclear p62 condensates, with recruitment enhanced under oxidative or heat stress conditions (PubMed:34385323). This partitioning occurs alongside chaperones HSP70 and HSP90, forming a stress-responsive complex within p62 condensates (PubMed:34385323). Condensate formation requires ubiquitinated substrates and active ubiquitination machinery, as inhibition of E1 ubiquitin-activating enzyme abolished foci formation (PubMed:34385323).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: DIMT1 undergoes RNA-dependent liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) that drives its localization to the Nucleolus, with wild-type (WT) and catalytic-dead E85A mutant forming dynamic condensates while the RNA binding-deficient 5mutA mutant is excluded to the nucleoplasm (PubMed:37024283). The condensates exhibit liquid material properties characterized by rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) and droplet fusion, with 5mutA showing reduced dynamics; no material state transitions were reported (PubMed:37024283).
Functional Summary: RNA-driven LLPS enables DIMT1 nucleolar localization essential for ribosome biogenesis and 18S rRNA processing, with disruption (via 5mutA) impairing ribosome assembly, polysome formation, and acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cell proliferation; catalytic activity is dispensable for these functions (PubMed:37024283).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by a positively charged cleft (residues Arg162, Arg174, Arg228, Lys253, Arg256) that mediates RNA binding, as mutation of these residues in the 5mutA variant abolishes both RNA binding and LLPS capacity (PubMed:37024283).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Total cellular RNA and rRNA act as essential extrinsic scaffolds, directly inducing WT-DIMT1 droplet formation in vitro in a salt-dependent manner (maximal at 200 mM NaCl), while absence of RNA or the 5mutA mutation prevents condensation (PubMed:37024283).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: TNRC6B undergoes partner-driven phase separation with Ago2 to form liquid-like condensates primarily in the cytoplasm (PubMed:29576456). These dynamic droplets associate with membrane-less organelles including P-bodies (GW bodies) and miRISC complexes, exhibiting liquid-like properties in vivo through rapid fusion and high mobility (PubMed:29576456). In vitro reconstitution yields viscoelastic condensates with partial fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), where material properties are modulated by Ago2 binding; no material state transitions were reported (PubMed:29576456).
Functional Summary: Phase-separated TNRC6B condensates accelerate mRNA decay by >100-fold through spatial co-concentration of target mRNAs and deadenylation factors like CCR4-NOT (PubMed:29576456). This enables efficient gene silencing by miRISC, with Ago2 retaining catalytic slicing activity within droplets (PubMed:29576456). The compartmentalization optimizes mRNA repression machinery organization and reaction kinetics in cytoplasmic foci (PubMed:29576456).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by TNRC6B's glycine/tryptophan-rich argonaute binding domain (ABD, residues 437-1056), an intrinsically disordered region inherently prone to condensation (PubMed:29576456). The multivalency of this GW-domain enables critical interactions with Ago2, establishing the molecular basis for droplet formation (PubMed:29576456).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: TNRC6B phase separation is extrinsically regulated by Ago2 through multivalent interactions between its GW-domain and three tryptophan-binding pockets in Ago2's PIWI domain (PubMed:29576456). Mutations in Ago2's binding pockets (K660S, P590G, R688S) impair droplet formation by 35-90%, confirming Ago2's essential scaffolding role (PubMed:29576456). Condensates functionally sequester target mRNAs and recruit deadenylation machinery, demonstrating RNA client selectivity (PubMed:29576456).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: EB3 (MAPRE3) undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) forming liquid-like droplets in vitro at micromolar concentrations (PubMed:37603768). It localizes to cytoplasmic microtubule plus-end networks (+TIP networks) that exhibit liquid-like properties including trailing foci formation and sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol (PubMed:37603768). No material state transitions were reported for EB3 alone.
Functional Summary: EB3 phase separation organizes +TIP networks that accelerate microtubule growth to 3.5-3.6 µm/min and reduce catastrophes by concentrating tubulin at microtubule tips (PubMed:37603768). This cooperative function with CLIP-170 enables spatiotemporal regulation of microtubule dynamics, with cellular +TIP networks exhibiting liquid-like properties including rapid trailing foci formation and hexanediol sensitivity (PubMed:37603768).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: EB3 intrinsically undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation as demonstrated by in vitro droplet formation (PubMed:37603768). A C-terminal tyrosine-deletion mutation (EB3-ΔY) retains intrinsic phase separation capability but loses cocondensation functionality with CLIP-170, indicating the C-terminal tail's critical role in partner interactions (PubMed:37603768).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: EB3 forms synergistic cocondensates with CLIP-170, generating homogeneous droplets 20× smaller than CLIP-170 alone with 1.4× increased EB3 partitioning into the dense phase – an interaction abolished by the EB3-ΔY mutation (PubMed:37603768). EB3 droplets moderately concentrate tubulin as a client protein, showing homogeneous distribution within condensates though with 40× less efficiency than CLIP-170 droplets (PubMed:37603768).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: IRSp53 undergoes partner-driven phase separation, requiring interactions with proteins like PSD-95 or Shank3 to form condensates (PubMed:35819332). It localizes to the cytoplasm and associates with the postsynaptic density, exhibiting liquid-like properties in its protein condensates (droplet fusion and FRAP recovery), while actin bundles within these assemblies display solid-like characteristics without recovery. State transitions occur in actin-PSD condensates where liquid-like PSD proteins organize around solid actin bundles (PubMed:35819332).
Functional Summary: IRSp53 phase separation enables synaptic localization and spine maturation in neurons by scaffolding postsynaptic density assembly and coupling it to the actin cytoskeleton (PubMed:35819332). Disruption via ΔPBM mutation reduces spine enrichment, while actin-binding mutants (K4E/RKE) fail to rescue spine defects, demonstrating that condensate-mediated actin bundling is critical for neuronal function (PubMed:35819332).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by the BAR domain enabling dimerization, the PBM motif facilitating PSD-95 binding, and the SH3 domain mediating interactions with Shank3 and actin (PubMed:35819332). Key mutations disrupt this behavior: ΔPBM abolishes PSD-95 binding, ΔBAR prevents dimerization, and K4E/RKE mutations impair actin binding (PubMed:35819332).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Essential extrinsic partners include PSD-95, whose PDZ domains bind IRSp53's PBM motif to drive co-phase separation (evidenced by droplet colocalization and sedimentation), and Shank3, which interacts via SH3-PRM binding to enable condensate formation (validated by ITC and mutagenesis) (PubMed:35819332). Actin further modulates these assemblies, with IRSp53 bundling actin into solid structures within liquid PSD condensates (PubMed:35819332).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: CDYL undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (class: PS-self) to form nuclear biomolecular condensates in kidney epithelial cells and normal kidney tissues. These CDYL-specific condensates exhibit liquid-like properties, characterized by rapid FRAP recovery, droplet fusion, and spherical morphology. No material state transitions were reported in the study (PubMed:35918147).
Functional Summary: CDYL phase separation enhances its enzymatic activity as a crotonyl-CoA hydratase, concentrating substrates to suppress histone crotonylation (particularly H3K18cr). This represses cyst-associated genes (e.g., STAT5A, COL5A1) and inhibits cyst growth in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). Pathologic downregulation disrupts this mechanism, promoting disease progression (PubMed:35918147).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by CDYL's intrinsically disordered region (IDR; aa 52-233), with lysine and arginine residues within this domain being essential for condensate formation. Mutation of these residues to alanine (KR>A mutant) completely abolishes phase separation capacity (PubMed:35918147).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators or partner molecules modulating CDYL phase separation were reported in the study (PubMed:35918147).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: PRELI does not undergo self-driven phase separation but is recruited as a client protein into Mieap-induced biomolecular condensates (Mi-BCs) within the cytoplasm, specifically localized at mitochondrial inner membranes (PubMed:38322995). These Mi-BCs exhibit liquid-like properties including fusion and partial fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), forming multi-phase structures with distinct Mieap-rich and enzyme-rich phases (PubMed:38322995). No material state transitions were reported under standard conditions (PubMed:38322995).
Functional Summary: As a client enzyme within Mi-BCs, PRELI contributes to cardiolipin (CL) metabolism, supporting CL biosynthesis/remodeling critical for maintaining mitochondrial cristae structure and oxidative phosphorylation (PubMed:38322995). Disruption of Mi-BCs due to Mieap deficiency causes abnormal cristae morphology and reduced ATP production, indicating PRELI's role in sustaining mitochondrial function through condensate-mediated compartmentalization (PubMed:38322995).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features of PRELI regulating its phase separation behavior were described in the provided data (PubMed:38322995).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: PRELI incorporation into condensates is extrinsically regulated by Mieap, which drives the formation of Mi-BCs (PubMed:38322995). PRELI localizes specifically within the Mieap-depleted phase of these condensates and participates in enzymatic reactions at phase interfaces, as demonstrated through live-cell co-localization and FuzDrop predictions (PubMed:38322995).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: RASD1 (Q9Y272) is a cytoplasmic protein that does not undergo self-driven phase separation based on available evidence (PubMed:39009833). While its material states include liquid, solid, and hydrogel properties, direct observation of phase separation behavior is not reported. However, it functionally promotes liquid-to-solid transitions in partner proteins' condensates (PubMed:39009833).
Functional Summary: RASD1's role in inducing liquid-to-solid transitions of RASSF8 condensates suggests a regulatory mechanism for Hippo signaling via YAP activity modulation, though pathological implications remain unexplored (PubMed:39009833).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features driving RASD1 phase separation were identified in the provided data. Key regulatory elements such as domains, PTMs, splicing variants, oligomerization properties, or repeat features remain unspecified (PubMed:39009833).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RASD1 modulates phase separation dynamics of partner proteins, notably promoting perinuclear coalescence and liquid-to-solid transitions in RASSF8 condensates when co-expressed, as demonstrated through reduced FRAP recovery and co-localization studies (PubMed:39009833). It also interacts with YAP, though the functional impact on phase behavior remains uncharacterized (PubMed:39009833).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Rph3A undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro and in the cytoplasm of HEK293 cells, forming dynamic liquid-like droplets that exhibit fusion and rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) (PubMed:36693856). This behavior is dependent on arginine residues within its intrinsically disordered region 1 (IDR1), with the R9A mutation abolishing phase separation (PubMed:36693856).
Functional Summary: Rph3A-mediated phase separation stabilizes GluN2A surface clusters and reduces its mobility, which is critical for sustaining synaptic function (PubMed:36693856). The ternary condensates formed with GluN2A-CTD and PSD95 demonstrate functional relevance in neuronal signaling pathways (PubMed:36693856).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by the N-terminal domain (NTD; aa 1-300), specifically IDR1 (aa 1-91) with conserved arginine residues essential for self-association (PubMed:36693856). The R9A mutation (arginine-to-alanine substitution in IDR1) completely abolishes phase separation capability (PubMed:36693856). IDR2 (aa 158-300) is required for recruiting partners into condensates but does not independently drive phase separation (PubMed:36693856).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Rph3A co-phase separates with the GluN2A C-terminal domain (CTD; aa 1244-1464), recruiting it into liquid-like condensates in vitro and in HEK293 cells (PubMed:36693856). Ternary complex formation with PSD95 significantly enhances Rph3A phase separation, leading to larger cluster formation compared to binary interactions (PubMed:36693856).

Gene Names: KDM2A CXXC8 FBL11 FBL7 FBXL11 JHDM1A KIAA1004
Overall Phase Separation Overview: KDM2A undergoes phase separation to form liquid-like nuclear condensates in vitro and in cells, as demonstrated by droplet formation assays and sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol treatment (PubMed:35887017). These condensates exhibit dynamic properties and are exclusively nuclear in localization, with no association with specific membrane-less organelles reported.
Functional Summary: KDM2A phase separation correlates with transcriptional repression, as condensates exclude H3K36me3-marked chromatin and associate with transcriptionally repressive regions (PubMed:35887017). This suggests phase separation facilitates functional responses of JMJC-KDMs in gene regulation by spatially organizing repressive chromatin domains.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically driven by KDM2A's amino acid composition, which is enriched in glutamate, arginine, and leucine residues, conferring a high predicted phase separation propensity (PubMed:35887017). Full-length protein constructs were used in experiments, indicating these intrinsic features collectively enable condensate formation.
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators or partner molecules were identified for KDM2A phase separation in the provided data (PubMed:35887017).

Protein Name: Mediator of RNA polymerase II transcription subunit 16
Overall Phase Separation Overview: MED16 (Q9Y2X0) does not undergo self-driven phase separation but is incorporated into liquid-like condensates through partner-driven co-phase separation in the nucleus, specifically within Mediator condensates at superenhancers (PubMed:32727915).
Functional Summary: Co-phase separation with NRF2 enables MED16-mediated recruitment of the transcriptional machinery to superenhancers, activating cytoprotective genes (e.g., ABCC3, RASEF) that ameliorate oxidative stress in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) by slowing cystogenesis (PubMed:32727915).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic domains, mutations, or features driving phase separation were identified for MED16; its incorporation into condensates is solely dependent on extrinsic partners (PubMed:32727915).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: MED16 co-phase separates exclusively with the transcription factor NRF2, which scaffolds condensate formation. In vitro, recombinant NRF2 (residues 1–208) forms dynamic droplets that recruit and concentrate MED16 (PubMed:32727915).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: RtcB (Q9Y3I0) is a cytoplasmic protein that partitions into stress granule (SG)-associated condensates formed by IRE1α, but does not undergo self-driven phase separation (PubMed:38714852). It localizes to IRE1α-SG condensates at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane during cellular stress, though its material state within these condensates is not characterized.
Functional Summary: RtcB enrichment within IRE1α-SG condensates creates a functional workstation that enhances the efficiency of the IRE1α–XBP1 pathway during endoplasmic reticulum stress by compartmentalizing the tRNA ligase with its substrate XBP1 mRNA (PubMed:38714852). This spatial organization promotes pro-survival signaling, while disruption of condensate formation impairs XBP1 mRNA splicing and compromises cellular stress resistance.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No intrinsic molecular features (domains, mutations, or sequence elements) driving phase separation of RtcB were identified in the provided data (PubMed:38714852).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RtcB enrichment in condensates is extrinsically regulated through its recruitment into IRE1α-SG assemblies, which requires stress granule formation scaffolded by G3BP1 and TIA1 (PubMed:38714852). This partitioning occurs specifically during endoplasmic reticulum stress, oxidative stress, heat shock, and glucose deprivation, and is abolished when stress granule formation is disrupted.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Talin1 exhibits low intrinsic propensity for phase separation and only forms small droplets with minimal material volume when bound to deregulated vinculin (Vn^DR) under crowded in vitro conditions (PubMed:38862544). It does not undergo self-driven phase separation with integrin β1D peptide or PIP2-containing SUVs (PubMed:38862544). Subcellular locations and membrane-less organelle associations were not specified in this study.
Functional Summary: Functional implications of Talin1 phase separation were not characterized in this study due to limited observed phase separation behavior (PubMed:38862544).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No specific intrinsic domains or mutations driving phase separation were identified. The autoinhibited tertiary structure of Talin1, regulated by intramolecular interactions, imposes a higher activation threshold for phase separation compared to Talin2 (PubMed:38862544).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Phase separation of Talin1 is weakly induced exclusively by deregulated vinculin (Vn^DR) under macromolecular crowding conditions, forming small droplets with drastically reduced material volume compared to Talin2 (PubMed:38862544). It fails to phase separate with integrin β1D peptide or PIP2-containing SUVs due to insufficient activation (PubMed:38862544).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: Talin-2 (Q9Y4G6) undergoes partner-dependent liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) in vitro upon activation triggered by binding partners (deregulated vinculin, integrin β1D peptide, or PIP2-containing membranes), forming dynamic liquid condensates in solution that mature into viscous/gel-like states over time, and 2D viscoelastic clusters on membranes (PubMed:38862544). It localizes to the cytoplasm and associates with focal adhesions in cellular contexts, though this association was not experimentally demonstrated in the study (PubMed:38862544).
Functional Summary: Talin-2 phase separation on PIP2-membranes enables formation of 2D anisotropic condensates that explain focal adhesion organization, providing dynamic liquid-like properties laterally while maintaining structured scaffolding orthogonally. This process strengthens talin-membrane interactions to withstand mechanical forces and recruits integrin components, potentially initiating integrin clustering and focal adhesion assembly (PubMed:38862544).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Talin-2 phase separation is intrinsically regulated by its dimerization domain and autoinhibitory interactions. Dimerization is critical for LLPS, as removal of the dimerization domain (Tn2ΔDD) reduces droplet formation. Reducing autoinhibitory interactions via the E1772A mutation increases phase separation propensity, while the Tn2S339L mutation (impairing integrin affinity) severely reduces LLPS (PubMed:38862544).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: Talin-2 phase separation is extrinsically triggered by binding to deregulated vinculin, integrin β1D peptide, and PIP2-containing membranes. On PIP2-membranes, it forms 2D phase-separated clusters that recruit integrin components, potentially initiating focal adhesion assembly (PubMed:38862544).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: RIP3 (Q9Y572) undergoes hetero-amyloid assembly through RHIM domain interactions, forming solid-like fibrils without classical liquid-liquid phase separation (PubMed:22817896). It localizes to the cytoplasm and associates with necrosomes, where it forms stable amyloid aggregates with partners like RIP1 (PubMed:22817896, 38982083). No material state transitions were observed under experimental conditions (PubMed:22817896).
Functional Summary: RIP3 amyloid fibrils activate kinase-dependent necroptosis by phosphorylating MLKL, executing programmed necrosis during viral infection (PubMed:22817896, 38982083). Disruption of amyloid assembly via RHIM mutations (e.g., V460P) impairs kinase activation, puncta formation, and cell death by >80%, demonstrating the pathological significance of amyloid aggregation in necroptosis (PubMed:22817896).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Amyloid formation is intrinsically driven by RIP3's RHIM domain (residues 388-518), which mediates filament assembly (PubMed:22817896). The V460P mutation within this domain impairs amyloidogenesis, reducing ThT fluorescence to background levels and disrupting necrosome function (PubMed:22817896).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: RIP3 forms hetero-amyloid fibrils with RIP1 (Q13546) through RHIM interactions, creating ultrastable complexes essential for necrosome scaffolding (PubMed:22817896). It is recruited to ZBP1 (Q9H171) amyloid aggregates during viral infection, with binding dependent on ZBP1's intact IQIG motif (PubMed:38982083).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: CD2AP (Q9Y5K6) undergoes self-driven phase separation (class: PS-self) to form dynamic, liquid-like condensates both in vitro and in the cytoplasm of cells (PubMed:34330769). It associates with the slit diaphragm condensate, where it exhibits liquid material properties characterized by spherical droplet formation and rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP). No material state transitions were reported (PubMed:34330769).
Functional Summary: CD2AP phase separation stabilizes slit diaphragm condensates to recruit Nephrin and link to the actin cytoskeleton, thereby maintaining glomerular filtration barrier integrity (PubMed:34330769).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of CD2AP is intrinsically driven by its coiled-coil (CC) domain-mediated oligomerization and multivalent interactions between its SH3 domains and proline-rich motifs (P1–P3) (PubMed:34330769). Disruption of oligomerization via the p.L539K/L625K double mutation in the CC domain abolishes phase separation capacity (PubMed:34330769).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: CD2AP co-phase separates with partners Dendrin and MAGI2, with its addition significantly lowering the threshold concentration for phase separation in the MAGI2-Dendrin complex (PubMed:34330769).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: JAM-A (Q9Y624) undergoes CXCL12-induced phase separation to form reversible, liquid-like cytoplasmic condensates described as 'protein nanoparticles' in breast cancer cells (PubMed:36179489). These droplet-like assemblies exhibit rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), fusion competence, and dissolution by 1,6-hexanediol, confirming their liquid material state. No material state transitions were observed under tested conditions. The condensates are not associated with canonical membrane-less organelles but function as osmotic pressure regulators.
Functional Summary: Phase-separated JAM-A nanoparticles elevate intracellular osmotic pressure, synergizing with cytoskeletal forces to drive membrane protrusion formation (filopodia/lamellipodia) in breast cancer cells (PubMed:36179489). This mechanism facilitates cancer cell invasion and metastasis, with pathological disruption of Par3-aPKC binding exacerbating condensate-driven invasion.
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: No specific intrinsic domains, mutations, or modifications driving JAM-A phase separation were identified in the study; experimental evidence exclusively utilized full-length CFP-tagged constructs without domain truncations or mutagenesis (PubMed:36179489).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: JAM-A phase separation is extrinsically regulated by the chemokine CXCL12, which triggers condensate formation, and by the scaffolding protein Par3 (O00254) (PubMed:36179489). Dissociation of Par3 from aPKC (e.g., via Par3-S827A/S962A phospho-disrupting mutations) promotes Par3 cytoplasmic translocation and enhances JAM-A condensation, evidenced by increased puncta counts and accelerated FRAP recovery. Condensate dissolution is mediated by 1,6-hexanediol and digitonin.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SPIN1 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) to form reversible, dynamic, liquid-like condensates in the nucleus both in vitro and in vivo (PubMed:38777743). These condensates are distinct nucleoplasmic structures that associate with nucleoli but do not match predefined membrane-less organelles (PubMed:38777743).
Functional Summary: SPIN1 phase separation facilitates H3K4me3 recognition, recruits the MLL1 methyltransferase complex to condensates, and enriches H3K4 methylation marks, activating tumorigenesis-related genes in the MAPK pathway (including MAPK4, MAPK6, and KRAS) (PubMed:38777743). This process promotes cancer cell proliferation and xenograft tumor growth, while IDR deletion impairs phase separation and suppresses tumorigenesis (PubMed:38777743).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: The phase separation of SPIN1 is intrinsically driven by its N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR) (PubMed:38777743). Deletion of the IDR (SPIN1-∆IDR) impairs condensate formation in vitro and in vivo, significantly reducing puncta formation capacity and dynamicity as evidenced by diminished FRAP recovery (PubMed:38777743).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: No extrinsic regulators or partner proteins modulating SPIN1 phase separation are reported in the provided context (PubMed:38777743).

Overall Phase Separation Overview: USH1C (Q9Y6N9) undergoes partner-dependent phase separation as a central scaffold for two distinct tripartite complexes: forming liquid-like condensates with MYO7B/ANKS4B in microvilli and with MYO7A/USH1G in stereocilia (PubMed:31644917). This behavior occurs primarily in the cytoplasm within receptor clusters, exhibiting liquid material properties both in vitro and in cells. No material state transitions were reported.
Functional Summary: The phase-separated condensates enable mechanical stability in sensory structures by assembling tip-link densities. In microvilli, the MYO7B/USH1C/ANKS4B complex stabilizes intestinal tip-links, while in stereocilia, the MYO7A/USH1C/USH1G complex forms upper tip-link densities essential for hearing. Disruption of this LLPS mechanism through domain truncations or disease-associated mutations in partner proteins impairs complex assembly and is linked to sensory dysfunction (PubMed:31644917).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation is intrinsically regulated by USH1C's NPDZ1 and PBM domains, which mediate critical multivalent interactions. Truncation of the NPDZ1 domain (ΔNPDZ1) completely abolishes LLPS, while deletion of the PBM domain (ΔPBM) significantly weakens condensate formation by disrupting binding to essential partners (PubMed:31644917).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: USH1C strictly requires specific protein partners for phase separation: In microvilli complexes, it co-phase separates with MYO7B and ANKS4B, where both partners are essential scaffolds. In stereocilia complexes, it forms condensates with MYO7A and USH1G, with all three components required for assembly (PubMed:31644917). Mutations in partner proteins (e.g., MYO7A R1245W/R1770X) disrupt multivalent interactions and impair condensate formation.

Overall Phase Separation Overview: SRC-3 undergoes self-driven liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), forming dynamic nuclear puncta in myeloma cells (PubMed:33589584). The condensates exhibit liquid-like properties, evidenced by rapid fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) and sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol dissolution (PubMed:33589584). Its phase separation is enhanced through interaction with NSD2 (PubMed:33589584).
Functional Summary: SRC-3 phase separation confers bortezomib resistance in multiple myeloma by recruiting NSD2 into condensates, elevating H3K36me2 modifications on anti-apoptotic gene promoters (e.g., ABCC1, BCL2) (PubMed:33589584). Disruption of condensates via SI-2 restores drug sensitivity, reduces tumor growth, and alleviates bone lesions in vivo (PubMed:33589584).
Intrinsic Determinants & Regulations: Phase separation of SRC-3 is intrinsically driven by its intrinsically disordered region (IDR; residues 1085-1424), which alone forms liquid droplets in vitro at concentrations ≥0.5 µM (PubMed:33589584). Deletion of this IDR domain (ΔIDR mutation) abolishes phase separation capacity, resulting in diffuse cellular distribution and loss of function (PubMed:33589584).
Extrinsic Partners & Regulations: SRC-3 phase separation is enhanced by the protein NSD2, which co-localizes with SRC-3 condensates, lowers the critical concentration for droplet formation, and stabilizes droplets against high-salt conditions (PubMed:33589584). The chemical SI-2 disrupts SRC-3/NSD2 interactions, dissolving condensates and reversing phase separation-mediated functions (PubMed:33589584).
